the many reasons why the sovereign is only worth lis. 6d.? lam in agreement with Mx Smith when he says that ss. was a fair economi, rent 11 years ago for a six-roomed cottage in c. side or back street, but I go further and sa) that in spite of rates having risen by "leaps anc. bounds," and pavement and other incidenta. charges having been presented and paid for, the economic rent of that same cottage should only ,he 58. 6d. to-41ay. .144 we know that the major-, ity of these houses are now paying from 6s. to 6s. 6d. and have been in most cases somewhere about Gs. for many years. The trouble began when the first leap in the rates took place ten years ago of 10d. in the X, followed the next year by another 6d. rise, making a total rise of is. 4d. This would be covered quite comfort- ably by raising rents 3d. per' week, say, on a £9 10s. assessment. About this time, too, the charges for paving, &c., began to come in, and we all should remember what a cry was raised by the landlords about the immense cost they ' were being put to. It varied considerably, ot course, and much depended on the type of land- lord or collector, and was anything from £2OO to £400; of course, all this alarmed the tenants and most of us thought ourselves lucky at being let off by a gradual rising of rents up to 6d. This occurred, perhaps, about eight or nine years ago, and I have often wondered what my proportion of these incidental and temporary charges really was. Now that Mr. Smith in- forms us they are about £lB for each house, I am ra_pre curious than ever to know how much of the. ,218• I am supposed in all fairness, to pay.- feel entitled to be my own assessor for once, for I find that when once this incidental charge is paid for, it remains a permanent -asset to the gross value of the property, although not rate- able. So I come to the conclusion that if each tenant paid half, say, £9, equity and justice .would be served. This sum being distributed, 'over seven years would easily be met by a charge of 6d. on the rent. Here we see that the tenant, by paying 6s. weekly, is meeting all equitable charges, both of extra rates, water rate and paving. Now, what happened at the

"TEMPERANCE SUBURBS " :--" A NOVEL SUGGESTION." Sir,—l was somewhat interested by Mr. J. W. Mealor's letter in. your issue of the 29th ultimo, suggesting the establishment of "temperance Suburbs" in the various towns. I should like to point out that although tremendous benefit .would undoubtedly accrue to abstainers from such an action, the position for those other- wise inclined would be somewhat unfortunate. What chance for reformation, for instance, would remain for the inebriate? Left amongst a population wholly drunken, with no perma- nent example of the advantages of sobriety at hand, he might only be expected to drink deeper and deeper of the bitter cup. Again, would your correspondent condemn the man who par- takes only of a nightly glass of liqueur for, say, medicinal purposes, to pass the whole of his existence in a community of drunkards if he did not give up that glass. Drunkenness must not be avoided, it must be abolished; and all experience goes to prove that the greatest re- forms have been effected when the reformers . have themselves,lived in the midst of the sin they sought to banish. The Hebrew leper was never cured because he was estranged from his fellow-men.

end of seven years? Did the landlord take off the extra 6d. per week, as he honestly should have done? Not he; instead, he raised the rent last October, and, on the top of this, we have Mr. Smith taunting us with neither knowing nor caring what our obligations are. To sum it all up, the rates have risen is. 6d. in the X during the last 11 years; a .charge on the rent of 4d,. per week on the average cottage assess- ment will more than cover this, and assuming that the paving charges have been paid during that time and should now be taken off, what is the argument against ss. 6d. being the economic rent capable of meeting- borough rate, water rate and interest on capital? As it stands at present I reckon I am paying 9d. per week above'. economic rent, and to that extent my sovereign diminishes to 17s. 6d. Finally, it is not a ques- tion of who makes, most profit, landlord or master, it is one of' fair rent or rack rent, and by that I mean an economic rent which will give the landlord , a fair return for his capital and enterprise, or a fleecing rent which will impoverish the tenant. Notwithstanding Mr Smith's attempt to glorify the speculator and mortgagee type of landlord, I think it comes a little bit too late in the day. Nemesis is al- ready on their track.
E. HEWITT, Secretary National Federation
of Caretakers.

FAIR RENT.

Sir,—ln your issue of last week there appeared a letter under the above heading, and I think all temperance workers will agree with me that not only is the suggestion a novel one, but at the same time a very bad one, and as a temperance worker I advise any of your readers who are interested in this glorious movement not to take such an idea into their .heads. It would be a thousand pities if the least active of tem- perance workers took any notice of such a sug- gestion whiah is nothing less than that the tem- perance workers should admit defeat and retire into' the desert away from such evil company. Your correspondent does well to admit that he hall never taken an active part in this good work, and I feel sure of this, that if he had, such a suggestion would never have ~been penned. by him. Does the writer ever think of the drunken men and women this organisation has been the means of rescuing from ruin and degredation, or the amount of trouble and time and expense the pioneers of this splendid move- ment have spent in trying to rescue the fallen and depraved? Then, after 80 years of fighting, bravely and strong, to suggest we retire and admit our defeat! No, a thousand times, No! But, instead of his being an abstainer who is only interested in this work, let him put his own shoulder to the wheel and by so.doing he will find, like thousands have before him, that there is joy and happiness in trying to save the drunkard, and that there is no more glorious and useful work in this world than trying to sweep away this cursed drink trade from out of our midst. Again, he says that because we are in a minority it creates a more strenuous opposition from the moderator. It is because we are still in the minority that we must fight on with our face to the foe, and not only fight, but fight hard and strong, until the battle be won.
3rd December, 1913.

Sir,—l read with interest the article of Mr. G. Smith in your issue of last week on increasing rents, and, whilst appreciating many of the Points he states, exposing the glaring anomalies in respect to by-laws, also the methods adopted by inconsiderate mortgagees,..&c., T cannot in any way agree with his argument in respect to higher wages for the industrial worker. To sum it up correctly from a trade unionist point of view, such an argument is sheer bunkum. My contention is that the speculative builders of Warrington and district, almost without excep- tion, have employed the cheapest labour on the market, botliin-the Manufacture Of joinery, and in the erection of their property. Mr. Smith would have us believe that the speculative builder in the past only existed to enable the artisan to live in better houses than the indus- trial manufacturer prefers the worker to live in. Surely your readers will exclaim that the speculative builders are Philanthropists! Mr.,Sinith says: "But is not the all-important riuestion, Are wages to 9 lew rather than are rents too' high ?" 'Consider this query along with the. fact that for the past 15 years to my know- ledge trade union joiners have never been em- ployed by the speculative builders in Warring- ton and district. The reason is quite obvious. The higher wages which Mr. Smith talks about have never been paid by him or his colleagues. Your readers could, to some extent, under- stand the effrontery of your correspondent in- viting all-property owners to join their associa- tion, "not exactly to fleece the tenant," but to continue to show him that although the specu- lative builder does not believe in paying higher wages, he at least is not going to be treated at the same ratio as his worker.
J. W. BRADLEY.

To. express my, own opinion. in regard, to the cessation of cottage building, until the specula- tive builder recognises lair conditions of labour to their own employes, the sooner they give cottage building up the better. , I ,am a member of the Joiners' Association knot a property owner), and I recommend all in the trade to join, not with the idea of fleec- ing the employer, but to maintain a proper stan- dard of living that is in keeping with the efforts he puts forth to produce the luxury which some theof speculative builders live in. In conclusion might I say that the present state of cottage weaving is to a great extent the reason why the investing public are carefully avoiding the.. purchase of house property, for the upkeep of such property after, say, five years' existence, is a very serious item, saying nothing about the inconvenience of the tenant in respect to smoky chimneys, draughts through badly fitted doors and windows, and the doctor's bills which inevitably follow.
TRADE UNIONIST,

div.p: THE IRISH DIFFICULTY.

Sir,—Allow me to express my dissent from Mr. O'Brien's version of the correspondence on the above subject, so far as I am concerned. I have in every letter kept close to the subject, and have repeatedly complained of the wander- ing from the subject matter in dispute. I en- deavoured to show the folly of stirring up strife • among the different sections of the Irish people, and suggested that they should conciliate each other; I have shown that it is unwise to entrust them with self-government until such recon- ciliation is brought about. An agitatOr is an- other name for a demagogue, and both mean a stirer up of strife without any intention of 4 allaying it.. A statesman is the opposite to these, and is one who works for the unalloyed benefit of his country. I have not in this cor- respondence attacked either Mr. Asquith or any other member of the Government, but as an individual with a little common sense, however small that, may be, I have a right to criticise the Government of my country. When I say I have no connection with any political organisa- tion; I expect my statement to be taken as true, though you or anyone are at full liberty to assess my opinions to any party you like. As • regards my Phariseeism, I leave myself in the hands of Mr. O'Brien, who, in his opening letter, says of me: "I have from time to time read many letters on various subjects from your cor- • respondent, Squod,' agreed with many, - sympathised with some, and differed with, others, but have always appreciated the earnest spirit of conviction in all." I might have said a great deal more on the subject, but, as my aim has been for peace anti orderly progress and not agitation and strife, this must be my final letter onfthe question at present
PHIL SQUOD

div.head: SCHOOL CARETAKERS.
div.p: SCHOOL CARETAKERS.

Sir,—We caretakers would like to reply to the report of the meeting of the Education Committee on the. 17th November, which ap- peared in "The Examiner," respecting an appli- cation from school caretakers for extra remuner- ation for extra work. Mr. A. J. Jolley said friction had arisen between the caretake-..s and the Committee, partly due to the fact tb it in ,Warrington they had both Council schools and a large number of non-provided schools, care- takers working for the same authority and re- ceiving their wages from the same source, the ratepayers' money. The Education Authority charge for fuel, light and cleaning of schools after school hours, and the caretaker only books for fuel and light; the time taken for cleaning before or after a party or concert is not booked. If this was taken into account and the person using the school charged with it, then handed over to the caretaker it might make matters a little better.

Why not have a deputation of the caretakers to draw up some scheme of pay for this extra work? We understand that it is the Education Authority who alone fix the caretakers' wages; therefore we are their servants and they should see that we are dealt with fairly. Mr. Jarmaa said: "The position is this—if the managors made a profit they were the people who should remunerate the caretaker. The extra ctuties had nothing to Zo with the Education Com- mittee."

If the Education Committee have nothing to do with the extra duties, how can he account for the duties of caretakers reading as follows: "To arrange.and prepare rooms required for evening school or meetings. To see that no portion Of the piernises is used for any meeting except with a written authority ,of the mana- g*re, given previous to the time when it is in- tended that the meeting should commence. To see that there is no istanding on the seats, 6:z.

div.head: NATIONAL SERVICE AND CONSCIENCE.
div.p: NATIONAL SERVICE AND CONSCIENCE.

Sir,—ln his last letter Mr. Townroe made a wrong deduction from one of my phrases con- cerning the elimination of parental responsi- bility tr)y the State in its treatment of boys Who refuse military service on conscientious grounds. This referred to the treatment meted out to boys in the Australasian •Colonies. One ,of the things I meant to convey was that the parent was not personally consulted in the matter, apart from registration. The boy himself is called before a magistrate to state reasons why he cannot sr•ve. According to their (National Service League) August notes, Should their prin- ciples become law, it is provided that an ex- emption certificate be granted in case parents obge,ct to their son serving in the Army, even if the son would not ask for such a certificate, and the declaration continues: "We would exempt the son so long as he was living, under the paternal roof."

Lwould like to ask Mr. Townroe whether such exemptions are granted either in Australia or New Zealand. Mr. 'rownroe is quite mistaken in his reference to a "noisy but small band" of resisters. In Australia alone the membership of the Freedom League at the end of September last was 55,000. If similar conditions prevailed here it would mean the League having a mem- bership of 550,000! It is only recently that the League was formed. And let it be said that the League find the greatest difficulty in getting the Press to state their case, or report their meet- ings. How different when the National Service League wish to • say anything! The. speech ,of Lord Roberts, delivered recently in Manchester, was printed, almost in full, by several Colonial papers. This may have arisen because his speech was cabled out free of charge to any paper that cared to print it. Mr. Brimelow will have much difficulty in convincing an unbiassed person of the validity of their guarantee to exempt the conscientious objector to military service. A grave miscon- ception •is abroad in the country, fostered by the National Service .League, and further strengthened by Mr. Sandys, M.P., when intro- ducing the National Service (Territorial Force) Bill on April 13th last. He said that the ex- emption provided in the Bill "was based, on the law of New Zealand, where all persons who have a conscientious objection are exempt from military service." On the authority of an 'interview, with the . Hon.. James Allen,. the Defence Minister of New Zealand, a similar statement has been made in our English news- papers and never contradicted. In the inter- view which two members of the Society of Friends had with Mr. Allen on March 7th last, he told them he had "found it impossible to meet the case of conscience." Those who are familiar with recent developments knew that hundreds of boys have been, and are being, fined and gaoled because of their conscientious
refusal to -bear arms. Which of the two are we to believe? 'Perhaps Mr. Brimelow will explain. •
H. GRAY.

div.head: LIVING WAGE.
div.p: THE LIVING WAGE.

Sir,—Many people have endeavoured to give us a definition of the living wage, but without a precise or satisfactory result; many advocates have been 'questioned and have found difficulty in explaining :their cause. Yet, in spite of this, the faith, the'desires, the hopes, the aspirations and the ambitions of such advocates have been. unshaken, and there is still a demand for some- thing more than the figures of a wages schedule. The. poor cry. out ,to heaven for a share of the water which pours forth from the Justice Foun- thin, and the cry having been heard, there .are signs of a remarkable upheaval in the Labour world.

The worker holds the conviction—the right conviction—that he does not get his share—fair share—of the common product, and demands that he shall receive at least a minimum—not of 30s. a week, but a minimum which will enable him to live as a "Citizen of no mean city." It is -useless to express the living wage in money terms, for 30s. per week can hardly suffice every family. The toiler .with, a wife and family can- not be placed upon the same lever as the man without dependents; the man in one trade or profession cannot be compared to the 'man in another; a worker in an agricultural area com- pares odiously to the town worker. No! The sole idea should be that every worker should ieceife a wage which would enable him to live as a civilised Christian, in moral, material, phy- sical and social comfort, and that no man should go with insufficiency, and another get more than he requires. Pope Leo XIII., as Mr. Philip Snowden says, stated that. the "Living wage meant sufficient to support a frugal and steady workman." • Questions as to amount therefore are useless; what is required is that a man may have enough—mind, enough—to enable hiisa to provide for the health aro2l physical well-being of his dependents, and tt) live as I have said, as a true-born citizen.

Every nidn has a right to live in this world. The individual has a right to receive a remu- neration from his employer which will satisfy his needs, for, says the late Pope Leo XIII., "if the workman, compelled by his needs, or influ- enced by fear of worse evils, agrees to harder terms, N4ich he Must willingly accept, because the master so insists, he becomes the victim of force that justice condemns." And the view of the Catholic Church has been that the labourer was worthy of his hire. But in this age of keen competition the unscrupulous employer, who at the expense of common weal draws upon un- limited supply of half-starved and helpless labour and sucks the very blood from it until it is used up, knows little of, and cares less, for the moral precepts of his business. For there is an incalculable loss of wealth to the State wrought by the under payment of the worker, who; in consequence of the "sweated wage,' is unable to educate, to clothe, and to train his family for life's fight. On. the other. hand the fair, wen- intentioned employer is driven by force of Cir- cumstances, by reason of keen competition, to adopt similar methods, with the result that the worker is " between the devil and the deep sea." What is the remedy? Well, Mr. Will Crooks suggested ,the remedy—the only remedy —when lie moved his minimum wage system in the House of Commons on the 29th May, 1911, that the State, and the State only, can, and should, 'enforce Common conditions in regard to wages, just as they have done in other depart- ments of industrial life. FRANCIS W. RODDY. . .

div.head: WOULD LOCAL VETO BE USELFSS?
div.p: WOULD LOCAL VETO BE USELFSS?

Sir,—Mr. G. E.'Holme's letters are always in- teresting, but after reading many of them in many newspapers, I am still at a loss to know what he really does advocate with regard to the liquor trade. Does he favour free trade in in- toxicants? If he accepts the right of a majority to impose the present restrictions on the liquor trade; it is difficult to diseover-bywhat,logic he condemns the right still further to restrict or even to prohibit. I think all temperance workers will be in agreement with Mr. Holme that the existence of practically unrestricted drinking clubs is an unmitigated evil, and all decent citizens are justified in their demand that the club shall be, at least, subjected to the same restrictive con- ditions as the public-house. Mr. Holine's argu- ment, however, implies that the club evil has sprung into existence owing to a too •great re- duction in licensed premises. Does he really believe that the number of public-houses at the present time is not, in most instances, far in excess of reasonable requirement? We do not imagine for a moment that the re- duction in .facilities for drinking would cure the confirmed drunkard. To suggest that we teetotalers do so, is somewhat begging tie ques- tion. It is the casual drinker (who so often, because of the many opportunities, develops into the drunkard) whom, we claim, would, be most affected by a reduction in the number of public-houses. A similar test applied to cafes and• coffee drinking •will'7amply bear out the contention. That habit has been created and fostered by cafe proprietors, who; by increasing the facilities, have increased the demand. It is invariably so with regard to tlie—aiile of luxuries. Does it work only one way, or are we right in maintaining that a reduction in facili- ties means a reduction (N. 8. not a.correspond- ing reduction) in consuniPtion? -;rewers are business men, and they would not maintain two public-houses if one could do the same trade. In 1909 the Brewery Manual stated: "During the years 1907 and 1908 close on 3,000 licences were extinguished on the ground of re- dundancy, and it will readily be seen thist many trade avenues have thus been closed to the brewer which he finds it exceedingly difficult to replace." Reverting to club drinking, while recognising in it a great source of mischief, it ought to be borne in mind that the amount of intoxicants consumed in clubs is comparatively insignificant as compared with the output of public-houses. Less than 21 per cent. of the total consumption of intoxicants in England and Wales is con- sumed in clubs (including golf ,and yachting clubs, cricket clubs, Freemasons' lodges, &c.). THOS. D. LESLIE. 17.1C.A., Warrington and Wigan, December 3rd, 1913.

Sir,—ln reply to the question "Would local veto be useless?" asked by Mr. G. E. Holme in your last issue will you allow me to publish the following quotation from the "Alliance News," issuecl November 20th, 1913 "A Parliamentary return has recently been made by the New Zealand Parliament which shows the exact amount of liquor which goes into the 13 no-licence areas of the dominion. 'While the sale of liquor is prohibited in these districts, the residents are at liberty to import from outside sources such liquor as they may desire for their own use. The total, consump- tion of liquor for the Dominion in 1912 amounted to 11,310,918 gallons. There are 186,262 persons residing in the 13 no-licence areas. This means that in the 63 licence areas the- consumption of liquor in 1912 reached on an average, 12.157 gallons per head, while in the 13 no-licence areas it only reached 1.811 gallons per head. In 1910 the returns showed that in no-licence areas the liquor consumed amounted to 2.1 gallons per head." So that the returns recently published tell us very plainly, I think, that local veto ox.. no- ormkeirsst, do 'neoutulag.Beree' with reulise licence does mean a decrease in the consumption of qthat wueo rt. e mOpuerr a fnrci ea nw.l closing of "public" houses and opening "secret" drinking places. We -want all liquor distriout- ing agencies to be on the sane ievel, subject to inspection, and ,undar .the same clntrol, and surely we can hope to. obtain this when so many .who do not agree with us generally are so em- phatic in pronouncing " club drinking" as the greater evil. BENJ. T. PARKE,S. 8, Willis-street.

div.head: INOREASING RENTS.
div.p: INOREASING RENTS.

- - . Sir,—The article Which appeared in your last week's issue under the above heading and signed by Mr. G. Smith, is not only interesting, as you say, but very illuminating. also. The impres- sion which it conveys to me confirms a previous suggestion that a certain class ,of landlord is trying to get controlling power over our local Property Owners' Association. The only re- deeming feature of the article is its semi-official figures, which, with your permission, I will gladly preSume to make use of. As a piece of special pleading for the ,speculator and mort,, gagee type Of landlord the article explains itself. We are to seek higher wages, so that exploita- tion may be easier, and we are to submit to rents being raised to the Manchester level, not- withstanding that house values here are 30 per cent. below that city. Moreover, the Rip Van Winkle innocence assumed by Mr. Smith would have us believe that rents have remained sta- tionary' for the \ last ten years or so, and we are to be rudely awakened to the fact that we have a lot to pay for, which has been charitably overlooked. We have been having "something for nothing" all these years, and now the slump has come; and the supply of tenants with more money than sense, who were willing to exchange ad economic rent for a fancy rent, has become exhausted, attention is now directed towards a scheme of rack renting in order to recoup pre- sent and prospective losses. May I present the tenants' case so far as ray knowledge and observation serve me, and inci- dentally show Mr. Smith and his friends one of

div.head: DOCTORS AND AMBULANCE WORK.
div.p: DOCTORS AND AMBULANCE WORK.

61r,—In your last issue you passed some stric- ...tres on the British Medical Association with •,-egard to its policy in connection with ambu- ,ance classes. After saying that there are hun- dreds of thousands of ambulance men in this country who owe their training to the self-sacri- ficing services of doctors who have lectured to them without fee or reward, you state : "But the Insurance Bill was,introduced, and by some process of reasoning which could only be dictated by political motives, the British Medical Association resolved that henceforth its members would be unable to lecture for nothing, and ambulance classes must pay a guinea a lecture or do without them." Let me state that the policy of the British Medical Association with regard to ambulance work was decided at the annual meeting held at London in 1910, when the following resolu- tion was passed: "That members of the medical profession should- be suitably remunerated for teaching subjects in connection with public health, such as nursing, first aid to the injured, and hygiene, and that the fee adopted by the London County Council of one guinea for each lecture is one which appears suitable for general adoption." This resolution, which was a recom- mendation from the Council, was the outcome of opinions expressed in different parts of the country some years prior to 1910, and had noth- ing to do with the Insurance Bill. The associa- tion's tion's policy with regard to the Insurance Bill was adopted,atthe au.nual meeting held at Bir- mingham in 1911, when the famous six cardinal points were enunciated and afterwards largely adopted by the Government. You will thus see that there was, and is, no connection between the association's policies with regard to ambu- lance work and the Insurance Act. Some towns, for example, Widnes, have already.accePted the 'policy of'the-association; and in'them-the ambu- lance movement is in a forward state. J. S. MANSON.

div.head: COUNCIL FOSTER FATHERS Age of Municipal Inspection to be Extended to Five Years A PURPOSEFUL SCHEME.
div.p: COUNCIL FOSTER FATHERS Age of Municipal Inspection to be Extended to Five Years A PURPOSEFUL SCHEME.

An important scheme whereby the Council will play the part of foster father to the chil- dren of the borough was mentioned at the War- rington Council meeting on Tuesday. At present children are inspected by Municipal nurses until they reach. the age of one year. This is now to be extended to five years, when the children will pass under the care of the School Medical Officer. For this work the Health Committee asked permission to appoint an additional nurse. Alderman JAMES MrANS said they now desired to give attention to the child life between the ages of one and five years. The death-rate between the years 1908 and 1912 showed the need for this work. The deaths in that period of ,children between the age of one and two were 517; two and three, _ 225 three and-four, 110; and four and five, 83. Even 'with these figures Warrington had one of the lowest death-rates, but it was still too high, and he thought it time they gave attention to the work. lie moved the adoption of the minutes.
Alderman BURTON, in seconding, said he thought the money expended on—tile work would be money extremely well spent. (Hear, hear.)
A MEDICAL VIEW.

Dr. JOSEPH- thought the Health Committee were being patted on the back over the appoint- ment of an additional ,health • inspector, /as if they had suddenly awakened to the fact that they required one. He wished to make it clear that it was merely an extension of a policy three and a half years old. The principle was adopted before the intervention of an outside organisa- tion, whose co-operation he, for one, cordially welcomed:, ,At the,same time,, there .was, a differ-, once between co-operation, and an attempt to oust or pioneer the legally-constituted Health Committee of the district.

They had in the committee an experienced body of men who worked earnestly when some of their critics might be comfortably enjoying themselves in armchairs. The committee were not narrow-minded, and they could accept sug- gestions and aids of any kind, but they ought to have sole control of the health policy of the town. - - _

_ .• Councillor HAWTHORN thought the new nurse might undertake the additional duties in the Education department as well as in the Health department. It would appear that if another nurse was appointed for Education Committee work alone, she would have to work only 20 hours a week.

ARGUMENT DISPUTED. Councillor ROBERTS disputed that argument. An additional nurse would still be necessary for the school work, and her spare time would be taken up with the clinic work. The Education Committee would require the full service of a nurse. 'Councillor PEMBERTON said ' the ' poorer class children could not battle against disease when the parents did not get the wages to keep them. Unless the children got sufficient nutriment, the visitation of a nurse would not help them to battle with disease. Finally the committee's suggestion was adopted. \ A QUESTION OF SMELLS.

_ The Health Committee reported that they Were in communication with Messrs. Bowmand, Ltd., with reference to the emission of offensive smells from their works. Councillor GOUGH : [think it's time the Health Committee, took it uP. It is an abominable nuisance, and- in InY own h,%use. the smells are abominable. (Laughter.) Only last night, when I went home, the stench was unbearable. (Laughter.) It is enough to breed an epidemic, Alderman JAMES EVANS said they were doing what they .could to detect the smells and have them stopped.

div.head: DISORDERS OF THE MIDDLE-AGED MAN.'
div.p: DISORDERS OF THE MIDDLE-AGED MAN.'

After the age of fifty cven the most healthy of men find it necessary to make some changes in their methods of life. They can no longer eat and drink whatever fancy. dictates, and tiley. require regular hours of rest and sleep. The man who has been so absorbed in his business or profession that be could give but little thought to his health, now begins to feel his work a burden. Some little weakness begins to develop. It may be dyspepsia in one of its multifarious forms; gout, or some uric acid disorder; or, worst of all, a nervous break- down. Whatever form the disorder assumes, it comes gradually, so graduaily that it is often- times well advanced before the busy man realises its significance. In all modern works on medicine, one fact is made abundantly clear—that nearly all dis- orders of this kind have their origin in the digestive area. It is too wide a subject to discuss here, but, broadly speaking, we poison ourselves by absorption from the intestinal tract. It follows that if the digestive organs could be kept in a healthy condition to perform their functions naturally, many of the worst disorders of middle age might be avoided. div.head: IN THE COURTS.
div.p: IN THE COURTS.
BOROUGH POLICE COURT
SATURDAY.
Before- Messrs. B. T. Fairclough (in the chair), A. J. Jolley, T. Pemberton, and Alderman Tinnion.

ON THE PLATFORM.-JOhll Monks, 8, Ellis-street, a partially blind young man, was charged with trespassing on the C.L.C. and refusing to leave when requested by a railway policeman, who stated that the prisoner loitered about the plat- form at the Central Station.—He was fined 2s. 6d., or seven days.

div.head: MONDAY.
div.p: MONDAY.
Before the Mayor (in the chair), Aldermen Smethurst, Bolton and Evans, Councillor J. Wilkinson, and Messrs. S. Wright, W. Roberts, W. Furness, T. Locker, and G. Pilling.

CHRISTMAS Music.—Music licences were granted to several picture palace ?roprictors for music to accompany the pictures on ( hristmas Lay. All the applicants did not appear, and the Chief Constableoexplained that probably there as some misunderstanding. Applications had been granted by the Watch Committee for the show, ing of pictures on Christmas Day from six o'clock in the evening until ten, on the under- standing that the films were submitted to him for approval.—This had been done and he had no objections.

div.head: TUESDAY
div.p: TUESDAY

Before Councillor H. Roberts (in the chair), and Messrs. C. Jackson Holmes and T. Locker. WANTED TRIAL BY JURY.—James White, labourer, no fixed abode, was charged with stealing a pair of boots from the shop of Messrs. Sterlings, Ltd., Bridge-street. The prisoner elected to be tried by a jury.—The evidence of the police showed that Mr. George Hackford, the manager of the shop, heard a noise outside resembling the falling of boots. He went to the door, but did not see anybody, and then proceeded to Rose and Crown-street, where he saw the prisoner, with one ,boot under his .coat and one dangling below. He taxed the prisoner with stealing the boots, and he replied that he would "punch his clock in" if witness did not take his hand off prisoner's shoulder.—Prisoner admitted stealing the boots, but was persistent in his determination to be tried at the Quarter Sessions.—Councillor Roberts: It appears to be an absolutely wicked waste of money to send this ease for trial. Subject, of course, to your legal right, it is an absurd and unnecessary extravagance.—Prisoner said he was drunk when he took the boots.—His request was granted. "NEVER MADE A BET.'"—Joseph Bate, 16, School- brow, was summoned for loitering in Bewsey- street for the purpose of betting on November 12th.—Detective-Sergeant Holland said that fol- lowing complaints he and P.C. Anderson kept observation on the Bewsey-street district. On November 12th they saw Bate speak to a work- ing man, who gave him something, which he placed in his trousers' pocket-- Two other men were seen to give him something, which he also placed in his pocket. He went into a shop in Bewsey-street, and came out immediately after each of the transactions. Bate was later arrested on, newspaper premises in Market- street, and when he was searched'a number of cards with the names of horses running on October 20th were found in his possession.— Defendant stated that he had never made or taken a bet in his life, whereupon the Chief Constable said he could not allow a statement like that to pass unchallenged, as it was known to the police that the defendant had been doing it with impunity. In order to submit evidence he asked for a week's remand, which was granted.

div.head: THURSDAY.
div.p: THURSDAY.
• Before Mr. W. Roberts (in the chair), Dr. Naden, and Messrs. W. Richardson and A. J. Jolley.

" Scoßcamo " CvmsTs.—Clarence Cooper, of 56, Dalton-bank, was charged with furiously rid- ing a cycle at Market Gate.—The police stated that defendant was riding at about ten miles an hour, and alleged that he lost control of hi, cycle and knocked :down a little boy.—The Chief Constable stated that cyclists thought they could go as fast as they liked. They were prose- cuting motorists for travelling at a, speed less than some of the cyclists. Theria had been several accidents lately, owing to the careless manner in which some cyclists had been riding their machines.—The Chairman, in ordering Cooper, who pleaded .not guilty, to pay 10s., in- cluding costs, said this kind of thing was really becoming most serious, and it would have to be stopped.

div.head: WORKHOUSE BEER.
div.p: WORKHOUSE BEER.
Should It Be Given to Inmates When Extra Outdoor Relief is Refused?
LADY GUARDIAN'S MOTION.

The inmates of the Warrington Workhon" must be sorely troubled. There is a threat that they will not have their usual supply of Christ- mas beer. Mrs. Simpson has given notice that at the next meeting of the Guatdians, to be hdd a week on Wednesday, she will moYe the Christmas Day dinner in the WOrkhouse be served without beer, so long as we, as Guardians, refrain from giving a little extrs relief to the outdoor poor." " That This was an echo at the Guardians' meeting on Wednesday of a debate in the House Com- mittee, when Mr. Garnett moved: "That inas- much as the Guardians' could not see their waY to grant fi small pittance to the recipients of outdoor relief, the Christmas extras for the Workhouse be not granted." This was with- drawn, and the House Committee reported that the Master had been instructed to order the extras, which, presumably, includes the beer. If Mrs. Simpson succeeds in carrying her reso- lution, the Guardians will be faced with a Per- plexity—the beer will be there, but none shall ,enter the inmates' pint pots. MORE GENEROUS GUARDIANS. . _

When Mrs. Simpson mentioned her motion, Mr. Bitooxs said: The beer has been already,, passed at. the House Committee, and no men- tion was made by you about it. Mrs. SIMPSON : I spoke against beer at another house meeting. Several Boards of Guardians wrote to the Warrington Guardians asking the latter to PaY on their behalf is. per week extra to their poor. resident in the Warrington Guardians' area as Christmas cheer. Mr. Bottomley, the clerk. said they would charge the extra money to the other Guardians. The Rev. A. M. MrrcnELL : Yes, and when the poor of other Guardians in Warrington are to get extra, our own outdoor poor are to get noth- ing. I move that we give our poor is. 6d. extra. The CLERK: At the last meeting you decided not to grant extra relief to our own cases, but that does not cover the payment to be made by you to • persons reaident in 'this •'Union Mit - be- longing to other Unions. FISH OF ONE; -FOWL OF THE OTHER. Mr. MITCHELL Oh! You are going to make fish of one lot and fowl of the other. You are going to give extra to outsiders but not to your own. Mr. E. L. BENT. the chairman: The Clerk jig only seeking instructions. Mr. Mrrcems.: I move that he give it to these cases, and I give notice that we re-consider the question of our own poor. (Hear, hear.) Thus the two notices of motion leave the question of Christmas cheer and beer in an interesting position for the next meeting of the Guardians.

div.head: STRANGE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD
div.p: STRANGE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD

DECISION. The CLERK intimated the receipt of a letter from the Local Government Board re the sug- gested appointment of Mr. Jones, schoolmaster at Padgate Homes, as relieving officer lo; No. 4 district. The Local Government Board wrote that they did not consider Mr. Jones had such experience as would qualify him for the position and suggested that the Guardians should adver- tise for candidates.

The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL' thought it was veri rough on Mr. Jones, who had been an officer of the Board for many years, and who had a good knowledge of the work. Mr. BILLINGS said they as a Board should not be actuated by sentiment. (Mr. MITCHELL: J 1113" tics and sentiment.) Finally it was decided that the Clerk should write to the Local Government Board and pre° the aaims of Mr. Jones. EXTENDED AREA. The CLERK intimated the receipt of a copy of a provisional order sought by the Lancashire County Council to have the centre of the ship Canal made the boundary line between Lanca- shire and Cheshire. Thelwall, Grappenhall, and part of Lymm districts, he said, would come into the Warrington Union. Mr. BILLINGS: Would it be a loss or gain to us? The CLERK: In our own district it would be - a gain in, area. Mr. BROOKS: Would we have to compensate other Unions? The CLERK: That is a matter for consideration. It is meantime a County Council *matter, and we are not fighting the question. It would mean a little increase in population. The matter was sent to the Assessment Com- mittee for Consideration. At a meeting of the Warrington Rural Dis- trict Council later in the day approval was ex- pressed of the scheme.

div.head: CHRISTMAS GEESE.
div.p: CHRISTMAS GEESE.
How to Prepare the Birds for the
Market.
HINTS IN THE FEEDING.

It pays better to prOdfice eggs during Decem- ber and January, when they are worth 2d. or 24d. each, than during the spring, when they are not worth, more than 14 or 16 a shilling. The laying stock requires to be generously fed Upon foods that are rich in carbohydrates and fat, as these are the two elements that assist so materially in* increasing the egg supply. barley meal is an extremely useful food for laying hens, though it is not employed nearly so extensively as it might be. Three parts bar- ley meal, two middlings, and one pea or bean Meal, one maize (when the weather is cold), and half a part of lean meat, is about as good a Preparation for laying hens as it is possible to Obtain. For afternoon' feeding wheat, barley, and a little maize are the most suitable. The Mixture of meals should always be supplied Warm.

div.head: FATTENING GEESE FOR CHRISTMAS.
div.p: FATTENING GEESE FOR CHRISTMAS.

There seems every likelihood of a big demand for geese this Christmas. Turkeys are .sure to command high prices. Already they are over a Shilling per pound live weigllt when bought Wholesale, so what the retail prices are I will leave the reader to imagine, says a writer in "Farm and Home." Whenever. turkeys are ex- Pensive it is always a. good sign fox breedeis.of geese, for customers unable to afford the ly`xtiiy Of a turkey have to be satisfied With geese. buiring the last few weeks •I have. seen many flocks of geese sleeping out at' night. This is not the way to get them fat; it. may answer Well for breeding stock until there is snow or heavy frost, but geese intended for Christmas Markets should get rather better treatment. intense cold always has 'a tendency to reduce Weight, and spoils the effects of good feeding.

div.head: NOT A WISE COURSE.
div.p: NOT A WISE COURSE.

SonIP people try fattening geese in the same pen withlowlS; Mit it Is not' a wise' proceeding: Fowls should not be allowed to eat much maize, while geese usually make the ground very dirty, especially in wet wea,ther. If -fowls and geese are kept together both lots should enjoy free range; this is the only successful way. Potatoes are useful for fattening, and maybe economi- cally. used 'if they can be had at a low rate. Geese like them, bAt there is the trouble of boil- ing them up. As Christmas approaches boiled fat_ can be mixed with the soft food. Barley meal and maize meal can be served by way of a change; geese like a little variety introduced, and it always pays. Some pure-bred varieties will weigh close on 201 b. each, but the average buyer does not want them so heavy, and prefers a weight of 151 b. to 161 b., while 121 b geese find a ready sale at remunerative prices.

div.head: HOUSING BREEDING DUCKS.
div.p: HOUSING BREEDING DUCKS.

Ducks require to be housed comfortably if they are to lay satisfactorily. If the houses are cold or damp, eggs are likely to be conspicuous by their absence. Many people seem to think that because ducks are hardy birds their housing ar- rangements may be neglected. This is, a great mistake, for, as.a matter of fact, there is no kind of poultry which respOndS-more readily to good treatment, than ducks: The house ilodslipt need to be, a.high one, for clucks, unlike ordinary fowls, do not perch. It is about four feet high in front, sloping down.a little towards the back. in order to allow the rain to drain away freely, this is ample. The shed must be well ventilated and must not be overcrowded, and the neglect of either matter is likely to lead to trouble. As far as possible, four square feet of floor space per bird should be allowsd.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 6, 1913.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 6, 1913.
FARM AND GARDEN.

The yield of .potatoes in England and \Vales, 6.55 tons per acre, is just about the same as in 1910 and 1911, says a Board of Agriculture re- port, and rather more than half rton above the decennial average • it is practically 1.1 tons more than last year. The total production amounts to 2,894,655 tons, which is some 650,000 'tons more than in 1912. Turnips and swedes have yielded 12.2 tons per acre, or about one-fifth of a ton above last year, but still nearly a ton under average; owing to the reduced acreage, however, the total 12/ million tons, is just below the production of 1912. Mangolds, with 18.15 tons per acre, are also a little better than in 1912,- but 1.3 tons below the average. In their case also the acreage has been reduced, and the total production, is 7,611,123 tons.

div.head: TO ESTIMATE WEIGHT OF PIGS.
div.p: TO ESTIMATE WEIGHT OF PIGS.

The weight of pigs may be estimated very closely, says the Senior Dairy Inspector of Vic- toria, by measuring in the following manner f Take the girth just behind .the shoulder in feet and inches, and the length from that point on top, along the curve of the back to the root of the tail. The head and neck weighs about one- sixth of the weight of the forequarters', and is estimated at about One-eighth the value. The girth and length as above, calculated by the rule to find the solid content of a cylinder: each cubic foot equals 3 stones or 141 b. (421 b. and one-third of afoot, or 576 inches, equals 1 stone. So, if the content in cubic inches is divided by 576, it equals imperial stones, and 8 stones equal I cwt. Rule 1: -Square the girth and multiply by the length, both in inches, and the product, multiplied by the decimal .07958, will give the content in cubic inches, which divide by 576, and the result is the I.'eight. Of the animal in im- perial stones of 141 b.; divide by 41, and the answer is in lbs. Rule 2: Multiply the square (if the girth .by the length, both in inches, ,and divide the product by 7,238, and the quotient is the weight in imperial stones.

div.head: lIIE MI.'S AILMENTS.
div.p: lIIE MI.'S AILMENTS.

The-pig is Subject' to Many ailments, more 'so than any other domestic animal—not to be won- dered at when we consider the artificial and un- natural conditions in which in most cases he passes his short life. Swine are bred, fed and killed solely for human .consumption. Why, then, are they usually kept in such insanitary and unhealthy conditions in defiance of the ordinary rules of health? If every day swine were permitted, weather allowing, to take half an hour's exercise away from the sty—the • larger -the space the better—a small one better than none—and in the interval all accumula- tions of fEecal matter were removed to a properly constructed depository, and the covered drain flushed out, their health would be greatly ha- proved, and freedom from many diseases they now suffer from secured. Have the sty com- fortable, with fair amount of sunlight, and bed raised on boards. This treatment would amply repay the pig-owner for his labour and trouble, and would reduce-swine fever quite as much, if not more, than the Board of Agriculture's laws. An eminent pathologist recently stated in a lec- ture that typhoid or enteric fever in the human, and swine fever, were both "dirt diseases." The present plan of • allowing* animals to., wallow. and of confining them to a limited space with six months' accumulation -of excreta!, is filthy.

div.head: IN THE GARDEN.
div.p: IN THE GARDEN.

Among rock plants Arabis and Aubretia have grown vigorously, and it will: be advisable to pinch off some of the long shoots. Stir the soil among the plants with a pointed stick, after clearing out any weeds.

Plant window boxes with wallflowers, prim- roses, and small evergreen shrubs. Nit bulbs of narcissi, hyacinths, tulips, crocus, and snow- drops among the plants, placing the two last mentioned in the front. .

Clear away all rubbish from the garden, and burn it; Left- on the ground it harbours slugs and other pests. A beautiful but old Nlicliaelmas daisy is aster tradescantii, which was probably the first of the many North American species cultivated in Europe. It was introduced into this country about the year 1603 by John Tradescant, who was gardener to Charles I. This variety has long elegant sprays of pure white flowers, which are borne in great profusion.

div.head: SWEET PEA SHORTAGE.
div.p: SWEET PEA SHORTAGE.

There is again a shortage of sweet pea seed. Last year there was a scarcity of good quality Sweet Pea- seekl on account of the general wet- nesi that prevailed, and this year it is feared they will be still scarcer on account of the long continued drought. It is not only at home, but also on the Continent and the United States there is a shortage, and if this is correct prices for good seed will be higher. Growers are ad- vised to make their purcTiases at once, as the seed will keep just as well in a drawer at home.

div.head: CLIMBERS FOR PRESENT PLANTING„
div.p: CLIMBERS FOR PRESENT PLANTING„
Clematis montana, creamy white, flowers in May. There is also a pink form. When estab- lished it is only necessary to remove weak shoots in February, as they flower on the old wood.

Clematis Jackmani, purple,, flowers in sum- mer. When established cut back previous year's shoots to within.six inches of the base in Febru- ary or March, just before growth 'commences. Jasminum oflicinale, white, flowers in sum- mer. When established prune' moderately after flowering, removing shoots that have flowered. only.
Ceanothus azureus, blue, flowers in July. ThiS is an attraitive subject.. ' •' • Wistaria 'multijuga; Mao-purple, sthtmer ; and 'Wistaria sinensis, mauve, May; are both beautiful climbers:
Climbing plants may be grown on walls, ['cf.- golas and over old trees.

div.head: RENOVATING BORDERS.
div.p: RENOVATING BORDERS.

Borders which do not need replanting may have the soil loosened with •a fork, and some well-rotten manure or decayed 'refuse laid on the surface. The winter rains will wash Much of the material into the soil, and will greatly benefit the plants next season. The thoroughly decomposed material from the refuse heap will be of service now, apply- ing it to borders where required. This com- post is a most valuable fertilising agent, and much good stuff, which is usually wasted, might be turned to better account. As refuse is added to the heap it should be sprinkled with salt, soot and lime, together with the ashes from rubbish burnt. The heap should be turned two or three times to aid decomposition, and when in a fit state may be used as a dressing anywhere, no matter what the nature of the 4oil may be.

div.head: HOW TO NEUTRALISE DANGEROUS STOMACH ACIDS.
div.p: HOW TO NEUTRALISE DANGEROUS STOMACH ACIDS.

Few people besides physicians realise the im- portance of keeping the food contents of ' the stomach free from acid fermentation. Healthy normal digestion cannot take place while the delicate lining of the stomach is being inflamed and distended by acid and wind—the results of i fermenting food n the stomach. To secure per- fect digestion, fermentation must be stopped or prevented, and the acid neutralised. For this purpose physicians usually recommend getting a little bisurated ,magnesia from the chemist and taking half a teaspoonful in a little hot or cold water immediately after eating. They recom- mend bisurated magnesia because it is pleasant to take, has Uo disagreeable after effects,- and instantly stops fermentation, •neutralises the acid and makes the sour acid food :bland, sweet and easily digested. The regular use of bisurated magnesia—be sure you get the bisurated, as other kinds of rutgnesia are of little value—is an absolute guarantee of healthy, normal digestion, for it overcomes and prevents that acid condition which alone is the cause of trouble.

div.head: Novelties Father Chrisfmas has Prepared for Old and Young.
div.p: Novelties Father Chrisfmas has Prepared for Old and Young.
"RAINBOWS CUT UP FOR TIES."
" EXAMINER " SPECIAL.

The whirl of .hr):. aeroplane 'propeller sounded overhead. Looking skywards, I espied a mon- ster airship, and at the helm sat 'old Santa Claus. A shrill whistle made the old chap look down, and, noting my presence, he switched off the engine power,-looped the loop in a thrilling manner, and brought his huge mechanical bird Co earth close- beside me. Shaking his grey beard free of moisture andvathering his red cloak around him, Santa sprang out, and; with extended, hand, came to greet me. "I have- to go through the same old Operation again, I suppose," said the genial old Father Christmas. "You want an interview, of course?"

-" flight!" I ejaculated, as Santa knew my mission from past experience. "I want ,to learn first hand what • novelties you have this year for old and young.", "flush! That's, a great secret. -Yes, I'll tell you, as I know you will keep my plans a secret, and only let the thousands of readers of 'The Examiner' know."
I assured him that only these intelligent people would get to know. "Well," added Santo, "we have had an ex- ceptionally busy year in Santaland factories— working night and do, my boy."
Novelties for flif. Ladies.

" Thar is good. You know what I want., sci drive along:" - "All right !" chuckled Santa. "As the ladies have been, I learn Mnyt 'The Examiner,' .very much in evidence during the past year, let us begin with them. .

"Now here is a new style. of hat, which I think they will call. a geld,' or a duck,' or something like that. I think I mpst call it the Tango,' for it is a creation of sq many steps, and just see how the. feathers whirl. Then. here .is the latest in jewellery. Sniff—how's that for a deli- cate perfume? In that big case are samples of the latest in low-cut dresses. No, I won't show you the samples, you Will see them on pretty, living models soon enough. ." All, me, but times are changing, and I dis- cover there is a section who do not trouble about dress, but about votes, and so the, Santa-, land factories have given special attention to the wants of this section. fiere are clockwork effigies of Mr. Asquith and Jr. 4 McKenna. All the ladies have to do is to shifike the figure, shout Votes for Women!' and the figure will cry Spare my life and take your vote!' Don't you think that iS truly a novelty"

div.head: For "Nuts and Nutesses."
div.p: For "Nuts and Nutesses."
"What secrets have you for we men?" 1 ques- tioned.

"Men are easily pleased. We alviays, in Santaland, follow out a Oteady plan. There are .gigar of the best irnike, pipes. and (At% things, from hats down 1p slippers, which we can always safely make ritid stock in Santalu,nd factories, sure .of a sterigy demand. " I find, however, that you have a new race of folk springing up----t e 'nuts and nutesses.' We find the pew .sehog of lads and lasses are harder to please, so the best brains in Santa- land have been hard at work designing striking novelties.

"For the female ' nuts ' we have designed some very manish dresses. No, they are not harems. can t really name them. These, hoWever, you will soon see for yourself, and, ' I ' doubtless the young damsels will give them attractive names.

"A new style of Trilby hat has been evolved ai tractions for the 'nuts; These will be par- atbisucutoloanuralryoe'•frili‘atedhfiealinmhte.ainsk'iVnetliheas;e been capturing all the rainbows, .and thee. we have cut up to get striking colours for ' nutty ' ties. Hush! that is a great secret." .
For the Children.
"Tell me, Santa, what you have got for the children?"

"Now, you have asked me something .1 can answer, for, of all the departMents in our busy factories 1 take most interest in, it is in those 'devoted to the m4king of things for the .chil- dren, and we have'designed scinie startling toys. "MY word, how things have changed since I started my annual Christmassy pilgrimages. The time was wlien it wax; sawdust stuffed figure was thoug4t ideal by the girls, but now they want something More real and lifelike. Even dolls that say ' Ma ' and shut eyes when laid down are out of vogue. We have to give the 20th century lass something more elaborate. "What is called the 'glad eye doll ought to be attractive. This is a tricky little chit who winks at you so knowingly. Then there is a mechanical doll, dressed like a South American girl, who, dances the Tango, when wound , up. Of the more elaborate toys we have a model nursery, fitted u'p with dolls' beds and 'other things, and lit with real electric light. Of course, we could only Make a few of these, and the girl will have to be very good before she gets one.

div.head: Scientific Toys for Boys.
div.p: Scientific Toys for Boys.

For boys we have an endless array, from a Jack-in-the-box to a football. The taste of boys is changing, however, and why I cannot say, except it be due to the newer methods of teach- ing_ given in your Schools:

"The Meccano outfit—we stock- them in all. sizes—is quite, the rage. These collections of bars and. bolts are very fascinating to.ys for the boys, as they enable 'the: lads: to . build, Many. things; froip, bridgesjo cranes,' and ,at the same time they inculcate into their minds many lessons in practical engineering. "Then we have turned out enormous quan- tities of model railways. These range from the small one, in which the engine is worked by clockwork, to the large railway system, with its crOssings, tunnels, stations, signals and loco- motives driven by steam. "We are always up-to-date in Santaland, and Are have made aeroplanes that really will fly— and so must I, for my time is now very precious. Ta, ta !" • The old man, with the agility of youth, swung himself into .the aeroplane, the engine puffed, the propellers whirled, and in a few minutes he was lost to sight in his dash back to Santaland. ' W. D. B.

div.head: CONDITION OF CHESTER ROAD.
div.p: CONDITION OF CHESTER ROAD.

• Councillor Osborne, at the meeting .of the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday, said be had received numerous complaints about the deplorable condition of. Chester-road. ,Alderman Tinnion said the Council had, powers to widen the road, and it would. take a considerable sum to do the work. When the widening took plac the road would be further from the river and greatly improved He thought it was a matter which ought to be attended to as early as possible.

div.head: VALUE OF CO-OPERATION.
div.p: VALUE OF CO-OPERATION.

A popular movement of education Must. not merely select the best minds of the workers and by a hot-house culture advance them far beyond the general level. The tutorial class may even- tually become a universal system recognised as the ordinary means of adult education, but until the way is prepared, only the more able or the more leisured will be touched. Most people are still unwilling to spend their evenings in "neither business nor pleasure." Some are too modest to venture amongst people whom they expect to be more intellectual than themselves. Others are unable to pledge themselves for a three years' -course, or cannot definitely set aside one evening a week throughout the winter. For thpse persons, who form the majority of any community, a study circle system has already been started in Bristol and Liverpool. The W.E.A. secures the services of a number of well- qualified leaders, often members of the local university staff, to offer courses of from three to eight or more " talks " on their various special subjects. These leaders are -chosen not only :for their knowledge, -but also for their general fitness for leading a small group of men and women in intimate study. Not only have they some definite knowledge to impart, but they are able to draw on the resources of their wider educatioia to illustrate and enlighten the whole discusgion. The names of these persons •and the HOES of the -courses they offer for the ensu- ing winter are issued in a syllabus which is dis- tributed- during tbe autumn among trade unions, adult schools, co-operative societies and likely individuals. Applications for Courses are -then maderby persons who, have formed- themselves into groups preferably:, of about- eight members. Time and place is arranged between the leader and the -circle.

In this way, men and women, who for any reason have been unable to join a tutorial class, have the chance of coming into personal touch with someone who has seriously studied what- ever subject the circle has chosen,from the sylla- bus. The secret of the success of study circles is intimacy. The ideal educational unit is that of the small group led by a man who is anxious not only to teach, but to learn, who is ready to see his subject through fresh minds, who expects to be thoroughly .criticised, and is forced,by thei very intimacy of the circle to put his best into his work. It was ever in such small. groups that men were inspired. "When two •or three are gathered together" in this way energy is in- creased, and sight made clear, as if in a keener atmosphere. Men come out of their shell of daily life and see the world as a whole. The vision will support them through the working days.

For Everyone. The ordinary man or woman is too ready to think: "This is all very well, but it is not for me. It is for the clever people and the people who. have time to spare. I have a family to keep." Study ,circles are for everyone. Those who spend their days even in heavy manual toil have found it refreshing to sit in a room with a few friends talking about science, literature, history, or philosophy, or discussing social pro- blems. Dock labourers have done it. If a man once started it he will never give it up. In every town there is probably already a rudimentary study circle system, in the form of Adult School lecturettes, or I.L.P. educational meetings, or other organisations of the same nature. This movement has to be extended and strengthened. Where there have been single " talks" by separate persons, let there be con-, nected courses started; for only after repeated meetings can you get the best out of any man, and only by continuous study can you expect to grasp a subject. The study circle is unhampered by regulations. It is responsible to no high State authority. Since all the work given by the leaders is volun- tary, the whole course and the trend of each ' discussion" may develop according to the needs of the moment. A poetry study circle which has given one night a week to selected poets will sometimes spend its whole evening in reading and listening to passages; at others it will develop into philosophical discussion of the nature of poetry. A circle which set out to study Germany in the nineteenth century has found it necessary to lay such secure foundations that its whole time will be spent in preparation, so that it ,will have to follow on with .a second course on the subject itself. Since the courses offered are generally shell it is possible for a keen circle to take several subjects in a winter. They may, for instance, spend six meetings on industrial history, and then take a course in the elements of political economy. -19Diey may branch into some entirely different subject, • but r disconnected...study, is on. the whole to be discouraged. A winter's work in study circles is an excellent preparation for a tutorial class in the following season. Though there can be no shadow of obligation to follow up with tutorial class mem- bership, the more advanced system should be able to draw many recruits from the other. Yet for a long time, and for most people, the study circle will necessarily be an end in itself. The scheme utterly fails unless it comes to be uni- versal. We must not rest until it is the common custom of all men and women to continue their education by some such means as this. In Bristol the scheme is well on foot. Liverpool has made a small beginning. Next winter it will be Warrington's turn. , We shall not found the great national culture which is our ideal till every member of the. nation is able to take his share in the work. A secure national culture must be rooted in _the nation's workers. Lest it become an artificial mannerism and no more, ciilture must rest upon' the experience of those who are most aware of the reality of life and death.

div.head: NUTS & SLACK, WASHED
div.p: NUTS & SLACK, WASHED
SCHouL ARCHITECTS.
Education Committee Controversy Re-fought in the Council.
LOCAL MEN FAVOURED.

The controversy over the question of whether the plans for a new school in Lovely-lane should be open to national competition, or confined to local architects, .tt tubject 'which has been the cause of several heated debates in the Educa- tion Committee, was re-fought in the Council on Tuesday night. The final decision of the Education Committee was to have competition only amongst local architects, - and this the Council confirmed by ten votes to nine, many of tile councillors not voting. Councillor PEDIRERTON raised the question by moving ,back the part of the Education minutes referring to the new school. His chief objec- tion was that there was no assessor to adjudi- cate upon the plans, and see that the specifica- tions were issued within reasonable time. With- out an assessor the matter might drag on for ten years. It was perfectly ridiculous the scheme proposed by the Education Committee. The competition would be limited to a few people. He had been told that only two archi- tects were' going in for it. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Gorqu seconded, as the Council had not sufficient information.

div.head: WITHOUT AN ASSESSOR.
div.p: WITHOUT AN ASSESSOR.

COunvinor I'. LINDLEY said they would get a good local competition without an assessor, and there was no fear of having unsuitable plans thrust upon , them. The interior of the new school was outside their control, and in the hands of the. Board 'a Education. They had only to design the exterior, and • their local architects were quite capable of that. Alderman TINNION said when the Police Build- ings were erected Councillor Pemberton had a good deal to say about employing outside architects, and in face of that it was surprising to find that he now wanted outside architects. In the building Of schools the committee had had experience, so had the Director of Education, the 'Borough Surveyor, and the Medical Officer, and surely they knew what was wanted in the way of requirements.. (Hear, hear.)

If they had an assessor they would be bound to select the plans he selected, and the assessor would cost in fees .R6O to .000, and if they 'did not accept the selected architects' plans they would have to pay the architect 11 per cent. on the contract, and that might amount to be- tween .2150 and £2OO. Surely in their joint wisdom they could get a school suitable for the requirements of Lovely-lane without the aid of an assessor? (Hear, hear.)

div.head: "SOMETHING BEHIND IT."
div.p: "SOMETHING BEHIND IT."

Councillor OSBORNE thought there was some- thing which had not been disclosed. There seemed to be something behind all the trouble, and ,it ought to be brought out. (Councillor Pemberton: " I have brought it out.") His feeling was that there were thoroughly efficient architects in Warrington capable of doing the work. If the whole of the architects were enabled to enter the committee would get a scheme which would satisfy everyone. Alderman• BENNETT thought that to ask archi- tects to compete- in an open competition for schools of that kind was similar to using a steam hammer to crack a nut—(laughter)—and it was, asking the world to witness that they were going to erect four brick walls and a roof. (Laughter.) With everything else equal, he favoured the local architects, who paid the rates as all had to do, and if they were not capable to build such a school their names ought not to be on the roll. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: " PROFOUND ASTONISHMENT."
div.p: " PROFOUND ASTONISHMENT."

Councillor ROBERTS expressed profound aston- ishment at the remarks of Alderman Bennett in comparing a school to house 1,000 or 1,500 chil- dren for years to a house of four brick walls and a roof. That from the apostle of the resthetic staggered one. (Laughter.) That was absolutely contrary to the professions of Alder- man Bennett for the past 30 years. (Laughter.)

Alderman BENNErr:-It is not so. It is meant for a bit of irony. Let me explain. I think the Committee, rightly or wrongly, are satisfied with brick walls and a roof, but I want them to go further. (Councillor Pemberton: "Shame," and laughter.)

div.head: "MOST _DISCREDITABLE."
div.p: "MOST _DISCREDITABLE."

Councillor ROBERTS: At one meeting when we decided to have an open competition and seek the assistance of the best expert brains in the country, Alderman .Bennett stigmatised that as bringing in a steam hammer to crack a nut. ,The further Igo into an analysis of his speech the worse it appears. (Councillor Pemberton: "Shame," and laughter.) This now is about the most discreditable utterance I have ever heard him make. (Councillor Pemberton: "Shame, shame," and loud laughter.) I do not often stand up to defend Councillor Pemberton. (Laughter.) I think this is the first occasion—it's unique. It is perfectly true that in days gone by he has opposed this kind of open competition, but he has changed his mind. (Laughter.) Councillor Roberts added that they would not violate any condition of the Architects' Assoc- iation if they had a limited competition. With that explanation he would not vote on the ques- tion.
The minutes were adopted, so now Warring- ton's architects only will compete.

div.p: VllOfiii ,%; LIBERALS.
Miss Crosfield's Remedy for Sweated
Women Labour.
FOR COUGHS & COLDS.

against it was: "You women don't care about politics; you don't understand them, or don't want to understand them; and don't want to bother about them." Mrs. Osborne said they had 2,431 members. "Does that," she asked, "look as if we do not care about politics, and does the work we put in for it look as if we didn't want to bother about them? 1 leave you to judge." (Applause.)

div.head: LEGISLATION PAST AND TO COME
div.p: LEGISLATION PAST AND TO COME

The ward teas and •slicials organised by the Women's Liberal Association are always un- qualified successes, and there was another large and enthusiastic gathering in the Bold-street Schools on Morkday, when members in the Town Hall and Howley Wards met together. After tea, interesting speeches were made by Mrs. Crosfield, who presided, Miss Truda Crosfield, and Mr. A. H. Crosfield. The songs by Miss Elsie Wilkinson were exceedingly Well ren- dered, as also were those by Miss Connie Wil- kinson al Mrs. Sanders. Mr. Bibby gave his humorous items in his usual entertaining man- ner, his songs provoking the utmost mirth.

div.head: GREAT ASSOCIATION.
div.p: A GREAT ASSOCIATION.

Mrs. CROSFIELD referred to the recent annual meeting of the association, and said they were all glad to see the association was not only prospering, but growing daily. At present they were one of the largest Women's Liberal Associations in the whole of England. (Ap- plause.) But it was no wonder the association was growing, because they had such a wonder- ful Liberal Government to follow. (Applause.) Since 1906, when the present Government came into office, it had passed quite a large number of Bills, considering it had been so handicapped by the Haus° of Lords. The Government record was exceedingly good, and amongst the many Bills which it had passed one of the most 'im- portant, and one which should certainly appeal to women, was the Children's Act, which came into operation in 1908 and was amended in 1910. (Hear, hear.) Under the Act, a child..under 14 years of age could not be imprisoned; they had instituted Juvenile Courts; regulations in re- gard to children going into the public-houses; the fire-guard provision: medical inspection in schools. She also laid special emphasis on the care of children's teeth and the Swedish system of drilling.

div.head: Tariff Reform Bogey.
div.p: Tariff Reform Bogey.

Speaking of Free Trade and Tariff Reform, she said the Tariff Reformer was always at his old game. He asked: "How is it, in spite of Free Trado, that the price of food has gone up during last year?" She would say that the price of food had gone up all over the world. Free Traders did not claim to be able to regu- late the price of food. It was the quality and quantity of the crops that detormined that. Under Tariff Reform food would be higher than it was to-day. In all parts of Europe, except in France, the price of food was much higher than in England. "If any of the Tariff Reformers get hold of you," she said, "I hope yon will get hold of them, and tell them we know very well that if Tariff Reform were in- troduced it would make the price of food higher raid not reduce it." After giving instances of taxatiOn in America, Mrs. Crosfield concluded: "After all, old Eng- land is the best, and that is why we mean to keep up the principles of Free Trade and Liberalism, and return a Liberal candidate at tie next election." (Loud applause.)

div.head: WONDERFUL LEGISLATION.
div.p: WONDERFUL LEGISLATION.

Miss CROSPIELD also referred to the splendid reoord of the Government, and said she thought in years to come people would point to this term of office, and would say that some of the greatest Acts affecting the welfare of the coun- try took place during those eight years. She thought we lived so near the period that we could hardly realise how wonderful had been some of the legislation since the Liberals came. in office. (Hear, hew.) First of all, there was Old-age Pensions. Mr. Asquith said ,the other day that one of the results of the Act was that outdoor old-age pauperism had been reduced 9i per cent., which meant that it had almost boon wiped out of existence. (Applause.) In 1909 there was the establishment of the Labour Exchanges, and 1910 was given up to fighting the power of the House of Lords. The Parlia- ment Bill was the outcome of that work, and the Act had rightly been called "the Act where- by the will of the people shall prevail." The Trades Boards Act and National InsuranCe Act were also passed. The establishment at War- rington of the Insurance headquarters for Lan- cashire, and Cheshire—the third great district in the country—was a fact of which we could all be proud. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: Women Workers'. " Living Death."
div.p: Women Workers'. " Living Death."

In regard to the Trades Boards Act she would like to say that that Act was passed in order that some of the poorest trades in the country should have some protection ;neted out to them —the trades so poor and sweated that they could not organise themselves. Five .millions eat of the 15,000,000 women in England over 15 years of age were wage earners, and it was that the least possible wage they could live on properly was 158. per week. But how wretched the wages of women were, for they only averaged 7s. per week. It was not work," she said, "but a living death, for some of the women workers." She agreed with Mrs. Crosfield that the in- creased cost of living had nothing to do with party politics at all. She was told one reason was the large production of gold in the world. If a large quantity of gold was turned out, the purchasing power of a sovereign was less. (Rear, hear.)

div.head: Woman Suffrage.
div.p: Woman Suffrage.

One remedy for the frightful sweating of women was a better training for young girls-7- 4heer, hear)—and there must be some Act passed ta limit juvenile labour. In Hie U.S.A. children were kept at school longer, in order that they might get a, better training to go out into the world. Co-operation should be their watch- word. They should co-operate in order to make things better. She would like to see some measure of women's suffrage, because the women played an important part in the coun- try, (Hear, hear.)
