div.head: COMPETITIONS.
div.p: COMPETITIONS.

The prizes given •to Bewsey Ward for the neatest baby's petticoat—not to cost more than one shilling—by Councillor Gough and Mrs. Pemberton, were won by Mrs. Whalley and Mrs. Boyle. The one for the Town Hall Ward for the, baby's pinafore,, not to cost more tlutn one shilling, and given by Councillor Lindley, was won by Mrs. Jolley. Mrs. CROSFIELD presented the prizes.

div.head: "A DOMINEERING WIFE."
div.p: "A DOMINEERING WIFE."
The sketch. "A Domineering Wife," was excellently given by members of the Adult School Sketch Party, and caused roars of laughter.

div.head: NOT SELFISH WORK.
div.p: NOT SELFISH WORK.

Mr. CROSFIELD, who was received with voci- ferous cheering, made a short speech, in the. course of which he said they were all proud of the Women's Liberal Association, and the ladies who gave such a splendid lead in War- rington. Might he take that opportunity specially to congratulate the two ladies to whose highly successful conduct Of affairs they, with the 'assistance of other ladies, had made the gathering that (waning so great a success? (Applause.) He would like to add a special word for Mrs. Osborne, who was such an indefati- gable worker. (Hear, hear.) He rejoiced to see such a splendid gathering, for it was only another indication of the constantly-growing in- terest women were taking in modern politics. He thought the Children's Bill, of which Mrs. Cros- aeld had spoken, was an illustration of the omprehensiveness of the work the Government had been engaged in during the .last seven years. The. Chancellor of the Exchequer the previous night had said that the Government cad the children of the nation as its wards, and the old folk of the nation as its honoured guests. They found the Government had been at work relieving those who were disabled and sick; •ind arranging for those who during slackness in trade were out of work. (Hear, hear.) •

div.head: Not for a Clique.
div.p: Not for a Clique.

That was not selfish 'work for one little favoured clique, but it was honest, great and good work for the entire mass of the people. (Hear, hear.) It was legislation which con- cerned the men so much that they should take the deepest pride and interest in it. It 'con- cerned the women also, for if there was one thing about Libefal legislation it was that it struck right down into the homes of the people. They had done a 'good deal in seven years, but they were not wearied of well doing. The Liberal party was full of life and energy, and it was going on with that Work' until, as the Chaneellor of 'the Exchequer said the ,pre- vious night,. all the slums and ...underpaid workers had disappeared. There was a' moun- tain of work waiting for them. The workers were being better paid, and the conditions were altogether better. He thought if they could manage to resurrect and revivify some old Inediceval baron and bring him back from his tuediwval castle—very picturesque, but a little smoky, a little smelly, a little insanitary, very draughty, and very dark those castles were— and show him our well-conducted industrial callings, he would be inclined to rub his smoke- reddened old eyes in astonishment. But all they had done was only an earnest of the still greater future which lay before the party, and the great work which all of them would help their chiefs at Westminster to carry through to a successful issue.. (Applause.) Votes of thanks were 'heartily accorded, on the proposition of Councillor LINDLEY, seconded by Councillor Gouou.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 6, 1913.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 6, 1913.
RUNCORN GUARDIANS.
The Question of Mental Defectives
is Discussed.
DUTTON SCHOOL QUESTION.

The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Guardians was held on Tuesday, Mr. Linaker, jun., presiding. Tee report of a conference representative of the Cheshire Poor Law Unions, held at Crewe, on the question of mentally defective persons was presented. It was unanimously resolved: " That in view of the Mental Deficiency Act it is desirable that the Cheshire Poor Law Unions should combine together for the purpose of pro- viding, or arranging for the provision of suit- able accommodation for chargeable defectives and epileptics, • and that an Executive Com- mittee should be appointed to work out details and arrange terms'for combination, and report and recommend to a future meeting of the con- ference. That a copy of the resolution be sent to each of the Boards of Guardians in the county." Mr. Spruce, as one of the delegates, moved that the Guardians_ fall in with the proposals.

Mr. Pilling seconded. Mr. Linaker said he would like to ask the delegates if any estimate had been given as re- garded the outlay needed. He was in sym- pathy with the objects, but he would like ,to if there was any estimated cost of new i,uildings, or for adapting buildings. That wab a matter which ought to be considered.

div.head: New Departure.
div.p: A New Departure.

Mr. Spruce said there was no sum named. It seemed to be a new departure, and it was hard to say in which way it would develop. •He could not say whether there would be new buildings, or whether existing buildings would be used. In the committee's opinion it would be better for the matter to be dealt with by Boards of Guardians rather than allow tilt County Council to come in and erect costly buildings for the purpose. Mr. Woodward said that the question waf, supplementary to the action taken by tilt North-Western Poor Law Office two years ag, with reference to dealing with defective chil then. They entered into negotiations for th, acquirement of the Workhouse in Loonsdab and Tarvin Unions for dealing with defectivi childre,n in the North-Western Area. Thep must have been an increase, and it was thought advisable to take further steps. He might say that the cost would not very much exceed the cost of those people now chargeable. Mr. Pilling: This is an Act of Parliament which comes into operation on April Ist. They would have to do something, and from what he gathered Guardians could do what was requited mote economically than the County Council. (A Voice: "Question.") After further discussion it was stated that each Union would probably have to pay so much per head. Mr. Pilling said they would have about eight in the Runcorn area. Mr. Spruce's motion was agreed to. Mr. Woodward was appointed to be the GuaP • dians' representative on the Joint Committet until the 15th April, 1914.

div.head: MID-DAY MEALS FOR CASUALS.
div.p: MID-DAY MEALS FOR CASUALS.

--- - The appended resolution was also passed, an 6 Mr. G. Piling was appointed representative on the Sectional Vagrancy Committee until April 15th: "That the Runcorn Union approves of the recommendations adopted at the conference of representatives of Boards of Guardians of Lancashire, Cheshire, Cumberland and West- morland, held at Liverpool on the 141 h Novem- ber, for the purpose of securing uniform admin- istration of the regulations with respect to casual paupers, and for the provision of a mid- day meal for casual paupers." The Clerk stated that the cost to the Board would be a 20th of a penny. The Knighton (Radnorshire) Union 'wrote asking the Board to .support the following reso- lution: "That the 'Guardians of the Knighton Union, finding the ',constantly increasing bur- dens of local rates for the maintenance of ob- jects which are national in their purpose appalling, call .upon the Government to enact that the cost of main roads and Of elementarY and secondary education be transferred from the local rates to Imperial 'taxation." Mr. Piling: A good idea. Mr. lorris moved that the Guardians support the resolution. This was carried.

div.head: DUTTON SCHOOL QUESTION.
div.p: THE DUTTON SCHOOL QUESTION.

. - - - Mr. Woodward moved the following resolu- tion: "That for the present no action be taken towards a re-transfer of any of the Homes' children from the Aston to Dutton Stihool." He said that, as chairman of the Education Corn mittee, he had to report with reference to tile overcrowding Which would take place at Dutton Schools if the children from the Homes were sent there. After some deliberation the Edu- cation Committee gave instructions to issue an 'order on the managers of Dutton Schools, rstat- ing that no children outside Dutton should be admitted to that school until such time as there should be such vacancies at the school as would enable all the children from the Homes •to attend: They had no power to exclude children from the schools, and that which he had said was the best course they could follow. The children now attending Aston Schools would be admitted at Dutton as vacancies arose. Mr: Pilling seconded. Mr. Morris moved an amendment. He was of the opinion that Sir John Brunner had ex- tended the schools in order that children from the Workhouse could he accommodated. That morning a' report came from the Superintendent of the Homes requesting the Guardians to pro- vide the children with bags to carry their dinners in to Aston Schools, as some of • the children had had their dinners stolen from them. He thought it was hard for the children to have to go all the way to Aston in winter. He moved that further steps be taken to get the children in Dutton Schools. •

div.head: Settle by Compromise.
div.p: Settle by Compromise.
After further discussiOn the Superintendent said that there were 16 children over 11 years of age going to the Aston Schools. Mr. .tinitows seconded Mr. Morris's amend- ment. _ _ _

Alderman Norman understood that if some of the outside children could be got away from the schools there would be room. Mr. Morris: That is the reason of my oppo- sition. Mr. Woodward said that if they did not re- duce the number at the Dutton. Schools the Education Committee would call on the mana- gers to enlarge the school. That seemed an unfortunate thing when by compromise they could overcome the difficulty. He did not hold a brief for the Dutton managers, but probably if there were an enlargement to-day the chil- dren from outside might all leave in about six months and the extra room would be practically useless. It was not such a great hardship for Children over 1.1 years of age to walk a mile to school. When he was nine years Old lie walked 'three miles to school. They did not want to put these children under a glass case and sur- round them with cotton wool, because that was not in their interests. They could be kind to the children,-but he did not think thay had the right to compel ratepayers to ixty for more room. He hoped to see all the children going to Dutton Schools, but he did not think they should press for that at the present moment. Mr. Woodward's resolution was carried, with the addition that the parents of children from outside should be persuaded, if possible, to take their children away.

In ,regard to the visit of the deputation to Messrs. Pilkitigton's glass works at St. Helens, who had offered vacancies to boys in the Homes, Mr. Spruce said they would present their report to a special meeting of the committee during the next fortnight.

div.head: Lki E DR. .LUDIIVIG titei..q).
div.p: Lki E DR. .LUDIIVIG titei..q).
One of the Founders of the Largest
Alkali Works in the World.
PRINCE OF APPLIED SCIENCE.

The late Dr. Ludwig Mond, Ph.D., D.Sc., F.R.S., one of those princes of applied science who have done so much for the welfare of the British people, was himself a native of Germany, where he was born in March, 1839. He attended the Polytechnic School of Cassel, his native place, and afterwards itudied chemistry under Her- mann Kolbe, at Marburg, and • the renowned Robert Bunsen at Heidelberg. After leaving the University, and whilst still little more than a boy, he held several important appointment 3 in chemical works in Germany. He first came to England in 1862, with the object of introducing his well-known process for the recovery a sul- Phur from alkali waste. While engaged in the development of this process in the works of John Hutchinson, of Widnes, he formed a friendship which lasted all his life with Mr. (now Sir John) Brunner, who • later on founded with hini the great firm of Brunner, Mond and Co. After a ' short interval of some three years spent in Hol• land in erecting and organising Leblanc Alkali Works at Utrecht, and his marriage wirli his eousin, Miss Frida Loewenthal, he settled down finally in England, and became a naturalised British subject. His first work consisted in the installation of his sulphur recovery process in a number of British and foreign alkali %Arks. Early in 1872, in the course of his travels, Dr. Mond met Mr. Ernest Solvay, of BritssAs, who gave him the fullest opportunity for examining his new process for the manufacture of soda hy the intervention of ammonia, the possibilities of which so struck Dr. Mond that he at onc.,e entered into an agreement with Mr. Solvay for its introduction into the United Kingdom, al- though the process' was only then in its infancy, and required many -improvements before it
father of Sir Alfred Mond, who spoke at Warrington last Friday night.
THE LATE DR. LUDWIG AIOND,

could be made capable of supplanting the ohi and well established Leblanc process. In 1875 Dr. Mond„ in conjuntion with his friend, Mr. Brunner, founded the firm of Brunner, Mond and Co., erecting works at Winnington, new Northwich, in Cheshire, a firm which has nols become the largest alkali works in the world, and employs style 4,000 workmen. During tilt early years of its existence, while the,neiv pro- cess was still being developed 'and imbroved, Dr. Mond worked day and night in the task oi remedying its deficiencies and perfecting it, methods. He practically lived a the works and often spent whole nights .there in order \ to be ready to deal immediately with any of the num- erous difficulties in the process of manufacture as they arose. Soon, however, the enterprist was an ensured success, the works were rapidb extended, and new branches had to be built at Middlesbrough, Sandbach, Middlewich and Silvertown. Zinc mines were acquired in Wales, as well as an interest in chemical works at Syracuse, U.S.A. In 1881 the firm was con- verted into a limited liability company, of which Dr. Mond we... 9 a managing director.

Pioneer in Labour Problem. The two founders of this great firm were among the first to deal with the labour problem in a thoroughly broad-minded and effective fashion. They granted an eight hours' day to all their employes, and provided for them a fine school and recreation grounds, entirely at the expense of the firm. What was, perhaps, of still greater importance was the rule which they insisted upon that no boy would be accepted as an employe at the works until, he had passed a high standard at school, Subsequently, in 1898, Dr: Mond joined with Sir John Brunner in providing for the men, at a cost of .tlO,OOO, a splendidly equipped recreation pavilion. While engaged in the arduous task of direct- ing these great works, Dr. Mond still found time to create a large number of other processes, for which he took out patents, in cOnnection with the manufacture of 'ammonia, soda, chlorine, the recovery of ammonia from nitrogeneous sub- stances, the economical consumption of coal, &c. At a later date he took out patents for methods and 'appliances which combined the two pro- blems of utilising coal in the form of gas, and recovering, at the same time, the nitrogen con- tained in the' coal in the form of ammonia, thus creating a new and: important industry, known as the Mond Gas, Which is rapidly developing here and abroad. One of his firms, the South Staffordshire Mond Gas Co., at Dudley Port, distributes Mond Gas to about 100 works over an extensive area.

It would take us much too long to dwell upon all the extremely valuable developments of Dr. Mond's inquiries into this problem. One of their most interesting results, from a purely scientific standpoint, was his discovery, in con- junction with Messrs. Quincke and Langer, of a new series of chemical compounds, composed of metals and c arbon monoxide, now known as metallic carbonyls. The further investigation of one of these compounds—nickel carbonyl— enabled him to devise a new process of manufac- turing pure nickel from its ores, thus laying the foundation of a very important new industry established at Clydach in South Wales.

In 1896 Dr. Mond founded and endowed the Davy-Faraday Research Laboratory at the Royal Institution at a cost of ,k 120,000. He was one of the Most generous supporters of scientific insti- tutions .in this country, including the Royal Society, the International Catalogue of Scienti- fic Literature (of which he was one of the founders), the. Royal Institution (Low Temper- ature Research and other funds), the .Universi-: ties of Cambridge, Liverpool' and Manchester. University College, London, the Lister' Institute of Preventive Medicine, &c. Indeed, Dr. Mond took the warmest interest in national education and in all that promoted the moral and material zulvanc4...ment of the community.

In addition to all this strenuous labour for the promotion of science,- Dr. Mond found time for the cultivation of art and music and gradually acquired an exceptionally fine collection of pic- tures, chiefly of the earlier Italian school, of which he was a great admirer. It will be re- membered that he bequeathed a number of the Most important Of these. works to the nation.

div.head: WOMEN'S QUESHONS.
div.p: WOMEN'S QUESHONS.
Dance That Has Effected a Revolution at Balls and Parties.

div.head: GENTLE SYMPATHETIC QUEEN
div.p: A GENTLE SYMPATHETIC QUEEN

Sincere Congratulations from all parts of the British Empire reached Queefi. Alexandra on Monday—the occasion of her 69th birthday. Since the lamented death of King Edward she has lived a somewhat retired life, but still de- lights to, gO about doing good in an inostenta- tious way. fler life has been a 'pattern to the womenkind of Britain. Gentle, gracious and sympathetic; she has joined in all the toys and sorrows of the people, and in the eventide of her life, retains in a marked degree their loyalty and affection,

The Queen of Autumn Flowers. Fashions change in flowers, as in so many other things. The tulip mania, and dahlia craze have vanished but the sweet pea, the llose, and the chrysanthemum retain more than a fleeting popularity. Perhaps no flower gives greater pleasure than the chrysanthemum. It comes at a time when all the glory of our gar- dens has departed, and brings a flower of the gorgeous East into our gloomiest days. All People loi-e the beautiful, many-tinted blooms, which Vary from .a deep crimson to a pure white. Much of the advance in the -cultivation of the queen of autumn flowers may be traced to the influence of the shows which are held at this period of the year. They stimulate the grower to devote the most assiduous care and attention to his blooms, and .demonstrate the achievements that are possible. There ,seems to be a tendency to turn from colossal double blooms to the single flowers, which never lose Louth of their native simplicity-, and are well adapted foi' indoor decorations.
The Tango Fever.

Dancing has received a treinendousAmpetus this autumn, and the Tango fever recall the excitement when the waltz was introduced just a century ago. There were then enthusi- astic waltz coteries, just as there. are to-day Tango clubs and parties, and when the highest. in the land took up the craze its triumph was ,issured. •Tango 'teas are spreading in all direc- tions from the, Metropolis to the big cities and small towns, and young people of both sexes tre practising with assiduity the sixteen hun- lred steps of the new dance. No longer .have the ladies to pine and languish for partners at balls and parties, the Tango has effected a revo- lution.

The Queen of Greece and British • Nurses. , The Queen. Sophia of Greece has expressed her appreciation of the services rendered by the nurses of St. Bartholomew's, St. Thomas's, University College and the London hospitals, during the wars in the Balkans. Each nurse, .before leaving for home, was presented with a gift 'from her Majesty, and Miss Tucker, who was in charge of the contingent, was received by the Queen and presented with a. gold pend- ant. Several lady doctors from this country went out to the war, and among them was one who lad hem.- the position 'of house surgeon in the London Homeopathic. Hospital.

div.head: Echoes 01 the Crimean War.
div.p: Echoes 01 the Crimean War.

Elderly folks—for no one is old in these days —who remember the Crimean War, will be in- terested to learn that there are living to-day, near London, two women, wives of soldiers, who shared the terrible hardships of that san- guinary campaign. One of. the brave women was but nineteen, when she followed her bu& band to the war, paying her own fare, for she was married "off the strength." A deep hole was dug for her behind the trenches, in which her husband lay before Sebastopol, and there her baby was born. Miss Nightingale and the wife of a corporal nur.Sed her. Later, she was removed to Scuiari, and helped—as did all the soldiers' wives—to do the men's washing. Her husband, after going through the war, was transferred from his old regiment and died in •

div.head: Ancient and 114Klei n Needlework.
div.p: Ancient and 114Klei n Needlework.

A most interesting loan exhibition of old and famous needlework has been held at Hinchin- brooke, Huntingdonshire, under the superin- tendence of Nirs Scott Galley. Among the ex- hibits was the wedding veil of Marie Antoinette, ,soine wonderful Elizabethan needlework, a counterpane in old Italian embroidery, Vene- tian tapestry hangings work.ed, by Queen Anne , and her ladies, a doll also of -Queen Anne's reign, and a Wonderful collection of Cretan em- broideries. Of samplers' there was a numerous selection,' besides laces of Various periods that had belonged to great ladies of the past. A piece of point lace, once the property of Queen Charlotte, w_aa a very fine example of that beautiful work. Several schools of needlecraft exhibited specimens of modern work, which, for beauty of design and•perfection of execu- tion compared favourably with that of other countries and other times..

How t? Use Veilings. Veilihgs are still popular, and fOr 'renova- tions have much to TecommenCtnem, for they gracefully cover up -many deficiencies of .the foundation over which they may bp used. There are many schemes in colouring; the -rainbow, lightning and sea shades being among the first favourites. These materials are, however, by no -means 'elle* therefore, before deciding to use them for the laudable purpose of bringing a half-Worn dress up to date, the cost. should be Made a matter of careful consideration, and the condition of the foundation thoroughly scruL tinised, or more expense may be entailed in the renovation than in .the purchase of a new gown. But given a good foundation, much may be done with a few yards of ninon, by means of a tunic or frills, and •draperies, which, with a sash, may be relied upon to convert a demode gown into a_charming frock in this season's newest mode.
The New Figure.

The Russian blouse, with a wide belt, is much ,in evidence. The belt gives a straight line from .the .shoulders to. the hips, for the waist is alto- gether undefined.. This line may suit. the slim and undeveloped girl, but it is, to Say the least., trying to the owner of prominent hips .and full 'figure. But much may be achieved and disadvantages modified 'by the choice of cor- sets. Coats fasten in divers fashions, some straight down the front, others at the side, or below the armhole, or diagonally. Many open widely in fhont, and are filled in with contrasting materials, such as .velvet, satin, &c., outlined with fur, which take the, place of, and are, to all intents and purposes, waistcoats. lin- mehsely wide cuffs . of .fur are seen on some ,of the wrap coats, wide enough to be used as muffs. In fact, some of these very roomy cuffs are provided with a snap and press button, sewn inside, to keep the arm and wrists warm, otherwise too much cold air would be admitted through the wide opening.

div.head: TARIFF REFORM FIGURES.
div.p: TARIFF REFORM FIGURES.
A Cornhill Calculation as to Motor Cars.

Speaking from the Conservative van at Corn- hill, the special advocate for last week on Tariff 'Reform" advanced as an argument in its favour that increased taxation made the cost of production greater than before, and if not adopted at the same time in other- countries. placed England at a disadvantage compared, say, with America, though a workman called out he should say France.

Then he illustrated by an example: If manufacturer of motor cars could turn one out ready for use at £l,OOO, and he employed 10 men, the cost through the burden of the Insur- ance Act was increased by .£1.20. This he re- peated three times. It does not take long to see. that if "argu- ments " of this kind become general, Tariff "Reform" will be ui a worse plight than ever. One hundred men under the Health Insurance would each cot an employer 3d. weekly for weeks, ot• £65 per annum. Supposing that half the men were skilled and came under the un- employment section, 50 at .21d. each . weekly for the year would .be £27 is: Bd., And if these ineu were continuously employed throughout the year the employer would be able to claim a refund of one-third of his contributions, bringing them down to .218. Thert4ore, the entire cost Of insurance (both•sections) would be £83,, against the sißaker's £l2O. ' However, this is not all, for it is not to be inferred that only one car would be produced in a year. With 100 men employed we would 'expect at least one car to be put on the street every week, in which case instead of a ear cost- ing .£l2O extra, it would bo T2s.. only. The speaker omitted all reference to medical benefits keep- ing the men at work and being better able to follow- their employment.

THE EXHIBITION CONCLUDED. End of Successful Missionary Effort.

s Over 20,000 people visited the Missionary Exhibition held for ten days in the Empire Warrington, and the promoters were sat- isfied with the results. The exhibition was brought to a close on _Saturday evening, and the last opening ceremony was performed in the afternoon by Archdeacon Spooner. Alderman Smethurst was in the chair. ' Alderman SMETIMRST, introducing the Arch- deacon, said it was all very well for people to sit by their firesides and read missionary books comfortably and contentedly, but it was not very well with those who offered their services and their lives to go and travel in the foreign lands and take God's blessings to people who had .not heard of them: People said .they needed missionaries ;at home, but he thought they had a good many missionaries in their towns working under various. organisations. (Applause.)

Archdeacon SPOONER said they ought to strike a note of thankfulness for the large measure of blessing given to that great effort. They ought to he thankful for the solidarity of the Church; first of all, becauSe of the fact that the Church, in corporate capacity, was beginning to realise some of the great responsibility which was being opened out in foreign lands, and he felt very thankful they were awakening to the realisa- tion of these responsibilities and opportunities. He had been a warm supporter and a firm believer in missions, and he rejoiced with the workers and those associated with the S.P.G. in their work. He urged the need for more support, as they wanted the exchequer" of the SP.G, to be filled to overflowing. Something k people had attended the exhibition, ait would have great effect if each one like became centres of missionary enterprise.

div.head: COUNCIL AND COW SNEDS.
div.p: COUNCIL AND COW SNEDS.
What Should The Air Space Be?

The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural District Council was held at Dutton on Tuesday, Councillor C. E. Linaker presiding The principal discussion took place on regula- tions as regards dairies and cowsheds. The Clerk said he had forwarded a copy of the local regulations in regard to cowsheds and dairies, which stated that the minimum air space for sows was 450 cubic feet, to the County Medical Officer of Health, who had replied to the effect that he did not think the Council had been well advised in passing such a resolution; for he was of the opinion that 450 cubic feet was far too small a cubic space to allow adequate ventilation taking place without causing draughts. The Leal Government Board said GOO cubic feet for cattle turned out to, grass, and 800 for those not turned out. The space in common lodging-houses was supposed to be 400 cubic feet per head. Councillor Lithker, jun., said he considered 450 cubic feet was quite adequate. , They were going to get starved cattle if they had 600 or 800 square feet. lie had built a shippon with 420 cubic feet per beast, and that was consid- ered an excellent building. He would not say anything about the cowsheds in town, but for their district 450 cubic feet was ample space.
ST. HELENS FANCILRS' SHOW. ,

div.head: Farmers Knew Better.
div.p: Farmers Knew Better.

Councillor Woodward thought the farmers of Cheshire knew what was better for their pur- suits than Dr. Meredith Yonge. He was glad the Local Government Board were getting more sensible in the matter. They had come down to 600, and they would probably come down to 400. If they were to turn milking beasts into 800 cubic feet space they would need fires. If the Medical Officer would 'go in Delamere Forest—Government property—he would find the largest shippon did not exceed 450 cubic feet per beast. A newly-built shippon there only allowed 420 cubic feet. Ile suggested that they leave the matter where it was. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Harrison: You want an even tem- perature and you..would not get it naturally with such large spaces. It was decided that the original resolution of 450 cubic feet.as the minimum be adhered to.
NO DRINK IN RUNCORN THEATRES. _Magistrates Come to Important Decision.

_ No drink is to be supplied in Runcorn theatres. This was the decision arrived at on Monday, when the magistrates held a special session to consider music and dancing licences. Mr..Laycock applied for, the transfer of the music, dancing and cinetna licences of the Palace Theatre, Runcorn, from. Mr. 0. Smith to Mr. David Stratton.

Supt. Owen said the, police had no objections, but he had been instructed by the Chief Con- stable to ask that the following rules be inserted on the plans: That no alcohol be consumed on the premises, that the theatre be Closed on Sun- days, Good Friday and Christmas Day, and that a Sufficient number of fire appliances be placed throughout the building, and that inflammable cotton wool or similar material be .not used for costumes or decorations.
Mr. Stratton undertook to carry out those instructions.
The licences were granted.

div.head: OLD FESTIVAL THAT IS EVER NEW.
div.p: THE OLD FESTIVAL THAT IS EVER NEW.
But is old, old—good old Christmas—gone? Nothing but the hair of his good, grey, old head and beard left? Well! I will have that, seeing I can- not have more of him.

Christmas is coming! And of all the old fes- tivals, that of Christmas awakens the strongest and most heartfelt associations. There is some- thing in it which mixes with our conviviality and lifts us up to a state of hallowed and ele- vated enjoyment. It is a beautiful arrange- ment, this season for the. gathering together of family connections, drawing closer the bonds of kindred hearts, of giving a world of happiness to children, and a world in which older people become young again. There's a 'charm about Christmas. It may be pitchy *dark outside in the village lanes, but, oh! the artificial sun- shine which comes from the blaze of the ruddy fire dispels all gloom. The wind may howl °lit- side and rumble down the chimney, but what can be more grateful than the sheltered 'security, the cosy hearth, and the scene of domestic hilarity? • We will not say that all the old ceremonials of . Christmas • have . disappeared, like the favourite sack of old Falstaff; neither must we be pessimists and say because the world has become more worldly there is less enjoyment and , more- dissipation. No! certainly not. Rather I let us say that " Pleasursi" has expanded info a broader but a shallower stream, and that it has gone out of the deep channels to flow into, the calm bosom of domestic life. We shall never let Christmas go. It is so delightful.

trepidation as the mature husband, goes along And finds the jeweller's, stationer's and picture shops tempt him to load himself with all kinds of pretty pretties for his bright-eyed, little girl, who, in her_ turn, thinks that that • cigarette case she saw would just suit Charlie, and finally it arrives at Charlie's home on Christmas morn- ing.

div.head: PREPARATIONS.
div.p: THE PREPARATIONS.

Oh! the joy of these shopping excursions! It holds a spell over every heart. And what a chance for the florists! All iheir shops are in their very best Christmas attire! High up are the bunches of mistletoe which are so bewitch- ing, and the holly berries are blushing by their side at the very thought of the fun in store. Oh! these evergreen emblems of peace and glad- ness, what a glorious effect they have on human hearts! And it is gratifying to see that home feeling so completely roused, which holds such a powerful place in every English bosom. Then there are the presents passing and repassing, those little tokens of regard and good cheer, those quickeners of good and kind feelings. What a pleasing effect they have in producing fond associations and stirring up deeper sym- pathies!

div.head: JOYS OF SHOPPING!
div.p: THE JOYS OF SHOPPING!

The eager faces of Men, Women and children, as they scan the contents of 'every shop win,- dow ! The dominant note is happiness tuned to its sweetest chord, nothing is gtruck in a minor key—even though the gift be for someone far away. Never mind! , The joy is just the same, he or she is not forgotten, the circle of love in- cludes all.

Here now we may stop before a draper's shop. What bewitching trifles! What dainiy lingerie! What warm gloves! What-. tempting furs! Then farther on we see that fathers, brothers, husbands and sons must not be forgotten. Why! that is just the tie for Jack! And what, a splen- did seasonable present for hubby. "He was just wanting a warm overcoat, and be shall have it, too," says his wee wife, and off she goes inside and orders it. But it must be a surprise-. "No. thank YOu!'. Don't send it till Christmas Eve." "Very well," says the knowing shop- man. He quite understands. And then off go the men 'folk to choose their presents. "Now what shall I get for in:G clever little manager? I shall have to be careful, pile's Sco particular, and wouldn't care for me to waste a penny. I must inspect things with judicious care. Why! that's the very, thing I beard her saying she wanted." And quickly be goes with a light heart, pays cheerfully, walks out and tumbles nast a brilliantly-lighted tobacco shop. "Ah ! the very thing. I've done such -a good spec. that I'll treat myself to a good cigar." Then the youths, with perhaps not so much

PARK, BATHS AND GAS.
Three Items Discussed at Warrington Town Council.
GAS SECRETARYSHIP.

The extension of the Victoria Park, the Baths, and the extra supply of gas for Jd. to the slot meter users, were topics discussed at the Town Council on Tuesday' night. Alderman BENNETT, introducing the subject of the proposed park extension, expressed satisfac- tion that the Parks Committee had agreed to purchase 38 acres of land adjoining the park for ..24,000 from the Earl of Ellesmere. It was he who proposed the purchase of the park in 1897, and the fact was one of the proudest recollec- tions of his municipal life. Ile had always had his eye on the remainder of the land, and he was glad the committee had been able to secure it on such good terms.

Councillor GOUGH thought the money could be better spent in purchasing land for open spaces in Bewsey and St. John's Wards, They had no recreation grounds, and why it should be proposed to extend Victoria Park he could not understand.

div.head: WARD OF POTENTIALITIES.
div.p: WARD OF POTENTIALITIES.

Councillor HEssnALL said the committee had a series of definite reasons for securing the land. One was that they had been threatened by the owner of the land that he wanted to build works on the frontages to the river and to the canal. The Corporation had already spent.from £12,000 to ..£1.4,000 on the park, and for that reason alone it was worth while to secure the additional land. The committee were not responsible for the making of Warrington, and there.was land adjoining Victoria Park which was not avail- able in BeWsei and St. John's Wards.. Latch- ford-Ward was the only ward in the town which had potentialities; because, while all other wards haid reached their boundaries, there was in Latchford land equal to at least one-fifth of the whole of the town unbuilt upon. The construe- „tion of the suspension ;bridge had also placed the park within easy access of a number of wards. The land in question was the very cheapest they had had the opportunity of buy- ing—in fact, when they deducted what they hoped to gain from allotments, the cost was in- finitesimal compared with land they had pur- chased elsewhere. (Hear, hear.) Councillor PEMBERTON : It is cheap because we have not been bled this time. Councillor DICKENSON was strongly in support of an open space in Bewsey Ward, but there was no prospect of getting land there at a reasonable price. The purchase was approved.

div.head: BATHS QUESTION.
div.p: THE BATHS QUESTION.

Councillor PEmerarroN asked when the baths were to be ready. He noticed that the com- mittee were to pull down some slipper baths not long erected. Councillor OSBORNE thought Councillor Pem- berton should go and see the baths it was pro- posed to remove. If -thry were not pulled down they would fall down. (Councillor PEMBERTON : Shame.) , These baths were in an -awful condi- tion. The committee had no intention of taking

div.head: WHAT CHRISTMAS MEANS TO THE CHILDREN.
div.p: WHAT CHRISTMAS MEANS TO THE CHILDREN.

Then come the children! How could we for- get them? They would not allow us, even if we would, for the bewildering display of toys is' everywhere, and the children's gaze is arrested at every step. The windows are full of Teddy bears, dancing pantomime fairies, dolls, rail- ways, motor cars, and even embryo aviators, who promise to do daring things, can %ratify their ambitions in a miniature aeroplane. Oh, the millions of .childish questions that happy parents are only too ready to answer. "Mother, do you think Santa Claus would -bring me a house and a lovely lot of dollies if I asked him?" "Daddy, do those penguins come all the way from the South Pole?" "What makes that aeroplane fly?" "Do all elephants wear waist- coats?" "Do giraffes live on chocolates?" "Daddy, see those two camels?" yes.” "Well, why has one only, one hump, and the other two?" "Mother, does Santa Claus buy his presents here?" "No, certainly not." "Well, where does he get them, then?" "In his own country." "Where's that?" "Didn't you learn it in school, Tommy?" "No, mother, not at all." "Well, where does he live?" "He lives in the Valley of Contentment, situated be- tween two little hills, Love and Harmony, and the, river which flows, down is called Tran- quility." "Tins it got a bridge over it like War- rington Bridge?" Mother nonplussed! ! ! ! _ .

Daddy goes home from his shopping, pockets bursting, arms aching, limbs weary, but face smiling. Witness', the onslaught made on the de- fenceless sire by the excited little ones. They scale him with stools for ladders to get at his pockets, they despoil him of his brown paper parcels, cling hold of his necktie, tug at his coat collar, hang round his neck, and even kick him in sheer irrepressible delight! What a multitude of wonders the pockets reveal! What shouts! What joy! What clamour! What ecstasy! _

And what trepidation iii poor Mother's heart when someone announces that baby has swal- lowed Mr. and Mrs. Noah out of the ark, or despatched the whole of the lucky pudding set —paper, too—from the jeweller's. Oh! inde- scribable relief at finding it's a false alarm! The multitudinous emotions all mixed with joy at this happy Christmas time!

div.head: SEASONABLE HINT TO TRADESMEN.
div.p: SEASONABLE HINT TO TRADESMEN.

Oh! Christmas presents, come in, come in, come in your hundreds, nay, thousands; we can do with them all! But as we are a little in ad- vance of the coming festive season, if the shop- men also wish to relish the joys of a real "• Nlow—ell" to the fullest extent, they can't , do better than acquaint our little Warrington world with the attractiveness of their dainty draperies, fascinating frocks, bewitching bijou- teries tempting toys, plenteous provisions, taste- ful turkeys and British beef. • Sweet are the uses of advertisement. Adver- tising under -.proper. conditions pays, ,and is as necessary to the shopman as a window display or the illumination of his premises. Who doesn't know that a good paper like "The Examiner," with its well-set, finely displayed, and artistically. arranged advertisements, influ- ences enormously the thoughts and spending power of the people? , A time like Christmas is one of the finest stimulants to shopping, it is a time when hands dive deep into pockets, money flows outwards like a-fast flowing river to the sea, for Christ- mas cheer knows no confining bounds. WO.

div.head: NO ROOM FOR PESSIMISTS.
div.p: NO ROOM FOR PESSIMISTS.

What's the use of . being a pessimist at such a time as this? Announce your goods and don't hide your light under • a bushel. Many papers are mere sellers of space, but "The Examiner" staff offers brains, and helps you to make your display a real trade-maker and a genuine at- tractive force.

And so amidst the general call to happiness, the bustle of the spirits, the stir of the affec- tions which prevail at this period, what heart, what bosom can remain insensible? It is the : season of regenerated feeling—the season for kindling, not merely the fire of hospitality in the hall, but the genial flame of charity in the heart. And so let us feel the influence of the season, let it beam into our souls from the happy looks of those dound us. Surely happiness is reflective like the light of heaven, and every face bright with. happy smiles and glowing with 'innocent enjoyment is a mirror transmitting to others the rays of a supreme and ever-shining benevolence. lie who can turn churlishly away from looking on or econtemplating the happiness ' of his fellow beings, and can sit down in the dark and repine in his lorieliness, when all around him is joyful he may have his moments of strong excitement and times when his gratification is all selfish, but he wants the genial warmth and the social sympathies which go to make up the charm of

div.head: MERRY CHRISTMAS.
div.p: A MERRY CHRISTMAS.

Here we have dear old Christmas, Then heap up the yule logs higher, How can we ever grow weary Of tales told round the fire? Then on with a jovial song or two,' And pass the Wassail Cup, For the springs of love should flourish— They should never be dried up.

Here we have dear old Christmas, But we—like the years—grow Old, With the ceaseless hurry and bustle, And the striving after gold. Bitt in kindness take old Christmas, And shake him by the hand, For he is right good company— The best in all the land.

Here we have dear old Christmas, Fling Discontent on one side, Pour Happiness around you From the flood of Plenty's tide; There may be lines to mar your fact, To wither up your heart, 'Tis not old Time, but selfishness, That does the greater part.

Be happy! then, be happy! Stir the logs into a blaze! Peace on Earth, goodwill to all, Amidst Life's dreary maze! •Be happy ! oh ! be ha.ppy ! The thorns hide not the flowers, Let kindness reign among you, You'll grow richer every hour!

Then here's to dear old Christmas Fill the bumper to the brim, And toast the dear ones far away, Altho' your eyes are dim; The golden chain that binds us, Grows tighter as we part. At Christmas time they're with us, 'Tis the call from every heart.

God's Will to all. It's full and free, 'Tis that which keeps away The frowning look and wrinkled face, And the dismal shades of grey. Oh ! let your life be glad, be glad, Tho. sadness comes so nigh, Just wait and hope, for then you'll See Silver linings in your sky. E.W.

CO-OP. PRESIDENT.
Mr. J. Upson is Elected to the

div.head: Position.
div.p: Position.
3s. 2d. IN £ DIVIDEND.

Mr. J. Upson has been appointed the new President of the Warrington Co-operative Saoety. The appointment was made at the quarterly meeting held in the Co-operative Hall on Monday evening, when about 300 members attended.

The report of the committee showed that the sales for the past three,' months had been :et77,894, an increase of .1:236 over the corre- sponding period last year; The membership at the end of the quarter stood at 13,318, a net inc`rease of 258 on the period, and the committee recommended that an interim dividend- of 3s. 2d. in the .2 should be again paid on all purchases, including butchery. The report was adopted with very little dis- cussion, except that a few remarks were made as to decreases in the coal department. Mr. Wadsworth- did not seek re-election, and Mr. J. Upson and Mr. S. H. Smith were nominated for the presidency for the ensuing year, and, on a vote being taken, Mr. Upson was elected.

Mr. Green Chappell was re-elected auditor for the ensuing twelve, months, and for vacancies on the committee Mr. W. Wright, Mr. W. H. Sherburn, Mr. S. H. Smith and Mr. J. Massey were elected, the latter for the remaining period of Mr. Upson's term of office.

div.head: TO BUILD COTTAGES.
div.p: TO BUILD COTTAGES.

The following resolution was submitted: "That the committee be E;Mpowe.red. to. consider the question. of building cottages where there is at present a shortage in any district covered by the society's operations, and to take action if it is financially possible to do so." This was carried with the hearty approval of the meeting. Mr. UPSON moved a vote of 'hanks to the re- tiring President, Mr. Wads. for his ser- vices to the society during the 13 years on the committee and as its President, and in doing so expressed the opinion that a,very great deal of time had been given by. Mr. Wads- worth, and also Mr. Bibby, who had been a member of the committee for 12 years, and that both these gentlemen were deserving of the thanks of the members for the work which they had done. The resolution was seconded by Mr.' S. IL SMITH, and carried unanimously.

div.head: SELF-RAISF.NG FLOUR.
div.p: SELF-RAISF.NG FLOUR.

The proprietors of McDougall's self-raising flour, which, they hold, is unequalled for all kinds of pastry, boiled puddings, and cakes, have issued a booklet giving recipes and hints most valuable to the household cook. Pastry made from McDougall's flour is beautifully light and flaky, so that the risk of indigestion is quite obviated. Yorkshire puddings made from it are specially good. A copy of the booklet, especially useful now, in view of the. coming season of good cheer, may be had on application.

Councillor PEMBERTON : These baths were only built a few years ago, and I think- Councillor DICKENSON :1 object to Councillor Pemberton making a second speech. Councillor PEMBERToN : I'm asking. a question. When are the baths to be ready? Councillor . DICKENSON : The new slipper baths will be opened this year and the plunge bath next year. The subject then dropped.

div.head: SLOT METER QUESTION.
div.p: THE SLOT METER QUESTION.

In reference to giving more gas for a Id. through the slot meters, the Gas Committee re- ported that the manager had been authorised to have the wheels of the meters altered, and to arrange with the meter makers to do the work, if he decided so.

Alderman JOHN EVANS said the committee de- cided upon the course suggested, because if they depended upon their own workmen Cie task would not be completed for some months. The work had to be done quickly.

div.head: SECRETARYSHIP.
div.p: THE SECRETARYSHIP.

Alderman JoHN EVANS stated that the Gas Committee had received with much regret the resignation of Mr. Frederick Taylor. He sug- gested that they should continue his services to the end of the financial year, when the ques- tion of the office would be considered. Councillor PEMBERTON : I hope we shall get notice when this is to be considered. We don't want to have two cash offices for one corpora- tion. It confuses the public. e Councillor HAWTHORN: It would be a great ad- vantage to have all the rates payable at Bank House. Alderman JOHN EVANS : The matter will be considered.

div.head: POOR PEOPLE AND COKE.
div.p: POOR PEOPLE AND COKE.

Councille-r-O-SB-OR-N-E- noted that the Gas Com- mittee had a surplui supply of coke on hand. They might give better facilities to the poor people to get the coke by supplying it in less quantities than 5 cwt. at a time. At thii season the poorer people would make use of the coke if they could get it ,in smaller quantities. Councillor PEMBERTON hoped the Gas Com- mittee would take into consideration the sug- gestion of Councillor Osborne about the coke. If they did not, other Councillors would bring in a special icsolhtion about the matter. Alderman JOHN EVANS : It has been done in former years. In hard times coke has been sup- plied in very small quantities. There has been no demand this season because the weather has been against it. The minutes were approved.

div.head: FOR THE CHRISTMAS PUDDING.
div.p: FOR THE CHRISTMAS PUDDING.

For the benefit of our lady readers we give them the best recipe we knoNx of for their Christmas Plum Pudding. Take threequarters of a pound of flour, two heaped-up teaspoonfuls of Borwick's Baking Powder, two ounces. of breadcrumbs, one and a half .pounds of suet, two pounds of raisins, one pound of currants, ten ounces of sugar, two ounces of almonds, one pound of mixed candied peel, salt and spice to taste. Mix the ingredients well together; and add six eggs, well beaten, and threequarters of a pint of milk; divide in two, and boil eight hours.

div.head: PASSIJIG WEEK.
div.p: PASSIJIG WEEK.
PROTECTED SOAP.

Those who remember the vain attempts of Mr; H4.01d Smith to prove that Crosfield's Works were run on lines which showed the wisdom of Protection—a shaving stick adver- tisement being pressed into the service of a desperate and moribund cause—will be glad of the assurance given on the relative merits Of Free Trade and Protection by Sir Alfred Mond, who has influence nowadays in the affairs of our great Bank Quay wOrks. As is well known, Sir Alfred is in close touch with the soap-mak- ing industry in Europe. Ile has discovered that as a result Of the German makers feeling themselves quite unable to compete with the soap Makers of Warrington and elsewhere, they sent a commission to this country to investigate , the cause. The Commission has now reported to the German soap manufacturers that 'the English can beat the Germans, because England is a Free Trade country. "English soap- makers," said the Commission, "can buy raw Materials at Free Trade prices. In Germany we have Protection, and we haye to pay more in consequence for our oils, paper, boxes—more for everything required., So long as germany is under Protection we cannot hope to compete [i.e., in the soap export trade] with the English soap induStry." Yet our Tory Member and his satellites, who 'weelAy' speak at the street corners of Warrington, say and ask &small section of an incredulous public to belpe Protection is a sblessing sent from the gods. The German soap-makers, speaking from actual experience, and not from Tariff Beform League cooked handbooks, do not say so. The Gellman Commission has unconsciously given a great message to Warrington: "Stick to Free Trade and throw out those who would tax one of your chief industries."

It Will be seen from his letter that the guinea fee was based upon the sum that was already being paid by the London County Council for this class of lecture, and that the Widnes Education Committee are 'paying the necessary Airst-aid lecture- fees. •As our 'object was ,to endeavour to get the Education Authority in Warrington to meet the charges, which, though small, are too great to be met by working people who are anxious to serve the whole community in a very useful way, these precedents may be remem- bered if the School Management Committee 'con- sider the advisability of beginning a class at the Technical School. div.head: PROTECTING CHILD LIFE.
div.p: PROTECTING CHILD LIFE.

It is pleasing to note the quiet and steady progress that is being Made with regard to the child life of the town. 'About two and a hall years ago the first Mothers' and Babies' Wel, come \V IS opened. Last week we recorded the fact that a second Welcome had been started in the 13ewsey district, with every prospect of success. A nei,v community of mothers and babies will thus. be tapped. It is also interesting to hear of the Idlest move of the Guild of Help, which originated the Welcome scheme: A conference is being called on the 9th December, at the Town Hall, to consider the problem of children under school age. Hitherto the infant in arms has had more public attention than the child between one and 'five years of age. There ought to be a representative gathering on that occasion, when Miss Janet Blair, who has done pioneer .work in Ancoats,. will open the discussion. The local Health Committee in this connection is to be heartily congratulated upon its decision to appoint an additional Lady .H9lth Visitor, Whose special duty will be to visit the homes Where there are children between the ages of one and five years. Few towns have yet real- ised the need for such work, and Warrington oughtio be proud to be in the forefront in such a development of public health work. Lanca- shire, unfortunately, is the black spot in Eng- land for .child mOrtality, but while many towns in the County Palatine are worse than Warring- ton, we must continually work for local better- ment. It is certainly an appalling fact that of nil the deaths in this borough no less than 40 per cent, occur before the age of five years. -

div.head: WARRIhGTON LEADS.
div.p: WARRIhGTON LEADS.
The Result of an Up-to-date Policy in
Education.
11 HEADMASTER'S TRIBUTE.

The annual distribution of prizes and certifi- cates to the students of the School of Art, Tech- nical Institute and Commercial Institute took place in the Parr Hall on Thursday evening. The Rev. Canon Morley Stevenson (chairman of the School Management Committee) presided, and Mr. J. L. Paton, Manchester Grammar School, presented the prizes. The CHAIRMAN said Warrington had some cause for pride in the success of its schools, because it was one of the first to adopt a certain system commonly known as the course system, whereby the student in the school did not merely take up one subject, as was the case sometimes, but he 'correlated a subject with others, and went through a course which was educationally much more beneficial. Mr. PATON said the results in Warrington dif- fered largely from those in other parts of the country. In Warrington they talked not about promises, but performances. They were before the others, and that night they saw the results of the policy inaugurated years ago. (Hear, hear.) That was a sound educational policy; not one of those policies shaped with the idea of catching the man in the street. It was, in the first place, by no means popular, but the com- mittee had gone forward and saw the excellent results. Ile thought that the employers of labour in Warrington had undoubtedly contri- buted to the result.

div.head: OLD HOME.
div.p: THE OLD HOME.
MADDISON CAWEIN.
An old lane, an old gate, an old house by a tree. A wild wood, a wild brook—they will not let me
be; In boyhood I knew, them, and still they call to me.
Down deep_ in my heart's core I hear them, and my eyes Through tear mists behold them beneath the old-time skies, 'Mid bee-bloom and rose-bloom and orchard lands arise.
f-k- Yr: • ..--14,401,-..v.• I hear them; and heartsick with longing is my
soul, To walk there, to dream there, beneath the sky's blue bra; Around me, within me, the weary world made whole.
To talk with the wild brook of all the long ago; To whisper the wood-wind of things we used to know When we were old companions, before my heart knew woe.
To walk with the morning and watch its rose unfold; To drowse with the noontide lulled on its heart of gold; To lie with the nighttime and dream the dreams of old.
To tell to the old trees, and to each listening leaf, The longing, the yearning, as in my boyhood brief, The old hope, the old love, would ease my heart of grief.
The old lane, the old gate, the old house by the tree, The wild wood, the wild brook—they will not let me be; In boyhood I knew them, and still they call to me.

div.head: V(1.1 NTARYISM'V. CONSCR IPTI ON .
div.p: V(1.1 NTARYISM'V. CONSCR IPTI ON .

The steps which should be token to popularise recruiting for the TeiTitOrials have been dis- cussed at a .deputation from the Territorial Association to Mr. ASQUITH. Lord HALDANE addressing a large meeting of those who are interested in the efforts of the Voluntary Service
Committee to promote military service without conscription, dealt most effectually with the fallacies of those who advocate compulsory service because recruiting for the Territorials is
slack. Our vital requirements are a, Navy which will guarantee food,-supplies in tithe of
war, and I—event invasion except by sporadic raids, arkl ,highly trained professional army for service overseas. If we tried to create a

large army on the Continental pattern, manned by compulsory service, we should not be able to get recruits for our overseas professional army, and the army which we did get would be useless for defence, aS we could be starved

out if our Fleet lost control of the seas. To try to maintain an overwhelming'. superiority nt sea and an army of the Continental type would mply spell bankruptcy. People on the Continent say to us: "You do not realise your own formid- ableness. ,With your small army and your great navy you can sustain a long war, but a prolonged war means starvation for us, because our fathers, ,brothers, and sons are taken away from us and the earning of money:' No nation is rich enough to give professional pay to a conscript army, and their families have to send money to the conscripts throughout the period of their service.

div.head: REFUSAL OF INSURANCE BENEFITS.
div.p: REFUSAL OF INSURANCE BENEFITS.

Sir,—The Committee of Inquiry into the working of the Insurance Act, instituted by the Fabian Research Department, has reason to be- lieve that some insured person § are being re- fused the benefits to which The Act entitles them; and that many poor people feel unable to resist what seems to them oppression. Will you allow me, through your columns, to invite all who know of any case of what seems to be wrongful refusal of benefits, to write (in strict confidence) to me, giving full particulars? Information is wanted as to the following cases among others :

1. Refusal of sickness benefit when the proved incapacity to work is caused by pregnancy, on the ground that this is not a disease. But the Act entitles to benefit for every " disablement," without specific disease; and Section 110 of the Commissioner's Rand Book explicitly recognises incapacity caused by the disablement of preg- nancy as a valid ground for sickness benefit.

2. Restriction of sickness benefit in pregnancy and maternity to a maximum of four weeks. There is no limitation of sickness benefit in the Act for members of approved societies, apart from the 26 weeks' maximum. . 3. Refusal to continue sickness benefit, when the doctor certifies incapacity to work, on the ground that the patient is found. (1) breaking the rules for persons on benefit (thereby incur- ring a fine only); (2) doing light household work deemed by the doctOr not harmful; (3) even "looking after her children"!

4. Refusal of .sickness benefit on the ground that, although unable to follow his own occupa- tion, the patient is capable of "'some" work. This amounts to a parody of the law, for no one is ever incapable of any work whatsoever, unless he is continuously unconscious. (Even the bedridden paralytic mai knit, or pick peas, or write a book!)

• 5. Failure to provide the " adequate " medical attendance and treatment, guaranteed by the Act for all cases without any ex6eptions. Par- ticulars are desired of all cases in which (1) panel doctors have required payment for ser- vices beyond the scope of their contract with the Insurance Committee; (9) panel doctors have been unable to give the treatment re- quired, e.g., surgery, eye cases, &c.; (3) hospital treatment was required and not obtained; (4) the prescribed drugs or appliances have not been supplied free of charge; and (5) appliances not included in the Commissioner's list (trusses, elastic bandages, spectacles, crutches, &e.) have been required and refused.

6. Failure to provide what is required by tuberculosis patients, such as (1) inability to gain admission to sanatorium; (2) refusal of the necessary means of adequate domiciliary treat- ment, .such as open-air sleeping arrangements or _necessary ventilation; (3) refusal to allow nourishing food, such as milk and eggs, which the Act empowers the panel doctor to prescribe under certain circumstances..

7. Refusal of maternity benefit or of sickness in connection therewith, on the ground of "mis- conduct," or because of alleged breach of rules. 8. Expulsion from approved society, for in- stance, on ground of "withholding material in- formation."

The committee welcomes testimony on both sides, and would like equally illustrative cases, in which, under the circumstances indicated above, _benefits had been given or continued, and instances of their advantageous results.
SIDNEY WEBB. (Fabian Research Department.) 37. Norfolk-street, London, W.C.

div.head: Miraculous Escape.
div.p: A Miraculous Escape.

Whilst following his employment as a painter and decorator, Samuel Ashbrook, who resides with his parents at 40, Rolleston-street, had a miraculous escape. He was working on a scaf- fold erected at Penketh Tannery, from which he fell to the ground, three storeys below. No bones were broken, and upon inquiry late last night he was reported to be progressing favour- ably.

div.head: Cotton Operatives' Dance.
div.p: Cotton Operatives' Dance.

There was a very- large attendance last night at the Empire Hall on the occasion of the cotton operatives' dance. During an interval Mr. J. Crinion, president of the Cardroom Operatives Amalgamation, and Mr. T. Shaw, secretary of the International Textile Workers, addressed the gathering. Mr. Crinion referred to the improvements which had taken place since the introduction of their organisation into the town. Mr. Shaw stated, that the Weavers' Amalgama- tign had a membership now of some 200,000, and was probably the largest amalgamation of any single trade in the world. He asked them to stand by their Union. (Cheers.)

div.head: MUNICIPAL HOUSES.
div.p: MUNICIPAL HOUSES.
Warrington Workers at the Mercy of the Landlords.
DEPUTATION TO THE MAYOR.
BY "A WORKER."

Organised trade unionism in Warrington is rapidly becoming u forte of the leaders of the Trades and Labour Council, and the result of such organisation is being realised by the tride unionists in general. Each meeting of the Council goes to 'prove, by the business trans- acted, that unity is strength, and the agenda on Tuesday evening was no exception to the rule. Mr. S. H. Smith presided, and he was supported by Mr. C. Dukes, secretary. Employers and Picketting.

The SECRETARY read a letter from the General Federation of Trade Unions, in which it was stated that persistent and well-organised efforts were being made by the Employers' Associationg throughout the kingdom to render Trades Unica' Acts very burdensome, and to destroy whatever protection the Trades Disputes Act conferred upon the unions. Efforts were to be made during the next session of Parliament to fur- ther limit the right to picket. " The emploY- ers' proposals," continued the letter, " are that pickets shall not number more than two; that they must be employes of the firm picketted; and that trade unions shall be financially re- sponsible for all the acts of their members. If these proposals become operative, the trade union movement will cease to exist as an effec- tive defence, or as a force capable of securing improvements in wages or conditions." This, said Mr. Dukes, would rob tiade union- ists of a large amount of liberty. Pickett' was a very difficult work to undertake, even under present conditions, and from a financial standpoint it would considerably weaken the position of trade unions. He asked them to support by resolution the protest which was being organised against this action of the Employers' Association.
The delegates unanim,ously endorsed the reso" lution.

div.head: Working-class Representation.
div.p: Working-class Representation.

4 For many months the ' Council have consid• ered the question of direct ParliamentarY Labour representation, and while action has been taken with regard to municipal elections, the larger subject seemed to be beyond the range of the members. However, the leaders have now come to the conclusion that the tiine for such consideration is ride, and the execiitive,, with the Object of securing the association e' political bodies, who have the Labour repre- sentation in view, placed the following resolt!i tion -before- the delegates: "That this Ceunci iircite the affiliation of the Independent Labour party and the British Socialist party with a view of pressing forward working-class reP sentation; also that a conference of all trade union branches be called to 'consider the advis" ability of putting forward a candidate at the next General Election."

A .wide discussion ranged round .the idea of introducing politics into the Council's PrOn- ganda work, and it was eventually decided to submit the resolution to all the trade unions affiliated with the Council. Scarcity of Houses.

The SECRETARY' said that for three years the property owners•had set themselves against the idea of erecting more houses. He was of the opinion that while the workers had been con- sidering the question of hours and wages they had left the landlord all alone in the field, viLith7, tsilu)aieenllreevfgnae selves reob:nuirUneaslyits:oai ftsniegtle.a:uoteiibhntehegane. we hfikatwdsN remits,atoihs le y.cault)srloite secured, rithroughnnkion.. ide, workers) fast)iheeL suti-re„: could not be secured anywhere, and the ques- tion of removing the slums seemed as far off as ever. Liverpool had a good type of building that might be copied; and lie thought the time had now come for the workers to make a move,; and he was confident in saying that the lanhl could be got and the money secured to buik. dwellings suitable for the comfort of the wor f ing classes. He was sure the only way out o the difficulty at the present was by appealing to the municipal authorities', and he moved the following resolution: "That this Council, rep- resenting the organised workers of the town, calls the attention of the Warrington Town Council to the growing demand for workmen's dwellings, and the lack of supply of the same- We are of the opinion that the Council should erect these dwellings at a reasonable rent, and that such accommodation should be provided with the least possible delay." Mr. HAMBLEDON seconded, and stated that such work was within the scope of trade unionists. for it was desirable to have good dwellings, us well as other benefits, for which they were asse ciated together.

"The King's Messenger." strong effort is being made by the Parish -Church to initiate a branch of the King's Messengers, and it is expected that one. will be formed this month.

div.head: New Curate for Warrington.
div.p: New Curate for Warrington.

_ _ A ne w curate for the Parish. Church will be Airdained as deacon on Sunday, December 21st. lie is the Rev. S. G. Stanton. A re-arrangement of the large parish has been found advisable, and the Rev. S. G. Stanton will take charge cl the Rowley district, which was formerly worked by the Rector.
Improved Accommodation for Belfast
Passengers.

For some time past alterations have been in progress on the Quay at Fleetwood so as to pro- vide a platform at which trains will arrive and -depart in connection with the sailingS of the -steamers to and from Belfast. The work has new been completed, and the platform was brought into use on Monday. The improvement enables passengers to step direct from trains on hoard the steamer.

div.head: Profit from Parish Church Bazaar.
div.p: Profit from Parish Church Bazaar.

The allocation of the money derived from the .recent bazaar in connection with the Warring- ton Parish Church has been made. There was -a profit' of £262 -16 s. 6d. available for distribu- tion, and amongst the sums allotted are the following : To the Churchwardens' Repair Fund £lO7 Os. 3d.; Church Institute, ..t6O; St, 'Clement's and St. George's Missions, respec- tively, ..t.25 16s. 3d. and ',,e10; whilst an allow- ance of -.1;20 has been 'granted for using the Day Schools for Sunday use. ,

div.head: People's College Conceri..
div.p: People's College Conceri..

The annual; concert of the People's College, Warrington, has Come to be reckoned as one of the Christmastide attractions, for the clever pupils there have always a first-class, as well as novel programme to present. This year's enter- tainme4, to ,be held in the Parr Hall on the 18th December, promises to be more attractive than ever. There will be solos, -part songs, choruses, and other up-to-date attractions by the pupils. It is an event which should on no accbunt be missed.

div.head: Sunday School Worker Honoured.
div.p: Sunday School Worker Honoured.

An interest ing presentation todk 'place at the Methodist Free Church School; Buckley-street, cui Sunday. Mr. H. Woolley, who is leaving Warrington, to take up a better situation in Dumfries, Scotland, was the recipient of a hand- some writing desk; given by his fellow workers, as a token of esteem for his past services in con- nection with the Sunday School and Band of :Rope. Messrs. J. Urmston, W. Shaw and A. Taylor spoke highly of the work accomplished by Mr. Woolley in the past, and how sorry all were to lose him. Mr. Woolley feelingly acknowledged the gift. :
Letter from Queen Alexandra. Mr. Arthur James Thorp, 160, Manchester-

road, whose father was rector of Ryme Intrin- eca, Dorset, on the nomination of the late King Edward, recently -wrote by request some verses on the. new children's ward for Yeatman Hos- pital, herborne, in aid ,of the funds; and, hav- ing sent a copy of them to Queen Alexandra; he received the following acknowledgment : "Sandringham, Norfolk. Dear sir,—l am com- manded by Queen Alexandra to thank you most sincerely for the copy of your touching 'verses, which you have been so good as to send for her .1111ajesty's acceptance.--I remain, yours faith- fully, Charlotte Knollys."

div.head: Citizens' Temperance Len ue.
div.p: Citizens' Temperance Len ue.

The Executive Committee of the Warrington Citizens' Temperance League held a meeting on Wednesday. Mr. T. Dale presided over a repre- sentative attendance. Mr. J. Simpson was elected representative to the Manchester and Salford Temperalnce. -Union.. The following resolution's- were adopted: (1) "That we record our appreciation of Councillor James Shaw's vote at the eilection of Aldermen on the 10th of November, 1913, he being the only councillor who did not. vote .for any person known to.; be directly connected with the alcoholic liquor traffic, to be either elected or re-elected an alderman." (2) "That this Executive Commit- tee of the W. C. T. League views with apprehen- sion the amount of drunkenness on the. streets of Warrington, specially among young .I,cop:e, and in view of the danger to citizenship r. spect- fully urges the Watch Committee to instruct the police to exercise increased vigilance 1-t: to the public-houses where such intoxicants are obtained."

Ormandy and Smoke Abatement. • - Dr. grmandy writes: ." I am really glad to know that you are taking active steps to make the public acquainted with the great and un- necessary evils arising from the smoke nuisance. I think that. the Warrington papers and the Warrington Smoke Abatement Society should urge .in season and out of season, the necessity for smoke inspectors coming. under the Alkalies Act. So long as the inspectors are appointed by local committees, and so long as their cases are heard before benches consisting largely of local • manufacturers, nothing will be done. War- rington should urge on .the Central Smoke Abatement Committee of Westminster the necessity for action in this direction, as only by this means .can anything be 'achieved. In larg, Places like Manchester the law can be enforced, because no 'individual or firm have sufficient weight to influence matters considerably, but in smaller towns the position is quite otherwise. Moreover, in Manchester these cases are tried before a Stipendiary, and not a local Bench."

div.head: Woman Suffrage.
div.p: Woman Suffrage.

- On Monday a meeting of the Warrington _Branch of the National Union of Women's Suf- frage SocietieS was held atAtkinson's Cafe. The members were entertained to tea by the Presi- dent (Mrs. Jas. Fain!lough), and Miss 'Crosfield and Miss Jessie Beavan, of Liverpool, addressed the meeting. 'Another • meeting was held at Atkinson's Cafe on Tuesday at -8 p.m. The .chair was taken by Miss Wilkinson, and Mr. J. S. Broome gave an address on "Women and Higher Education." An interesting discussion followed. .

Mrs. Malcolm, who has just been elected the .civic head of the Burgh of Dollar, was elected to a seat, On the Dollar Town Council six years ago, the first lady to enter this branch o public work in Scotland. The first lady Provo st is an ardent champion of the woman's forward move- ment, but not of the militant type. She is strongly convinced that where women are con- cerned, there should not be taxation without representation; but she hopes that if women do get the vote it will come in a. constitutional way.

div.head: AVarrilltj ton Rand of Hope Union.
div.p: AVarrilltj ton Rand of Hope Union.

The new branch of the Temperance Guild, for members over 14 years of age held its first-re- union in Cairo-street Schoolroom the other .evening, when about 80 members were present. In the 'absence of Mrs. Dodds, the president, through indisposition, Mr. T. D. Leslie took the .chair, and gave ~an address, in which he ap- pealed to all the young people to be in earnest in fighting the evil of intemperance. The whole .-audience afterwards repeated the pledge in unison: - Mr. F. Gandy gave an encouraging • report of the Guild membership and appealed to those present to get others to join. Miss Duck- worth delighted .the aUdience by singing two solos, and a pianoforte solo was exceedingly well played by Master J. Mills. .During, the evening Mr. T. Dale,, on behalf - of the Executive Com- mittee, presented Mr. Harry 'Woolley with a beautiful writing bureau, with suitable inscrip- tion, in recognition of his services to, the Union us assistant secretary for many years. Mr. 'Woolley has now left the town, and, in conse- quence, resigned his position as assistant secre- tary. Mr. Woolley, in 'acknowledging receipt of the gift, thanked the Union for the most useful article, which would, he trusted, be used for - many years in helping on temperance work Wherever he might be situated. Refreshments were provided by ladies of the committee, and afterFards games were indulged in most heartily. Mr. T. Tanner acted as accompanist to the musical itenis.
KrratEN RANGES, FIRE GRATES, TlLES.—Large 'Rtock, reasonable prices.—J. S. GARLAND. 11-911- 'Monger, 51 to 55, Bridge-street, Warrington.
Fever Abating.
The scarlet fever epidemic in Warrington is slightly abating. Eight eases were reported last week, and there were 53 in hospital.
Telephone Manager Dead.
Mr. John Lemon, who was telephone manager in Warrington prior to going to Blackburn, died in a nursing home at Preston on Thursday.
The Late Mr. Edwin Woods.
The Mayor, at Tuesday's meeting of the Town Council, moved a vote of condolence with the widow and family of the late Mr. Edwin Woods.

div.head: Male Births Equal Female.
div.p: Male Births Equal Female.
Eighteen males and eighteen females were born in Warrington last week, giving a birth- rate of 26, compared with 28.4 in the same week last year.

div.head: Convalescent Council Members.
div.p: Convalescent Council Members.
The Mayor, at the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday, expressed his sympathy with Alder- man Pierpoint and Councillor Birtles on their illness and pleasure at their recovery.

div.head: New Curate for St. Paul's.
div.p: New Curate for St. Paul's.
The Rev. Edward Down]] am, 8.A., at present in charge of St. Mary's, Lowton, has accepted the curaey of St. Paul's Warrington, and will commence his work early in January.

div.head: Territorials Dine.
div.p: Territorials Dine.
"D " Company of the Territorials held a supper and smoking concert on Saturday. Cap- tain Roberts presided. There was a• good gathering of officers and men, and they enjoyed the programme.

Warrington Photogi•aphic Society. At Tuesday's meeting the lanternists showed the slides, numbering 100, circulated on tour by "Photography and Focus," selected from the prize-winners and the runners-up in the 1913 annual competition.

AVhist, Drive at the Town Hall. The annual whisbdrive of, the Municipal Offi- cers' Guild was held last night at the Town Hall. About 135 were present, and a most enjoyable evening was spent. The arrange- ments were in the hands of Mr. A. E. Rains- worth.

div.head: Latchford Baptist Choir.
div.p: Latchford Baptist Choir.

At the choir supper an interesting presenta- tion was made to two members—Mr. J. R. Con- way and Mrs. Conway late Miss Eva Grounds), who, have recently been married. The present consisted of a set of carvers and other cutlery. The presentation was made by Mr. I. Wilkinson.

div.p: International Peace.

_ The meeting of the Wycliffe Church Y.P. S. on Thursday night, the Rev. T. T. James in the chair, was devoted to a paper by Mr. H. Eccles on "International Peace'. The spealc.er asked if it was possible or desirable. having been discussed, the subject was put to the vote, with a result of 33 affirmative and three negative,
