div.head: Beautiful Christmas Present.
div.p: A Beautiful Christmas Present.

"The Seven Cries from the Cross" is the title of anew book 'published by the Rev. 11 lorgan, l'adgate, author of " Christ at the and "The Calls of God." It is tastefully bound,. and the price is one shilling net. It consists of devout meditations on the wonderful and memorable words of. Jesus during His Cruci- fixion. . Copies'. may be obtajw.d. on application to the Rev. W. A. Beckett, Bewsey, Manse, or W. H. Smith's Book Shop. - Sankey-street, or Smith's BooksWl in Central Railway Station.

div.head: "Nlaking Good Citizens."
div.p: "Nlaking Good Citizens."

Some 509 members of the combined Boys' Brigade united in a march round the town on Thursday night, after being dispatched from Warrington's Town Hall with the good-will and best wishes of the Mayor. The event was the first combined parade and was under the com- mand of Lieutenant-Colonel F. M. Appleton. Life was added to the-spectacle by the introduc- tion of torchlights and the colours of the C.L.B. and Boy Scouts. The Mayor hoped the lessons they learned in the Brigades would help to make them better citizens.

div.head: Lifeboat InWttition.
div.p: The Lifeboat InWttition.

Two plays, entitled "The Peacemaker" and "Why .Cupid Came to Earl's Court," will be presented in the Parish Room, Latchford, on Thursday, December 18th, in aid of the funds of the Royal National Lifeboat Institution. The characters will be taken by Mrs. James Fairclough, the Misses Gladys Adams, Broad- bent, S. Broadbent, M. BrOadbent, and Messrs. Brian Dickson, C. H. Clarke, W. B. Forshaw, 'Montague Preston, and Withers. The plan of the reserved seats may be seen at "The Hollies," Latchford.

Merry Time for the Youngsters. The annual social in connection with the "Admiral Nelson" Lodge, took place on Tuesday evening and proved successful. Songs, &c., were given by the folloW'ing : The Misses Rigby, Jenks, Cross and Walker, and Messrs. R 4 Lightfoot, J. B. Poole, W. Webster, H. Hare, and W. Dennett. A fine exhibition of dancing Was also given by Master Partridge. Mrs. H. .Webster, Mrs. H. Taylor and Mr. Pemberton were the accompanists, whilst Messrs. William Webster, W. Holbrook and W. Bennett 'acted as M.C.'s.

div.head: arrington Philomathic Society.
div.p: arrington Philomathic Society.

At a meeting of the above society, held at the Old Academy on Wednesday evening, the Rev. Dr. Mellor, supplementing the subject of a debate which took place amongst the members some six weeks ago, propounded "Suggestions Towards the Industrial Reorganisation of Society." He endeavoured to show how the worker. could be made master of his work. The way towards doing this was to put industry itself /on a democratic basis, and to reintroduce the conception Of fellowship which once had a place in industrial life.

div.head: Ambulance Ladies at Whist.
div.p: Ambulance Ladies at Whist.

The Ladies' Division of the St. 'John Ambu- lance Association held a whist drive at Atkin- son's Cafe on Thursday. The Mayor and Mayoress attended. The Mayoress presented the: Certificates and medallions gained at a re- cent examination, and also the whist prizes. The winners were :!-T-Certilicates : Misses Ban- ning, 3egg and Burgess, Mrs. Baskerville, Mrs. Gaskell, Mips Kirkhan, Mrs.' Molyneux, and Miss Williams. Medallions: Mesdames Alcock,. Wailhurst, Fisher' and Cook. Another interest- ing presentation was that to Mr. fl. T. Williams, who received an Oak occasional table in appre- ciation . of his services as :practical instructor. The winners of the whist prizes were: Ladies, Mrs. Fisher and Mrs. Gaskell; gentlemen, Mr. Cartwright and Mr. Molynenx.

div.head: Ambulance Men at Supper.
div.p: Ambulance Men at Supper.

The Crosfield Division of the St. John' Ambu- lance Brigade held a hotpot supper on Wednes- day night in the Central Hotel. First Officer Cawley presided. The toast of " Crosfield Divi- sion" was proposed by Sergt. Newns, who im- pressed upon the men the necessity of sticking together, and then they would have a division of the best kind. If they were not wanted for national help they would still be ready to help their fellow men, who were unable to help them- selves. They had now a membership of 42, which was very creditable. The following were the artistes: Sergt. J. E. Newns, Corpl, J. 0. Robert, Privates F. R. Wallington, H. Cook, A. Webb, E. Newns, and Assistant Scoutmaster T. Y.,Young. Private W. Pacey accompanied.
Stockton Heath Sale: Proceeds.
The proceeds of the two days' sale of work at the Wesleyan Church, StocktoF Heath, amounted to £67.
A Hockey Ball.
The annual ball of the Stockton Heath Hockey Club was held at the Parr Hall last night. The Mayor and Mayoress were present.
Property Sale.

Messrs. John Mainwaring and Co., auction- eers, report the sale by private treaty of the freehold house, "Latchford Lodge," Latchford, offered at their recent sale. The purchaser is the tenant, Mr. Robert Lowe.

An inspection of the " D " Company of the Free Church Boys' Brigade was held last night in the Thewlis-street Mission, when Councillor Roberts presented the company with drums and bug:es. He, with Captain Crosfield, afterwards inspected the boys and offered to furthei help them when occasion required. Colonel Grounds was in command.

div.head: Swan Sale Rooms.
div.p: The Swan Sale Rooms.

• In connection with the closing of the above rooms, Mr. and Mrs. R. Lowe gave a tea and Social evening to the local auctioneers and brokers and a few of their friends at their resi- dence, Latchford Lodge, Latchford, on Tuesday .evening. After tea Mr. F. Hickman and Mr. George Ashton proposed the health of their host and hostess, and success to the new Market Gate Sale Rooms. Mrs. Gandy, in supporting, on behalf of the brokers of the town, expressed a hope that their relationship would continue to be of the best. They wished Mr. Lowe success in his new sale rooms at Market Gate. The evening was spent in an enjoyable and varied manner, Mr. Hickman ably taking the musical portion. The whist drive was won by Mrs. Arthur Hill, Mrs. Hill, sen., 'being seconth Mr. Abraham Shaw and Mr. John Chandler were the successful gentlemen; The billiard handi- Cap was Won by Mr. Joseph Matthews.

div.head: Christmas Day Trams.
div.p: Christmas Day Trams.

The Tramway Committee decided that the trams should ,run, on Christmas Day, but in an outburst :.of seasonable generosity the Town Council on Tuesday evening 'decided • that the Tramway Committee .should reconsider the pro- posal with the View of giving the tramway em- ployes a holiday on the one festival day iii the year.—The Deputy Mayor, Dr. Joseph, said that the committee had declined a petition from the tramcar drivers to discontinue the car service on Christmas Day. The committee did not de- cide against the petition On any mercenary grounds, but, simply, because they thought the discontinuance of the car service would be against the. public convenience.—Councillor Broadhurst 'moved the matter back, and this was carried.—lnquiries last evening showed that no definite decision had been come to by the committee.

div.head: LARGE GATHERING.
div.p: A LARGE GATHERING.
Over 800 Citizens Attend at the
Town Hall.

The Town Hall was transformed on Thursday afternoon from a place of almost cold, classic dignity into a bower of beauty. Flowers and plants constituted the background, and the varied raiment worn by the ladies completed the colour effect of the moving picture.

The occasion was the first "At Home" of the new Mayor and Mayoress, Councillor and Mrs. P. Peacock, and the gathering proved one of the most brilliant spectacles ever seen in the. old mansion house since it became public property, and none in the days of its lordly occupant could have been more pretty or more attractive. The guests, who numbered over 800, were received in the Council Chamber by the Mayor and Mayoress, who were supported by the Town Cleik (Mr. J. L. Whittle). A touch of the official element was added to the scene by the presence of the mace and sword, with the re- spective bearers of these emblems of civic dignity in close attendance. During the reception and afterwards Mr. R. IL Pearson's Band discoursed selections, and variety was added by a well-executed violin solo by Mr. Pearson, and a pianoforte solo, cleverly played by Miss Jones. The guest A were also supplied with refreshments, and all spent a pleasant afternoon.
The decorations in the Town Hall were from

the conservatories in the Park, and the scheme was tastefully executed by Mr. R. Whitfield. Mr. and Mrs. Mitchell were responsible for the catering, which proved dainty and highly appreciated by the visitors. •

div.head: Sir Geo. Tonlmin, M.P., and Ulster's Threat of the Sword.
div.p: Sir Geo. Tonlmin, M.P., and Ulster's Threat of the Sword.
MR. ARTHUR CROSFIELD AND CONSCRIPTION.

Another successful meeting was held under the auspices of the Junior Liberal Associatiott in the Co-operative Hall on Tuesday evening. Sir George Toulmin, M.P. for Bury, and Mr. A. H. Crosfield were the principal speakers, whilst Mr. Henry Bradburn presided. There were also on the platform Mrs. Crosfield, Miss Crosfield, Mr. E. G. Hughes, Mr. George Toui- min, Mr. E. A. Sanders, Mr. E. Lloyd Jones, and others. Miss Gertrude Hall, of Bolton, was the vocalist, and she pleased the audience immensely with her well-rendered songs, espe- cially with her finished rendition of "Home, sweet home." She is a singer of exceptional ability, her voice being rich in tone, and well modulated.

IMPORTANCE OF THE LAND PROBLEM. The CHAIRMAN said there should not be any monopoly of land in the country. (Applause.) He believed the land was common heritage, as much as common fresh air .and sunshine. It was not possible for' any one person to mono- polise fresh air and sunshine. They were en- titled to those things and also to their little corner of land. Everything depended on solv- ing the question of the land, unemploYrnent, bad housing and over-crowding---(hear, hear)— and they must .get that question settled at the earliest opportunity: (Applause.) •
S!P, GEORGE TOULMIN'S souNo ADVICE. To Maintain the King's Peace.
Sir GEoanE TonLmin dealt with the many clues-
tions at issue in a pointed and lucid manner, and at the outset referred to the Ulster ques-

tion. He said that within the last month or so Lord Derby had said two things for which he would be honoured. (Hear, hear. ) One was that he had put his foot down on that mis- chievous and disloyal attempt to drag the King's name into the Ulster question. The other was , what he said the previous day—" The Army does whit it is told." (Applause.) There were some very mischievous views expressed and mischievous speeches being made in regard to matters which ought to be fundamental— beyond and above party—and one was that the King's peace should be the duty of all of them to maintain. They must all help to maintain that and fight out their political battles as they

liked. Let them be turned out at the nlaxt election, if they had done wrong, by votes, but do not let them have specimens they had had of endeavouring to influence policy by threats. That no Englishman could tolerate. They dare not give in to the sword, or the threat of the sword, for if they did they would be the ser- vants of the sword, and that they would not be. (Cheers.) They would take the voice of their fellows and accept the vote—especially when they had "one man one vbte"—(applause)— but not threats. He thought that the least one said, about -Ulster the better. They should thus givel a better chance to those who were endeav- oUring to secure the best settlement and better conditions all round. That Would be better than the violent talk they had been having.
A Voice: :` They, will all be getting their lodg--

ings down here.") "I hope," added Sir\Georie, "that won't come about." (Applause.) Let them give a common-sense and reasonable chance and let the House of Commons have the opportunity of hearing the different- plans anyone- had to bring forward. That was the place for questions to be settled, but in the meantime let them wait in patiefee, trusting to our wise and calm and strong Prime Minister. (Ap- plause.)

Attackihg the Bases of Society. There were some who would change the whole bases of society. (Hear, hear.) It was a big job, and not a job for one generation, never mind one Parliament. Our life was so complex and hung one point on another. They ought not to wait until women asked for the vote;
they ought to ask them to take it, and show their intuition and enlightenment in those things which counted for the moral health of a community. _ _

After giving many details of the wretched con- ditions of the people, and expounding on the various beneficial measures of the Liberal party, Sir George agreed that the land question should be tackled, for it was through that that better conditions would come. It was to that, and MA vested interest, to -:which the Liberal Party must give heed. (Applause.)

TO RECTIFY A SAD MISTAKE. Mr. GEORGE TOULMIN, proposing a vote of thanks to Sir George Toulmin, said they in- tended to rectify the mistake made at the last election, when the next election came, by send- ing Mr. Crosfield to the House of Commons. (Loud cheers.)
The vote was carried by acclamation, and ,Sir GEORGE Tot:"aux replied.
WHAT OF THE SHOOTING?
Mr. C. E. PARKER said it was difficult for either

friends or opponents to make out What the Ulster people were going to shoot, and when they were going to shoot. Would they shoot when the Home Rule Bill goes through next year, or when rejected by the Lords, or when, it having become law, they were asked to elect their Mem- bers. of Parliament? (Laughter.) '
The Liberal Phalanx Against Compulsory Military Service.
of it all was realised only when he was gone. He congratulated the Chancellor that he could

in • his own 'lifetime see some of the fine •results of his work; and in speaking to Mrs. Lloyd George he took the opportunity of referring to the way in which the United States—now that the democrats were in power under their splen- did leader, President Wilson—were taking leaf after leaf out of the book of progressive modern Liberalism and Radicalism. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Whether they considered the work achieved, the work they had in hand to-day, or the work that lay before them for the future, it was work that was calculated to stir' the
patriotism and fire the enthusiasm of every Junior Liberal who • had joined the club in Horsemarket-street. .(Applause.)

div.head: MR. CROSFIfLD AND THE PROGRESS OF
div.p: MR. CROSFIfLD AND THE PROGRESS OF
HUMANITY.

Mr. CROSVIELD said he was sure it was a very pleasant custom they had in War- rington of mixing music and politics, as they had done in such an excellent manner that night. Certainly the quality of the music had been very good—(hear, hear)—and certainly the quality of the politics had been equally good. (Hear, hear.) Sir George Toulmin's speech was entirely out of the common, and they all must have been struck by the way politics were going right into the home. The reason he was late in coming to the meeting was that he had just had a very long interview with a' deputation of ladies, who had come to see him on the suffrage question, and that made his wife and himself half an hour later than they would otherwise have been. He had just got to the meeting in time to listen to the Chairman' S speech, and he was glad to say that he•agreed with him in the way he had struck the note of the wide future to which Liberalism looked forward. (Ap- plause.) Poor humanity about touched its nadir in the dark, cruel middle ages. We had been on the up grade ever since, and he liked to feel that we were now travelling a good deal faster than poor humanity had ever travelled before. (Hear, hear.) He took his hat' off to science and educa- tion, and the spread of knowledge and its wider feeling of humanity, to which we owed our pro- gress. We in England had had a share in this work of advancement, involving, as it did, a more merciful 'condition of things than the human race had ever known; certainly it was no exaggeration but the literal tenth to say that in the last seven years we had had an epoch- making period in the whole history of Great Britain. We had done something for our own people, and something in the way of example to the world at large to help on that upward movement of humanity. (Applause.)

The Fortunate Chancellor. It was only a week ago that his wife and he met the Chancellor of the Exchequer and Mrs. "Lloyd George. (Applause.) They met at an evening party in London, and had a long talk together. He took the opportunity of congratu- lating the Chancellor of the Exchequer upon having been so fortunate as to See already so much of his work bearing fruit in this world, where it was often the sad fate of a man that he spent his days and years in toil, and the fruition

div.head: Divided, Bankrupt Party.
div.p: The Divided, Bankrupt Party.

After referring to eke Tory party as a most afflicted party and a party of negation, Mr. Crosfield said the Unionists were so bankrupt in policy that they were left to-day with noth- ing except .the preposterous policy of Protection, to which Conscription had now been tacked on: (Hear, hear.)

~ He would not say much about Protection, but if they read the remarks of the President of the Liberal Association in the Parr Hall the other night they would have a pretty ,good sum- ming up of the state Of paralysis in which the Tory party found itself to-day, owing to the conflicting opposed, forces inside it own party, and owing to the irreconcilable absurdities of its Protectionist policy. He was not going into the absurdities of Protection, for he thought they had done enough in detailing the impos- sible and rotten finance, commercial fallacies and all the rest of it summed up in "Protec- tion." (Hear, hear.) He was told on good authority that if it were not for the pressure which to-day was being put on from Birming- ham the Tory party itself would chuck Protec- tion. Most Tories would like to do it, because they were so utterly Sick of the experiences they had had in the last ten years of that attempt to place taxes on food and clothing, and to intro- duce all the other paraphernalia of Protection, not forgetting the poisoning of our public life with it. (Hear, hear.) The pressure from Bir- mingham was still put on, and so, apparently, they were going to stick to it. It seemed to him rather like the whole Tory party laying itself out for suicide. (Laughter and "Hear, jhear.")

div.head: Crazy Craft of Conscription.
div.p: The Crazy Craft of Conscription.

He did not think they were going to mend the situation for themselves by tacking on this— what its advocates called compulsory service— what the Liberals called conscription—because really, did any British crew ever embark upon the turbulent' seas of politics in a crazier craft than those people who were setting out to ask the constituencies of England to return them to power in order that they might re-introduce Protection and actually land us in for this odious system of Conscription? The first objec- tion that they as Liberals raised to the pro- posal to adopt compulsory service was that we did not need it. . (Hear, hear.) Our needs in England, for the defence of our shores and the upkeep of the Empire, began with the com- mand of the sea. Our navy was in the fore- front, and that fact controlled, dictated, and really settled the whole of our policy of defence. Their opponents turned to them and asked for H' a nation in arms" to defend these shores. That was .the way it was first put, but if the navy was destroyed it did not matter how big. the "nation in arms" became or how many millions of soldiers they had. . The more they had the worse for them, because they would be the-sooner starved out.

div.head: Our Preparedness.
div.p: Our Preparedness.

Therefore, as the navy was a matter of life and death for us, he thought the Government had been justified—having first of all raised money on the lines of democratic finance—in maintaining at great sacrifice, its supremacy on the water. He thought., if we had sooner checked what had been done in that direction, we should have the less spbedily brought about that settlement by private negotiation between the Great Powers, which was bound to come; and which he ventured to say would come before very long. Next to that they had the finest striking force for oversea service at the disposal of the Empire, of any Great Power in the world, in their highly-paid, well-equipped voluntarily recruited Regular Army, and in addition to that cihey had the force of the Territorials, which- was fully equal to coping with any raid- ing that might be possible in these islands. They had heard a good deal about 70,000 men coming over here. If any attempt at all were made, well, it had been agreed—Mr. Balfour was ! the first to point this out after consultation with the Defence Committee, and Mr. Asquith and Others had since endorsed it—that no nation in its senses would think of invading Britain with fewer than 70,000 men. What the. Liberals said was that if there were 70,000 men coming over, they would present such a target to our navy that they could not possibly miss. (Hear, hear.) They were protected against an invasion of that character, and what did that -mean? It meant that the most that could be achieved was a raid of a smaller number than 70,000; and, . really, with the Territorials that we had at home and the 'stiffening of Regulars we had here always available, he submitted it was pre- posterous to say we were not capable of dealing with any raid of that character. .(Hear, hear.) Would any people'on the Continent be so mad as to attempt one? He said "mad" deliberately, for unless a raiding force like that was able to keep up its communications over the sea it was bound to be smothered out in a very short space of time; and we had always that overwhelming superiority of the fleet threatening anyone who attempted to send a force of that kind. (Ap- plause.)

Risking a Challenge to Fight for Supremacy. "Conscriptionists," proceeded Mr. Crosfield, "are all the time fairly active, just waiting their opportunity. If you listen to them you will always find they have some pretext or other, but always some, for increasing our mili- tary forces. They won't ask you to cut down the navy. No, they say we must keep our naval supremacy, but we must have a nation in arms' besides. Ladies and gentlemen, may I put this to you? We have a supreme navy and ,we have something else. We have a mercantile marine which is pretty well equal to the ship- ping of the rest of the world. I won't put it as high as that, but at any rate you have a mer- cantile marine which is the envy of the world, and which, guarded by the navy, would be capable of shipping those hundreds of thousands, or those millions, of men who, in years to come, if the conscriptionists had their way, are going ,to form our 'nation in arms.' What are _going to be the feelings of the people on the Continent who see that besides our command of the water we are able to launch at any point we chose, a force of that kind? I will tell you. If the con- scriptionists here succeed, they would play straight into the hands of the Jingoes—in Ger- many especially, and in other countries, too— who would at once say: 'Now we must haw

our navy on a level footing with Britain's, to prevent our country being invaded by this nation under arms.' What should we say? Oh, we cannot stand this competitive naval building; we must go and add another £10,000,000 a year, or ithatever it might be, to keep our supremacy at sea.' And you would speedily enough have this vicious cir2le working much more rapidly even than it has done in the course of the last decade." (Hear, hear.) Liberal Phalanx Against Conscription. He thanked them for allowing him to speak on that question of excessive militarism. He looked forward with faith to the more perma- nent preservation of the relations of peace be- tween the Great Powers of the world. (Ap- plause,) One reason for that was that -self-in-

terest was now an enormous factor making for the peace between the nations of the wowld. lie did not think we should have helped the cause of peace if we had failed to do our share in.keep- ing ourselves strong enough to preserve the in- tegrity of the Empire and our shores. (Ap- plause.) We had done it and we were not going to be driven by .any dodges into pushing our military expenditure and the developing of armaments to the exCessive point we were urged' to go. He was thankful when the Chief Whip• of the Liberal party at Manchester the other day said that the whole power of the Liberal party, with all its splendid reserve forces, Nvould be a solid phalanx to resist that attempt at con- scription. (Loud applause.) He thanked the Chairman for giving him the opportunity of dealing with that question, which was not an imaginary danger. lie noted that Lord Lans- downe had' not adopted the principle, and they could not get Mr. Balfour to commit himself to it. He, however, did not place too much faith in Tory leaders, for they had too much pliability about them. What about the rank and file of the party? They had gone to their annual conferences and passed resolutions in favour of' conscription; but they just looked across the water and saw what conscription meant to the pepple there—how like Protection it had grown. They should not trust to the promises that forced military service would only extend for 'a few weeks or months. It was quite clear that if'they got the thin end of the wedge in they would drive it further. (Hear, hear.) Let them set their faces against the thin edge in both Protection and Conscription. (Hear, hear.) They should not yet look on either as dead issues. Protection was in a bad *ay, but they would have to lop another head or two off that hydra-headed monster of monopoly before it was finished. They had scotched the reptile, but they had yet got to kill it. When they foiled Protection he would like them to make a proper job of it and knock Conscription on the head at the same time. (Loud applause.)
(Regd. Trade Mark.)

div.head: MR. CROSFIELD AND THE SUFFRAGE.
div.p: MR. CROSFIELD AND THE SUFFRAGE.

Mr. E. LLOYD JONES expressed the hope that when Mr. Crosfield had finished thinking about what ,the ladies had said to him he would de- clare on the right side. The sooner women got the vote the better, for he believed there was no more progressive force in the town than the Women's Suffrage movement. (Applause.)

div.head: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
div.p: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.

STIRRING PLAY AT THE ROYAL COURT. Sensationalism abounds in the well-known "Village Blacksmith" production, which is visiting the Royal Court Theatre this week. The character of John Strong, the blacksmith, is irreseparable from the name of Mr. Sam Livesey, whose performance is as near perfect as can be expected after his connection with the play for a number of years. Kate Strong is excellently interpreted by Miss Cassie Le Grand.

div.head: "The Pet of the Ranch."
div.p: "The Pet of the Ranch."

The visit next week of Mr. and Mrs.: Harry Lyndon's company in ".The Pet of the Ranch" is interesting, not alone for the Status of the play, but from the fact that it includes Chief Eagle Elk, who is described as the only full- blooded Sioux Indian in Britain. The play it- self is from the pen of Mrs. F. G. Kimberley, who excells as a dramatic authoress.

div.head: ‘!CHRISTMAS EVE" AT THE HIPPODROME.
div.p: ‘!CHRISTMAS EVE" AT THE HIPPODROME.
A novel method of introducing a misical turn

has been struck by Theo. J. Johnson --who brings a band in the scena "Encamped," through the instrumentality of the Colonial Boys. Mac- kinnon's Scottish Meisters provided a really acceptable turn, and the Gerbola Trio are worthy of praise. Another touch of comedy is presented by the Yorkshire Comedian, Fred Ward, whilst a pretty episode is given under the title of "Christmas Eve," in which a little girl interrupts and chats in a childlike manner with a burly burglar whilst he is in the act of "doing business."

div.head: Six Ceylons.
div.p: The Six Ceylons.

The Six Ceylons come to the Hippodrome next week with their attractive sketch "A Dream in an Opium Den." A real human sketch, "The Vagabond," will be presented by E. D. Nicholls and Company. Violas, the mysterious; ,Prof.
Norton, ; Viplet King, queen of violin- ists; the Belford Trio; with a most sensational turn, and others are also due next weet.

"THE CALL" AT THE PICTUREDROME. Visitors to this comfortable picture theatre will find in "The Call" all that appeals to the human mind. It has a well-written and excel- lently,played plot. This picture, in two parts, will attract the attention on the first three nights, whilst for the latter part of the week "The Fascination of the Dance," a dramatic story of love and, brigandage, will bc the special feature. There are matinees evety day, and the evening performances are continuous.

div.head: "CASTE AT ANDREWS'.
div.p: "CASTE AT ANDREWS'.

Andrews' Picture Palace at Bridge Foot is the Mecca of the pleasnre seeker, and for next week the attraction for the first three days is a repro- duction of Tom W. Robertson's comedy "Caste" The patrons of the latter part of the week will be treated to -.a two-part drama, "Grist to the Mill," which embodies a powerful story packed with interesting 'situations. The rest of the programme is composed of comedy, tales'ef the Wild West and dramas of good standard.

STAR FILMS AT NEW PICTURE HOUSE. An excellent programme has been arranged for the patrons of the New Picture Rouse for next week, when the two "star" films will be "A Prince of Evil" and "After Death," the first for Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, and the latter for the remainder of the week. In addition there will be pictures of travel, of, which " Catalonia", will be the pick; also • comedy will hold its own.

!` SIXTY YEARS A QUEEN." Warringtonians are-to have the opportunity of seeing the great historical film which is to por- tray the life of the late Queen Victoria. This picture, shown at Park palace next week, cost £20,000 and took 18 months to produce. There are 11,000 different 'tharacters appearing, and this entailed the making of 3,000 special dresses, and ,tB,OOO was paid in wages to the performers. To further gain the interest of the children the .management have arranged an essay competi- tion for children under 14 years of age, the first prize to be 10S. 6d.. the Second 7s. 6d., and third ss. Such a fine picture cannot help but be Of more than general interest. •

AN IRISH ROMANCE AT THEATRE ROYAL. The typical Irish romance "Kathleen Mavour- neen " is being presented this week by the Stock Company at the Theatre Royal. In the leading -role Miss Malvein establishes herself a favourite, and Mr. 11. Vousden does him- self credit as Terence O'Moore.

"Jealousy " Next Week. The Royal Stock Company are again to appear at the Scotland-road theatre next week, when they will present the romantic drama " Jealousy." It is a strong play, which should lead to packed houses.

STOCKTON HEATH
TOWNSHIP TITTLE-TATILE,
The wind blew; the hail flew! Then we met the village optimist, And he very cheerfully said:

"It's a fine day for the farmers!" After that we fairly staggered through the gale. Stockton Heath is smiling at its dear And near neighbour—Grappenhall. It is threatened with being taken Into the ancient borough of Warrington. That is, if the Lancashire County Council Can persuade Mr. John Burns To alter the ancient boundary line Between Lancashire and Cheshire. Then the centre of the Ship Canal Is proposed to form the boundary.. But the "Heathens" cannot smile long. Warrington means' soon to annex all The outside districts at a gulp. Some say honest John Burns will Never cede Stockton Heath to Warrington, Because it is in a different county. He gave the best chunk of Staffordshire To Birmingham, the latter city being Located formerly entirely in Warwickshire. What he does on a big scale he Will be ready to do on a smalL scale. Persons heavily laden with parcels were Seen about the Heath on ThurSday and yes- terday e'ens. This was a sure sign that the Sale Of Work at the Wesleyan Church MIS Ding quite a boom in trade. A very handsome surn was secured. A "Heathen" has another grievance about The swing bridge en rOule to Warrington. As he was crossing "the bridge of sighs," While Thursday's gale was al, its height, His hat was blown on to a Barge being towed beneath the bridge. He Wants now to know where he will Have to go to claim his lOst headgear. Perhaps he had better apply to the Receiver of Shipwrecks at the-Mers.ey port. His hat would be a wreck, that is certain; And it was last seen On a ship— Shipwrecked was the hat, wasn't it? If the Receiver of Shipwrecks has not GA it—well, ask the bargee.
First Snow.—The "Heathens" had their first taste of winter on Thursday. In the morning snow coated the ground. At Hill Cliffe it lay over a quarter of an inch deep.' It soon melted.

WESLEYAN WORKERS' ENTER- . PRISE.

div.head: Pretty and Successful Sale of Work.
div.p: A Pretty and Successful Sale of Work.
THE SPEECHES AND STALLHOLDEHS.

The Wesleyan Methodists of Stockton Heath launched upon a , two days' sale of work on Thursday, by means of which they intended to add to the coffers by at least .t5O, and last night they were well on the way to realise their wish. This sum is needed for the work of renovating the church and school, and then they are hop- ing to make a much-needed extension of the school premises. At the opening on Thursday the attendance pointed the way to success. The stalls were tastefully decorated with divers- coloured bunting, and, stretched across the ceil-, ing, were festoons of flags and streamers, mak- ing the school a picture of tasty decoration. The Rev. W. A. .Beckett, the superintendent of the Warrington Circuit, took the chair, and he was accompanied, on the platform by Mr. P. M. Oliver, who opened the said, and Messrs. S. Moss, F. Pendlebury, F. E: Penketh, J. Miller, and R. Miller. Mr. Beckett stated that the sale of work was being arranged for the express purpose of rais- ing funds for the decoration of the church and schoolroom. There had been no renovation since the building was erected. For the work contemplated they would have to raise .150 dur- ing the two days. If they did that at the sale it would save the trouble of getting it later on. (Laughter.) Anyhow, he trusted they would more than realise their expectations. (Ap- plause.)

div.head: Mr. P. M. Oliver's " Experience."
div.p: Mr. P. M. Oliver's " Experience."

Mr. P. M. Oliver, declaring the sale open, said he had not done much in the way of opening sales of work, and his only experience in open- ing things had been in opening ginger beer bottles. (Laughter.) That told him the best thing to do in opening anything was to open it quickly—(laughter)—and at bazaars and sales of work the fewer words said the better, because bazaars meant business. They ,v.ere there not to talk, but to raise a certain sum of money, and le hoped they would raise more than they' ex- pected. , The first bazaars were held in the East, and they were the market places of the people, and where the sellers meant business. Even to-day when an unwary Englishman went to one of these plates he ,was immediately besieged by all sorts of people, and requested to buy all sorts of things. At first, perhaps, a sovereign would be asked for an article, but eventually it would be bought for 'a shilling. (Laughter.) The bazaars had come from the East to the West, and had very Much improved in the coming. Those who spent at a bazaar always did well, because at all those he had been to they always seemed to get full value for what they paid. • At the same time they not only made a good bar- gain, hut they also helped forward a good cause. (Applause.)

Many of their chapels in Cheshire were now very old. They found them in out-of-the-way corners, little brick places, without any preten- sion at beauty. Those chapels were built in the old time when it was harder to be a Non- -conformist than it was to-day. Those places had now become beautiful with age, for they were covered with ivy, and the sentiments and memories that lingered about them added to their beauty. Yesterday- there was a good attendance for the second day's opening ceremony, when the efforts were !stimulated by the handsome sum of .t 37 which had been realised the previous day. Mrs. Penketh, a well-known lady. in Church circles, declared the sale open, and Mr. Taylor, who is equally well known, presided. Mr. Taylor said Stockton Heath was not what it once was. He remembered it 38 years ago, and then it was a small village, but they lidd since made great progress, and the Wesleyan Church had progressed with the people. Mrs. Penketh stated that if she had plenty of money .the Stockton Heath Church. • would not be begging for such a small sum. div.head: 'IRISHMEN RUN AMOK.
div.p: 'IRISHMEN RUN AMOK.
Lively Scene in a Public-house.

The tale of two Irishmen throwing pint pots about and assaulting two barmaids was related at the Stockton Heath Occasional Court on Tuesday afternoon, when John Wade and Owen Carney, . farm labourers, were charged with doing wilful damage to two pint pots, the pro- perty of Mr. Williams, licensee of'the Ship Inn, Walton Superior. Wade was further charged with assaulting Florence Hughes, a barmaid, and also with breaking Or window in the door of the inn, whilst Carney was charged with assaulting Kate Rattican, also a barmaid. The magistrates were Mr. R. C. Parr (in the chair) and Mr. C. Jackson Holmes,.

Mr. Steel, who appeared to Prosecute on behalf of "Mr. Williams, licensee of the Ship Inn, said on November 23rd, a week last Sun- day, at five minutes to ten, the two men charged were with some other Irishmen in the taproom, and Miss Rattican told them it was Closing time, and they should get ready. Wade said. "No, it is not ten o'clock; I Want another pint of beer," and he further said, "If you don't serve me I will smash your head in," and Car- ney said that he would throw the glass at her.

div.head: Police Called In.
div.p: Police Called In.

Mr. Williams went into the room and pots were broken by the accused men throwing them dawn, and later Mr. Williams went to the tele- phone, and asked the Stockton Heath police to come down to his house. Meanwhile Miss Hughes, a barmaid, went into the room, thinking she could pacify the two 'men, who were using most disgusting language. When the prisoners real- ised they were not going to get any more drink. Wade made a rush at Miss -Hughes, but missed her, and then ran at her 'a second time and hit her on the, top- of her bead. • 'She-fell, but ,a gentleman-cght her. 'lmmediately Wade had done that he rushed out of the house, and as he was going out he deliberately put his arm through the window in the door. Carney then got hold of Miss Rattican by the back of the neck and knocked her on the table, and then he too ran out, but a Mr. Warburton gave chase' and caught Wade,- who was taken back to the. public-house to await the arrival of the poliee.
Licensed Victuallers' Association Intervene.

Mr. Steel said that he was also instructed by the coraMittee of the Licensed Victuallers' Asaociation. The desire of the cOmmittee .of the astociatiou was that the members should, as far as possible, carry out the wishes of tiiit Bench, and Mr. Williams considered it his duty to bring the case and lay the facts before the Bench. The men should not be able to do these things and thew get away "scot free." He asked for a substantial penalty. The injury to Miss Hughes, said Mr. Steel; might have been very serious.
Mr. Thomas Griffiths Williams, Kate Patti- can and Florence Hughes gave corroborative evidence.

- Mr. Arthur Warburton. theatrical manager's assistant, 9, Rylands-street, Warrington. stated that he heard both the girls scream. He gave chase after the prisoners and succeeded in tak- ing Wade back, where he was detained in the taproom.;

div.head: Barmaid Sustains Concussion.
div.p: Barmaid Sustains Concussion.

Dr. Hutton was called and said that the young woman Florence Hughes was unconscious for some time. She was suffering from slight con- cussion which could have been caused by a blow, such as stated in the evidence. P.C. Worthington gave evidence of arresting the prisoner Wade, :and obtaining a warrant to arrest Carney. Wade said he only pushed the young lady. out of the way, and Carney Said he had been going to the house for five years, and had never said a wrong word to. anyoneman, woman, or child. Both admitted breaking the pots. After a brief retirement, Mr. R. C. Parr said they considered these very bad assaults. More- over publicans • had to be. protected in keeping their houses in proper order. John Wade would have to go to prison for six weeks with hard labour, and Owen Carney for one month with I hard labour.

div.head: Held Up Unnecessarily.
div.p: Held Up Unnecessarily.

Councillor Hayward said there should be dis- cretion on the part of the bridgemen. On November 21st he 'was crossing Stockton. Heath Bridge, and the car which was coming dowi: could have crossed the bridge in half a minute, but the gates were closed, and the car was hell up. It ,was two and a half minutes before a steamer came level. with the bridge, and it was quite calm that morning, so there could be no question of the wind. The Superintendent of the Warrington Tramways was also there, and they noticed that the tram was held up for seven minutes. If they had. kept the gates open another half minute the car could have got over, and then there would have been two minutes to wait before the steamer came - up.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.
LINES FROM LYMM.

Lyinm had a Mayor on Monday. . True, he was borrowed for the occasion, But he was a real, live Mayor. Knights and Primos gathered to greet him. It was a memorable gathering. The visilor was the Mayor of Warrington, Who Mlle to meet his brother "Buffs." The local 13.A.0.8.'s made a great night of it. oddfellowS are very good fellows At the ancient pine of bowling. The Lymm Oddfellows have won A challenge cup, open to the Warrington 'district And they have greatly rejoiced thereat. TWprize presentation was a great funcl,jon, And the Oddfellows proved very jolly fellows.

Bowling Oddfellows.—The Lymm. "Trafford Lodge" of the Independent Order of Oddfellows, Manchuter Unity, held a social on Saturday evening at the Fleece Hotel, to celebrate the first bowling main held- by the Lodge, and the winning of the cup and bowls presented by Sir Gilbert Greenall to the Warrington District ,Lodges. Prov. C. S. Webster, Warrington, and 'P.P.G.M. Herbert Wkitelegg responded to the respective toasts of "The Manchester Unity" and "The Trafford Lodge." Much optimism as to the success of the Order and the local Lodge ;was nxiireSsed. in the various , speeches. ,Bro. Owen Davies occupied the chair, and pleasant musical items were contributed by Mr. G. Bowen, and Bros. Boyle, Brooks, Dennett, Holt, Jolley and Whitelegg. The winners in the recent cup competition. were 1, Bros. A. Clare; 2, I. Wilson; 3, J. Hirst; 4, W. Challenor; whilst -he successful competitors in the local main were: Bros. Owen Davies, 1; A. Clare, 2: A. TwiSs, 3; and W. Daniels,' 4.

Mayor and the " Buffs."—The weekly meeting of the. Lymm Lodge of the was held at N. 743 Old Fleece Hotel on Monday. There wa's an unusual large attendance, the occasion being the visit of his WOrship the iMayor of Warring- ton (Bro. Councillor P. Peacock), accompanied by Councillor J. Chrimes, and Knights Walsh, Davies, Taylor, Miller, Smalley, J. Wolfenden, Wilkinson, Sutton, and many Warrington brethren. The Lodge was opened by Primo Burn; and afterwards transferred into the hands of Primo J. Wilcock, C.G.H. Harmony was ex- cellently rendered by Knights Davies, Wilkin- son and. Sutton, and Bro.. L. Thomason. The Knight ,Quartet Party, consisting of Messrs: Davies, Taylor, Miller and J. Wolfenden, are to be congratulated upon the splendid harmony they rendered. Primo Wilcock, on behalf of the Lodge, moved a vote of thanks to Bro. P. Peacock, which was afterwards supported by Primo Burn, and Bros. Holt and Atherton. Bro. Peacock responded in ,well-chosen words, as did Bro. Councillor J. Chrimes. At the termina- tion of the proceedings th:3 meeting was described as one of the most enjoyable held since the formation of the Lodge.

United Service.—The monthly united service of the Lyxnm Free Churches was held ,in the Wesleyan Church on Wednesday night. The Rev. Hugh Williamson, Warrington, preached to a good congregation from the words: "For the Son of -Man came not to be ministered into, 1)14 to minister, and to give His life it. ran- som' for many. He that hath seen, Me hath seen the Father." Mr. H. S. Brown officiated. at the organ.

Missionary Services.—The annual Missionary services were held at the Congregational Church on Sunday. The Rev. J. Richardson, a retired missionary, who has seen 28 years of active service in Madagascar, and six years in South 'Africa, was the preacher. At the morning ser- vice he told the children of the difficult task the missionaries had in endeavouring to get tho heathen boys and girls to learn to speak the truth. He afterwards dealt in a striking man- ner with "The objections Of Christian people to Missionary Societies." For the evening service, which was well attended, the preacher took for his subject "Travels in 'Madagascar." There was also a good attendance at the Christian Service Band meeting on Monday night, when Mr. J. D. B. Smith spoke upon "The objections of people to missionary work." The collections, which were for the London Missionary Society, amounted to £l2, including the sum of £5 col- lected by the scholars.

div.head: CHURCHMAN WANTS DISESTAB-
div.p: CHURCHMAN WANTS DISESTAB-
LISHMENT.
;unit, Pointed Facts About the Welsh Church Question.
AN ULSTER WAR BENEFICIAL.

The question of religious toleration in Wales was the theme of several addresses given to a good attendance 'at a Liberal meeting 'held at the Primitive Methodist School, Eagle Brow, Lymm, on Tuesday evening. Mr. E• Wynne Jones was to have attended, but at the last moment. this was found impossible, and Mr. J. !I. Whitworth, the new chairman of the Altrine- ham Division Liberal Association, and Mr. F. Milne, secretary of the Altrincham Liberal Association, together with Mr. R. Barker, secre- tary of the Lymm Liberal Association, came to the rescue. Mr. J. D. B. Smith presided. The Chairman said that he believed in the justice and right, not only of Welsh Disestab- lishment, but the freedom of all religion from State interference and fetterings of any kind, and he further believed that the disestablish- Went of the Church, would mean a' great Stimu- lus to that body, and in no way would injure it. (Hear, hear, and applause.)

div.head: Carried Social Standing.
div.p: Carried Social Standing.

• Mr. Milne said that belonging to a• national church carried with it a certain amount of social standing, and many people could not under- stand why the Nonconformists wanted to stay outside. _ That had arisen out of a religious toleration, which let every ,individual man or woman choose .the form of worship which wits nearest to their belief and hearts. That was fill right in the large towns, but it was more difficult to be a Free Churchman in the court- try .districts, where the leaders of their society were the squire and the parson. Let them transfer the case to, Wales. and think what it meant there, because, .after all, the claims for Wales were more pressing, more urgent, and more distinct than it was in England. In Wales they had a population in its characteristiiis and in its language entirely distinct from England; they had a people who were impulsive, eager, and. full of the idea of freedom.

Alien to Welsh Life. • This zealous nation had in the midst of them church Which .was entirely distinct from the national life of .that: people. (Hear, hear.) Why was that? It was a strange thing, but it came from the fact that the Church in Wales. though in its early days it migbt have been on the Side of the people, had gradually got divorced from the people. It was well known 4-''a-17 for many years the Bishops of that Church ',01:1d not speak the language of t.le people in Mir dioceses, the people they were appointed to a.dMinister to. No wonder Nonconformity ad glt hold of the movie. it election after f.leetion. for the last 25 years, the Welsh people had sent a majority of its members to the Trore of Commons, a.slcino• for disestablishment. They .11 ad now passed the -Bill !wire through Irouse of Commons, and it would soon be (I.nplause.) They could not disestablish a chur-h without disendowing it. and in dis- ^ndowing -Lhe Wrlsh Church every -care had 'n-san taken that all life intere4s should. not be o,eslroyed. The money that was being taken by the disendowinic was an apparently small Q.-Im. which was not going to be ,i.ven to other d.euominations. but to be used solely and simply for national purposes. (Applause.)

div.head: Churcliman's .V;Pvis.
div.p: A Churcliman's .V;Pvis.

Nrr U. 'Barker. who is a Churchman. said that in apnroaching this ,cp,est,;,,, it must be remembered that the Welsh Fstablished Church was not in anv way the national chnreh. but merely a branch_ of the Church of England in Wales. ACcordinc to ancient records there must have been a church in Wales. probably a branch of the. ancient Irish Church, previous to .the coming of An!rnstine in 597, and that 'viten lie came he already found a branch of the Irish Church in ecr.nnation of Cornwall, and i was driven back intfi 1717e(1.Vir11:11 lulls. portion cPnglish Church was not nronerlv established until the seventh century. when the 'frnown land was defined into narishes. TTe eonld not say when the Church of England established herself in Wales, but the diocese of Bangor wais said to date from about' 550 A.D. Assuming that to be :correct, it spoke well for the nationalism of the .Welsh that through the centuries they .had lent to their own peculiar methods of worship. The Church of England in Wales did not meet the spiritual needs of the people, and was it right to force upon -them 'a religion they did not want and which many of them believed to be 'sinful?

div.head: As a Churchman.
div.p: As a Churchman.

As a High, Churchman, he. was theoretically in favour Of disestablishment. He did not wish to be supported by people who did not believe in his doctrine. Then he thought Churchman had a right to control their finances and appoint their own parsons, and not leave itn the hands of Patrons who could appoint anybody they wished. Under disestabliShment they would have a right to do this. .and also revise their Praver-book, without going through the present cumbrOus formalities. The endowments to be taken away would not affect the present par- gons. who Would have a life-long interest. He thought that as a church they would stand to (-rain -enormously bY''ilisestablishment, not only in Wales. but in England. Mr. -Whitworth discoursed at length upon the Welsh Church vquestion. and concluded by re- ferring to the •satisfactory work which the Liberals in the. Lymm district were doing for their cause.

"The Noisy Brother." Mr. G. L. div.head: NURSING ASSOCIATION. Mother Most Successful Year.
div.p: THE NURSING ASSOCIATION. Mother Most Successful Year.

MORE FINANCIAL. AID WANTED. The Grappenhall Nursing Association, like many kindred bodies, finds its work greatly ham- pered by the absence of sufficient money to carry on the society's operations as they ought to be carried out, and a strong apPTal was made at the annual meeting, held .at the Hall, Grappen- hall, 'on Monday evening, for extra financial assistance. • Mr. Aylmer Frost presided, and the report of the hon. secretary showed that during the past year there had been under treatment a total number of 74 patients. The cases were com- posed of 31 medical and 43 surgical, and out of these 47 patients were cured, 20 made convales- cent, and six showed no improvement, whilst the same number died. The total number of visits paid reached 1,802. Last year the figures were 78 patients, with 1,748 visits. The report was adopted unanimously. The hon. treasurer, Mr. R. C. Parr, submitted his report, Which,, he said, did not show as good a balance sheet as last year, 'because they com- menced with .23 3s. 9d. in hand and had left off with a debit balance of .23 3s. Their expendi- ture could not have /been less, the chief items composing it were the nurse's salary .2.83 '78., and outlay involved by the National Insurance Act .21 6s. The only unsatisfactory feature was that the people who benefited most by the ser- vices of the nurse had only contributed .23 55.. 6d.

div.head: Praise for the Nurse.
div.p: Praise for the Nurse.

Mr. Aylmer Frost proposed a vote of thanks to the officers and the nurse, and referring to the committee, he said he was sure those present would agree that the committee had done their duty satisfactorily, and although the hon. treas- urer could not show them a vein/ encouraging balance sheet, he had done his best, and mGre than that they could not expect. With regard to theirs nurse, they had been running for five years, and she had done her duty well, and she deserved all the praise she got. The duty of a-nurse was a really difficult ere, for she sent into all kinds- of houses and Sa w people in all kinds of different conditions, and it was very, very difficult for anybody to get on with everybody, and he thought the nurse did it with remarkable success. From all sides he heard words of praise for not only her skill as a nurse, but for the kindness and tenderness to the patients, and he was sure the longer she stayed in the parish .the more she was Woved by all who came in -contact with her. Capt. Elgood seconded, and the resolution was adopted. More Money Wanted.

Mr. Aylmer Frost said that it was a shame that the people who beneBted by the nurse's skill only subscribed such a small amount. If they got £3 odd a year out of 1,800 visits, it did not come to very much per visit. , They knew that the poor could not pay anything, but there were some who really could. , Mr. It. C. Pair: We had a subscription card printed. Miss Appleton: Some do 'pay. Captain Elgood suggested that one or two boxes should be erected. ,
Mr. Frost: You might try that.' One lady said that if the poor people gave sixpence a year they Would never miss it. The matter was eventually left in the bands of the committee. The Office Bearers.

div.head: '1'111.: 1011 ND ‘RY LINE.
div.p: Lancashire and Cheshire Border.
NEW LINE IS SUGGESTED.

The question .of supporting or protesting •against a proposal,- to 'alter the ,boundary line of Lancashire and Cheshire was discussed at the Runcorn Board of Guardians and the Runcorn Rural District Council meetings at Duttoin on Tuesday. • Mr. Reginald Potts, Clerk to the Cheshire County Council, wrote stating that the Lanca- shire County Council intended proceeding by way of Provisional Order of the Local. Govern- ment Board to alter the boundary between the two counties by making the centre line of the Manchester Ship Canal the boundary from the easterly side of the Borough of Warrington to the north-easterly side of the parish of Carring- ton. This proposal affected the two Unions of Runcorn and Bucklow, and also the two Rural District Councils, the parishes in the Runcorn Union being Grappenhall and Thelwall, and in Bucklow those of Lymm (Urban District), Car- rington, Partington and Warburton. lie had, on behalf of the County Council, informed the Local Government Board that they strongly ob- jected to the proposal, and had submitted that any alteration hi the boundaries of the two counties should only he made as the result of a joint representation by the two County Councils, .and expressing the hope that the Board would not proceed in the Matter. The Bucklow Union were strongly protesting against the proposal, and if the Runcorn Authorities protested it would perhaps strengthen the position of the parishes affected.

Grappenhall in Danger. The Clerk said the suggestion was that the point should be near Latchford Without and Grappenhall, and extend Up to Irlam Locks. If the scheme were successful Lancashire would take up a portion of Grappenhalli and,a,smaller still quite fair portion of Thelwall, from Che- shire. They wanted half of the Ship Canal from those two points, and they would draw the rates for that area instead of Cheshire, which received them now. The County Council and the BucklOw Rural District 'Council were also opposing it. lie would advise the Guardians to oppose it also, and suggest that the parishes. of Grappenhall and Thelwall be asked to oppose. Mr. Linaker moved that they oppose the idea and act as the Clerk suggested.
Mr. AntWiss seconded:a-nd this was agreed to. Mr. Roylance asked if the parishes served would be called upon in the matter.
The Chairman: They must co-operate. • (Hear, hear.)
The Rural District Council also passpd similar resolution.

div.head: , PADGATE.
div.p: , PADGATE.
GIRL'S ALLEGATIONS.
Patitiate Builder in a Sensational Case.
.1N EXTRAORDINARY STORY.

An extraordinary case which occupied the attention of the magistrates at the Warrington County Sessions for the whole of Wednesday was brought from the Padgate district, when Rockselena Lodge, a single woman, of Ivy House, Padgate, applied for an order against James A. Houghton, married, builder, ."Grestones," Padgate. At the commencement the magistrates were Mr. W. P;Rylands (in the chair),Councillor H. Roberts, Messrs. C. E. Parker, R. C. Parr, J. Ball and G. Mather.

Mr. E. C. Burgis, Manchester, appeared for the complainant, and Mr. As Browne, Warring- ton, for the defendant. Mr. Hurgis said Houghton was a man who occupied a fairly substantial position, and, he believed, was connected with the chapel at Pad- gate. The girl Appeared to have led a virtuous and chaste life. She was 20 years of age that day, and at the time was living at home with her parents. The child was born on December 14th, 1912.

div.head: Question of Money.
div.p: A Question of Money.

She first met the defendant in February, 1912, .when he Was engaged by the landlord of the house where the girl resided to repair a window. One Morning in March .defendant went with another man to the house to do work..- The girl came downstairs, and defendant, afterwards sending the other man away on some pretext, suggested 'that they should walk through the fields. He persisted in putting his arm round her. She repelled him, and said she would tell her parents. Defendant replied, A girl of your age should know better than that." De- fendant told her he was not married. At a later date he was repairing the windows upstairs, and the offence complained of then took place. It was alleged that similar conduct took place sub- sequently. When seen by the girl's father on the morn- ing that the child was born, defendant alleged that another man was the father, but at the girl's bedside he did not deny the paternity. The complainant's father said he would accept .2200 or :.C250, and defendant • said the furniture and property were in his wife's name., •
It was alleged that Houghton had introduced a ,man named Ridings to the girl as named Russell, but it .afterwards came out, through, an interview at Houghton's house, that the name was Ridings.

div.head: Document.
div.p: A Document.

Later, Mr. Lodge was shown by the defendant a letter which purported to come from Ridings, offering to give the girl £250. He (Mr. Burgis) would call Ridings, who would say be never wrote such a letter, but that he wrote an en- tirely different 'one, in which he denied •puier- nity.- An arrangement was made that the de- fendant should take Mr. Lodge to Liverpool, and see Ridings and thaw the £250. Defendant then secured a letter from Lodge, declaring that Houghton was not the father. Houghton, it was alleged, drew this letter up, and Lodge signed it. They. went to Liverpool, and it was said that Ridings was away at Southport, but that he had got the money. A man named Roberts then came on the scene, and the defendant suggested that a document already prepared should be signed- by Lodge and handed over to Roberts. The document was to the effect that Lodge with- drew any accusations against Houghton, but Lodge refused to hand the document over Until he had got £250. Another appointment was made, but defendant failed to keep it. They had ascertained, proceeded Mr. Burgis, that defendant had seen Ridings, who declared his innocence, and pointed out in a letter to defendant that he only met the girl on May 30. The result was that the defendant was placed in the possession of an envelope frOm Ridings bear- ing the date December 14th, 1912. A letter was shown Lodge in that 'envelope purporting to be from Ridings, in which, it was alleged, Ridings offered 1250. He (Mr. Burgis) contended that defendant wrote the letter himself.

div.head: Girl Cross-examined.
div.p: Girl Cross-examined.

Having given evidence in support of counsel's statement, the girl was cross-examined by Mr. Browne. She admitted she had kept a diary, but it had been lost. She had never seen it since Padgate Walking Day last year. Mr. Browne: Did you tell Mr. Ridings there were a lot of other people with whom you had been out a
Did you tell him. about a certain Vicar in Warrington?—No.
And that he had .made propaals to you? Witness: I might have done. I have known several vicars.

Did you•tell Mr. Ridings, whilst out with him. that a certain Vicar had made proposals to you? Now, be careful. Yes, I did. Mr. Browne: Did you tell him a certain Vicar had made improper proposals to you?—No.

div.head: JVIINGS BY AN .OLD • JOURiiALIST,
div.p: JVIINGS BY AN .OLD • JOURiiALIST,

Hibernian "Volubility. Mary McLoughlin's prayer from the dock .of the -Borough Police Court, first for the Chief Constable and later for the new Mayor of War- rington, reminded me of an old trishwornan Whom I once found standing helplessly by the Post Office with a letter packet in one hand and a postage stamp in the other, exclaiming "Wirra, wirra, phwatli Oi do?" I ventured to inquire as to her trouble, and she said: "An' Shure, it's a letther Oi got Patsy's gun, the scholar that she is, to wroite to my hhoy in Ameriky, an' now phwat'll Oi do wid it at on, at on?" I affixed the stamp for her, and as I handed it back, she .began to call upon all the *saints in the calendar to guide and protect me. "An'," sh'e proceeded, "may the hivens be yer bed, an' may on the howly angels ," but by that time I was beyond earshot.. !teal Life. •

Dealing with "The problem of Education," Dr. Mellor argued that genuine education was concerned rather with the sphere of apprecia- tion, enjoyment and crbative activity than with the sphere of production,. and Mr. Paton, the High Master of the Manchester Grammar School, holds that it is the business of the truly ' educated to forego mere money-making and self-sacrificingly to add to the sum of human knowledge with the sole object of benefiting their less fortunate fellows. t have known many an ordinary working man, taking that view, accomplish a good .deal. I as person- ally acquainted with one James Needham, who recently died at Hebden Bridge. lie was a moulder employed in a local foundry, and for the latter half of his three score years or so gave his leisure, to the study of mycology, with the result that. he gained eminence in the scien- tific world as an authority on fungi. A Tod- inorden man named Nowell distinguished him- self in like manner by original botanical re- search. His learning in relation to mosses was Special and peculiar; and it was in recognition O f this that he was offered a lucrative position at Kew—which, however, he unhesitatingly de- dined, preferring, if poor in a sense, to remain Unfettered and to pursue his hobby in his native woods and fields. It would r)e easy to multiply such instances from one's own experiences.

Heraldry Gone Mad. • The reference to the "lion rampant" in the description of the decorative scheme on the occasion of the local Scots' celebration of St. Andrew's Day recalled a more elaborate but Wholly inexcusable one which I met with some Years ago. Without apology to those who will very properly disregard it, I give it •here for what the general reader may deem it worth. The abandoned writer thus misused his talents and debased his knowledge of heraldry "On a field per pale mur. and barren, a Jeru- salem .pony rampagent, braying . raucously ; springing from a dock-(en) in base, aspiring hungrily to a thistle in dexter chief,' drooping Prickly. Crest, on a wreath borne 'jauntily a Scotsman sans breeks, improperly; departing joyfully and arriving gleefully, and having for motto—' Ah I my country, my country, how I love thee from a respectable distance!' "
Dickens.

The reminder respecting Mi. Mackie's lecture on "Dickens' Land" before the Photographic Society sent me for the thousand. and first time to a postcard album which I cherish among my /host prized possessions. It is a good-sized one, and is filled to overflowing with Dickens illus- trations, the delightful accumulations of a series, Of years. Beginning with a portrait of the Master, it includes views of Gadshill ; the Bull. Inn, Rochester; Dotheboys Hall, Maidstone ; the "Leather Bottle," Cobham; Lincoln's Inn Gate- Way; the "Little Inn," Canterbury; the old Curiosity Shop, &c., and the many immortal Characters over whose joys and sorrows I laughed and wept as a youngster, and whom to-day I love as heartily and sincerely as ever.

." F.C.G." • May I supplement the eclitorial conimenda- Lion of the genial. caricaturist whose weekly -cartoon is henceforth to adorn these pages? One of the points to which prominence was given was that Sir Francis Carruthers Gould is extraordinarily successful in resisting. the temp- tation to be offensive. A few years ago an ex- hibition of his pOlitical cartoons was held, in London,- and it was' noted that those who took Most delight in his Work, who were loudest in their appreciation, and bought most freely, were themselves the victims of " F.C.C.'s" witty pen pen which; as he has himself written, etches "with vinegar, not with vitriol." That the victims should buy and treasure their own caricatures is a, fact that speaks volumes 1,9 r the chivalrous manner in which the first car- toonist Of the age wields his pbWer. Sir Fran- cis has represented himself as' a mail-clad knight returning from the wars; and on his saddle-bow he carries the head-of Mr. Cham- berla4n, in token that this is the principal spoil taken by his spear-like pen.' In yearsTast, he Was always "going for" Mr. Chamberlain, but that statesman never objected to the treatment; on the contrary, he apparently enjoyed it. Speaking once at a complimentary dinner to Sir Francis, the late Sir Henry CamPbell-Banner- man gave the following testimony : "I have the highest authority for saying that his pictures do not give' offence. Some time ago 1 was taking my humble cup of. tea on the ter- race of the House of Commons, when I heard a voice which was well known to me. I stood in somewhat strained relations at that time to the owner of the voice, so I buried myself more deeply in the 'Westminster Gazette,' which I was reading at 'the time. The owner of the voice sat down beside, nie. I still remained deeply immersed in the paper, but. .the owner of. the, voice addressed me, and I had to lower my paper and recognise the Presence of Mr. Joseph Chamberlain. He said: Are you look- ing at the pictures there—are they not good?' Yes, they are always humorous,' I answered. And always goo-natured,' Mr. Chamberlain replied. lam glad to hear you say that,' answered, because you are so often the subject of them.' 'Yes,' was the reply, 'but. I ruttier. like that, and I always say I have nothing to com- Plain of in them.'" As has been observed., elsewhere,' the first characteristic of "F.C.G.'s" work is that it. is free from offence; while his political enemies Ote innumerable and he shows them no mercy, he has not a single personal enemy.

Other Remarkable Qualities. leet me further. quote .one . who, knows. Sir , . . „ t'ra.ncis personally, as I cannot myself claim to (10, although I am, of course, proud to rank With his admirers. According to the authority Ilow cited, he is a man of the strongest political ?Pinions. He works frankly for the sake of the Liberal cause; and holds that strong convic- !ion is the first quality requiied in the car- toonist who would be successful. Another 'great characteristic of his work is the wonder- Way in which it sums up a complicated poll- .l situation so that a man can see the whole Iklea at a glance. "We in the House of Com- Inrs," Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman once !` occupy an hour in .expressing what Sir vraneis says in a few lines." The third is the Dower of its absolute simplicity. Ile always strikes at the heart of a situation. "The R"eater the simplicity, of treatment.," he de- clares, "the more quickly the eye sees the essence-meaning., The complex picture which l'equires explanatory labels and a little guide- ' book will not do for the present day. The 4ituation must be boiled down into a pictorial .tract" Yet, however simple. his methods, I4.l2wever familiar., his . material—whether 'a 'lli moos picture, a nursery fable, or a natural ,:htst'°rY note—his cartoons always have the '''orm of freshness and newness, and the Ualityof surprise. And over all his work is le gloW. of his never-failing humour.
Continued in next columne.

This large task ,was undertaken by the Ger- man Oriental Society. The ,npn in charge 'has been Dr. Robert Koldeway, who, with a small army of Arabs and a miniature railway to re- move the rubbish, has burrowed here with fine patience year in and year out. He found that Babylon is a fine illustration of the process We described last week. -Here 'there, are the ruins of not one city, but a dozen. Of course, he is 'looking for relics of the mighty' city built ,by Nebuchadnezzar, but he says in one of his reports, "Magnificent as are the relics already discovered of the second Babylonian Empire, they represent but some of the later stages in the long story of human civilisation upon this site. Though Nebuchad- nezzar's Babylon lies: buried many, feet deep beneath the ruins of subsequent dominions, it rests upon a siiccession of earlier strata, which go back not improbably to a date yet more remote. from Nebuchadnezzar's than his is from our own." ' Possibly explorers will some day get to the very bottom of the ruins. If they do they will find relics which take' us to the very dawn of. things, for Babylonia seenis to havebeen the cradle of civilisation. But many years of dig- ging must elapse before the lowest strata is reached.
