div.head: City of Temples, Gates, Mighty Walls and the Famous Hanging Gardens.
div.p: The City of Temples, Gates, Mighty Walls and the Famous Hanging Gardens.
HOW IT LOOKS AFTER 2,500 YEARS.

In our brief article on Babylonia last week we tried to explain the process by which the cities of the East had fallen into heaps and been buried, arid how city had sbeen built upon city in the course of the ages.
d•a• - This week we shall try to describe the ruins of the great old city of Babylon, and some of the surprising things which have been found

there. . Babylon is specially interesting to us because Of what we have read in the Bible. The Jewish people were taken into captivity to this great cent.re, and one of the most plaintive of their old hymns tells how, "by the waters of Babylon," they sat down and wept as they thought of the homeland. It was here that Nebuchadnezzar had his throne, and it was the scene of the events recorded in ,the Book of

Daniel. Everything that old historians told about Babylon showed how much they had been im- pressed by. its vastnegs. The Bible gives us this idea, and describes Nebuchadnezzar as say- ing with pride, "Is not this the great Babylon Which I have built to be the house of my king- dom?"

Other historians painted' such extra Ordinary word-pictures of its size and magnificence that no one could help feeling that they must be exaggerating. Strabo,• the Greek chronicler, says that the massive walls and Hanging Gardens were among the seven wonders of the world, and he gave descriptions which seem to us like pieces of wild imagination. In explan- ation of the Hanging Gardens we are told that the wife of the king had been accustomed to a hilly country, and could not endure the flat plains of Babylon, whereupon the king began to raise some miniature mountains, which rose one above the other in terraces, each decked with trees and flowers. Herodotus gives us some details of the walls and gates. He tells us that the city was built in the form of a square, each side being fourteen ; miles long. These walls are said to have had a hundred gateways, each having a massive gate made of brass, and, dotted round the walls, 250 towers for defence. However much we may have doubted these statements, or similar statements made in the Bible, it has not been in the power .of anyone to contradict them. Jeremiah, the - prophet, predicted that "Babylon shall become heaps," and his word came strangely true. It fell to ruins so completely that for many centuries no one knew for certain where it had stood. But the mounds remained, and about fourteen years ago the work of digging through them was begun.
Told For Young People.

one of. the most favoured deities of the Baby- lonian people. The gateway was built by Nebuchadnezzar;. it stood at the end of the Sacred Road,' and 'would be the gate by which the proud king would enter and leaVe the city. It is a double gateway, flanked by massive brick towers, of which we are able to give a picture. .

If the reproduction upon this page is suffi ciently clear, the reader will be able to dis- cern some decorations which adorn these enor- mous gate towers. They consist of row upon row of bulls and. dragons, represented in bril- liant enamelled bricks. Some of the figures aie flat, and others stand out in relief from the walls. It fias been reckoned that there were 495 of these figures, and they are surprisingly well preserved.

div.head: WALLS.
div.p: THE WALLS.

Near by the gateway a portion of the city wall is uncovered. This Would run round the entire city,, but only a small portion of it can be Studied. Some idea of its massiveness May be gathered from the fact that it is more than twenty-four yards thick. Whether it was ill ty- six miles long, as Herodotus said, we are not likely to know just yet. hr. Koldeway says, "Years of labour will Mill ,be required to trace the ground plan of all the palace buildings adjacent to and protecting the royal dwelling, built by, Nebuchadnezzar."
And he has been digging there for fourteen years.
Not for a generation or two shall we be likely to know the true extent of Nebuchadnezzar's Babylon. .•
THE SCENE OF BELSILIZZAR'S FEAST.

A very interesting portion of the palace is a great oblong hall, which has an alcove at one end, arranged, probably, to contain a throne. This would be the scene of the great banquets, and would present a brilliant scene when thronged by: the king's guests in their gorgeous Eastern garments. Here Belshazzar and his lords would hold their drunken orgy, while Cyrus was surrounding the city and pre- paring for its oVerthrow. Bible readers would survey these ruined walls with interest as the one upon which the hand traced the message of doom.

div.head: OLDER EMPIRES BENEATH.
div.p: OLDER EMPIRES BENEATH.
And beneath these vast relies are the remains of yet another great city built by Nabopolassar, Nebuchadnezzar's father, for, strange as it seems to us, one set of buildings were built upon

div.head: GREAT GATE OF ISHTAR.
div.p: THE GREAT GATE OF ISHTAR.
The Chief Entrance into Ancient Babylon.

div.head: UNCOVERING TIIE PALkCES.
div.p: UNCOVERING TIIE PALkCES.

Happily, when Dr. -Koldeway began his work, he hit upon some of the most important ruins. There .was a very large mound, which the natives called "The Palace." And a palace it Droved to be. Not one, but two palaces of King Nebuchadnezzar were uncovered; two temples also, one of them, a small temple of the goddess Ninnitikh, and a larger one dedicated to the god Ninib. The next important discovery was the site of the great Temple of Bel, the city god of Baby- lon. Next they uncovered the great road, called the Sacred !load 'of the City, and traced its course from, the Temple of Bel .to the Royal Palaces. .Then came another flni. discovery, 'which must have greatly delighted the .explorers. They .came. upon the gate pillars of a colossal gateway, and Dr. Koldeway found that it was the great gate ,of Ishtar, which .was the pride of old Babylon. It ought to be explained that Ishtar, was the goddess of .love and war, and

the ruins of another set. And deep. beneath are the streets and walls of -the city of the first Banylonish Empire, some of which were built 5,000 years ago and razed to the ground by the Assyrian conqueror, Sennacherib. These older remains, howeVer, are not so well preserved as the later ones, for by the raising of the bed of the River. Euphrate alluvial deposits have saturated the lower layers• and done much damage to the brick walls.

As the years go by we shall hear of fresh dis- COVeries from the plains of Babylonia., and we are giving these brief and simple descriptions in oftlei- that our young readers may be better able to appreciate and .understand the work of the explorers and the relics they are bringing to light.

It will be of interest t Bible students if I add a paragraph to say that among the in- scriptions which have been dug up the names of Abraham, Jacob and Rkseph have been read. Of course,. these are net the people we know in the Bible, but it proves "that the names were commOn at that period. We wilt copy one docu- ment to show what they are like:

div.head: JOTTINGS BY JOURNALTST—cont.
div.p: JOTTINGS BY JOURNALTST—cont.
Honorary Freeman.
As I Write I have before me an appreciative

character sketch which appeared in a-since de- funct magazine, and it is so full of good things about my subject ,that I am strongly tempted to reproduce it in extenso ; but that may not be.. The place and circumstances of " F.C.G.'s " nativity were, mentioned in last' week's note. hi the pages to which I have just alluded I read that on the 30th ‘JuIY, 1903, Sir Francis went to Barnstaple to receive the first honorary freemanship of the town that he had left as a boy to seek his ..fortune. It was "in recogni- tion," as the address put it,'" of .the signal and distinguished position attained by Mr. Gould, artist—and journalist, a native of the town, by the exercise of his, untiring energy, which has brought him to such world-wide reputation and esteem in his profession:' that the Town Coun-

cil made the presentation, in a beautiful silver casket, embellished with chasings of the build- ings designed by his father (who, as explained last week, was an architect). They spoke, on this occasion, of his 'gifts as a caricaturist, of

his fidelity, originality, and humour; and claimed that he was playing an important part in the making of history. In returning thanks, he remarked that one of the most interesting features of English life was that party politics made no difference to social amenities; and said that he had always been treated mr7ith extreme generosity by those whom he had attacked in caricature. "Englishmen," he added, "in my opinion, do not mind how hard one flits, pro- vided one hits above the belt." "Where do you get your ideas?" This is a question that is put to Sir Francis hundreds of times in the course of a year. 'Any difficulty in the. way of :finding ideas., however, has never troubled him. The only problem is to find and use ideas for cartoons which shall be so striking, simple;,

and distinct that the dullest member of the pub- lic could not fail to see what they suggest. For he is, at once a scholar, a tfaVeller, a linguist, a book-lover and litterateur, an artist with a fine taste in pictures, and a naturalist with a

deep love and knowledge of everything that flies, or swims, or crawls, or runs. "In my search for ideas on which to base cartoons," he 'once said to the writer whom I quote, "I have to cover a wide field. Mythology, fable, natural history, ancient history, and folk-lore— all these afford ideas. One may often, for the purpose of illustration, try to find harmony between the character of men, and of animals or birds. There'. are mulish men, owlish men, elephantine men, men as slow as tortoises, as swift as hares, as fond of turning tail as rab- bits. So I often put a man's head on the body of an animal, when, from my point of view, I perceive a harmony between, them for my poli- tical purpose." ".Examiner" readers will already have noticed this.
Built by Nebuchadnezzar.

div.head: CONCERNING A LAND-LEASE TO ABRAM,
div.p: CONCERNING A LAND-LEASE TO ABRAM,
THE FARMER.

To the patrician says Gimil-Marduh as fol- lows: "May Shamash and Marduh (two of their gods) give thee health! Mayest thou be well and strong! May the god who protects thee bestow favour upon thee! Concerning thy health I would make inquiry. May thy welfare before Shamash and Marduh be forever! "As for the four acres of land belonging to Sin-iddinam which thou didst direct me by letter to lease to Abram, I have leased it unto Abram. Unto thy command I shall never be neglectful."

As this latter datqs from several generations before Abram. th patriarch, it cannot refer to him, but it shows that the name was a.Baby- lonish one. A hundred years or- so before Abram the farmer's time, there-was a Jacob, and we have also the name or Joseph. So that When the- names Ja,cob and Joseph were adopted the patriarchs were not inventing new names, but choosing. some which had long been in use in the land of. Babylonia, in which Abraham was reared, and from which he went out in search of Canaan. A. M.

The World's 1 ribute of Interesting Items of News. QUAINT AND AMUSING.

A liindoo baby is named when it is twelve days old, usually by the mother. Sonietimes the father is not satisfied with the name selected by the mother, and suggests another name. In such a case two lighted candles of equal size are placed over the two names, and the name under the candle that burns the longer is given to the child.
Appendicitis in Ancient Egypt.

Presiding at a lecture given at the Camera Club on sonic researches among the ancient Egyptian tombs, Captain H. •G. Lyons, F. 11.5., late Director-General of the Egyptian Survey, said that some of the bodies in the tombs were wonderfully preserved. Not long ago in a tomb at Assouan, the body of a girl was covered, and anatomists who examined it were able to make out beyond all question, so e.Ncel- lently had the soft tissues remained, that she had suffered from appendicitis.
Comfort and Speed at Sea.

In Atlantic liners the average stateroom area per passenger has increased ,in twenty years from 17i sq, feet to 80,sq. feet, sits "Engineer- ing," and the average area of public rooms from 16 square feet to 40 square feet., and the trial speed from 22 to 26 knots. In Channel steamers equally great advance has been Made. The speed has advanced from 20.64 knots to 25.07 knots: The present-day results for Channel steamers were got with geared turbines and water-tufie boilers in the Newhaven and Dieppe steamer Paris.
A Horse's Sagacity.
Ilesponsibility for the following rests on the

"New York Tribune." A Long Island farmer turned his favourite- horse-out to pastureilast summer, first removing the animal's shoes. Then he went on a holiday himself. On his re- turn he remembered that the horse required shoeing, and was greatly surprised when .the Village 'blacksmith rang him; up and informed him that the operation had already been car- ried out. It appears that the horse had escaped from his pastures, thinking it was time for his winter shoes, and had presented himself at the black Smith's shop. •;

New Light on Siberia. Siberia has probably been tip subject. of more mis&mceptions than any other country. Through the modern novel which deals with Russian life it is pictured in the minds of most people as a land of perpetual winter, extremely barren, its only industry being mines worked by Convict labour whose unwillingness is over- come by the constant application of the knout, until eventually death gives them a happy re- lease. Siberia in reality is Russia's Canada, says a writer in the "Russian Review," and Canada, as portrayed by the novelist, is a land flowing with milk and honey, where everyone is rich and everyone is contented.

div.head: 13-Year-Old Officer.
div.p: A 13-Year-Old Officer.

Greece boasts the youngest non-commissioned Army officer .in the world. lie is only thirteen, and was a cafe waiter when hostilites broke out. As the Military authorities refused to accept. him on account of his age when he volun- teered for Service, he managed to be taken the 18th Begiment. At part in the light., athi°enbt using the rifle Of a soldier who had been killed, nbay. he took and his bravery at the battle of Saranoppros caused him to be admitted to the regimental ranks. Subsequently he was promoted, first to corporal, and then to sergeant, and was deco- rated by his Sovereign. •

div.head: Wateful Americans.
div.p: Wateful Americans.

The American people are the ineBl, wasteful on earth. They waste everything in every pos- sible way. But it is waste of food that is most striking, in comparison with the frugal habits of our Continental cousins, Says thd " Kansas City ,Journal.; *Americans not Only 'live high," as the saying goes, but they live almost riot- ously. The average man who sits down at an hotel table will' order twice as much as he can eat. He nibbles at this and that, and in the end spoils enough for a family. The American cook sends enough good food to the garbage can every day to sustain a family as large as the one she cooks for.
Lace Industry for Quebec.

- To the many flourishing industries of the Pro- vince of Quebec, Canada, it is possible that the manufacture of lace and lace-making machinery may soon be added. Two leading •British lace manufacturers, Mr. D., J. Jardine, M.P., and Mr. E. Ririline, who employ some 3,000 workers in, Nottingham, have recently paid a visit to Canada for the express purpose of ascertaining whether the time is ripe for the establishment of this industry in the Canadian Dominion. It is thought that the tariff at present in force is scarcely high enough :to Warrant such an under- taking without some Government concession, but hopes are entertained that such a conces- sion may be secured.

div.head: \ Mixed Bathing in Olden Times.
div.p: \ Mixed Bathing in Olden Times.

Mixed bathing .was a • question that caused trouble under the Roman Empire, It came in with the collapse of austere Republican man- ners, and the Emperors Hadrian and Marcus Aurelius found . it necessary, to issue orders against it. Alexander Severus also forbade the opening of." balnea mixta "in Rome. Later on we find great diversity of view. in Europe, on the matter. .In the fifteenth century Bohemian and Spanish travellers were ,astonislted at the goings on at Bruges, Malines and Brussels. The Spaniard observes that "(lie bathing together of men and women, skin-bare, is here reckohed aS innocent as is, with us, a visit to church." The public baths at Swiss Baden, where only a railing separated the sexes, scandalised Poggio Bracciolini.
Forced Marches.

Creditable as was the march of 37 miles in 12 hours made by the 19th French Infantry, in their recent mahceuvres, it is worth recording that the Ist Battalion Royal Scots last year did ' pi. miles in India in 12 hours without a man falling out. But General Craufurd's forced march with his famous Light Division to Tala- vera during the Peninsula War has, if accurate, never yet been beaten. Napier credits these splendid soldiers with having; covered over 62 English miles under the burning rays of h Span- ish sun in July, each man carrying from 501 b. to 60lb. in weight, and of the entire division only 17 stragglers were left behind. In 26 hours Craufurd reached the battlefield. The late General Sir George Colley," however, threw the gravest doubts on this. Celebrated .march.,? which. -1 put at`4o miles, not 62, and he further pointed out that the _ distance between tho places given' makes the march one of 82 milesl a still more remarkable feat.

div.head: T WORLD OF LETTERS.
div.p: T WORLD OF LETTERS.
Literary Oleanings.lChristmas. Numbers

The Story Teller, always a first-class collec- tion of reading niatter, is an especially fine Christmas number. There are " The Song of Life," by W. J. Lock; a long, complete novel, "The Guard' of Honour," by Andrew Soutar; and stories by E. P. Oppenheim, I. A. R. Wylie, Tom Gallon, Winifred Graham, Walter E. Gro- gan, Frank H. Shaw, Capt. Dallas, and Brinsley Moore. It is certainly .0. big sixpennyworth.

div.head: World.
div.p: The World.

The new vitality which has been a notable feature of ." The World" during the present year is very marked in its Christmas Double Number, which, while Maintaining the high literary reputation so long enjoyed by that

popular "Journal for Men and Women," has every appearance of prosperity and well-doing. In addition to the usual weekly features, there is a modern revue entitled "The Ideal World Exhibition," written by Mr. Philip O'Farrell ("The Super-Nut "), and illustrated by Mr. Wil- fred Hawells (" Owl "). This revue is as bright and inconsequential as every other revue. Most of the leading personages and incidents of the day. are lightly and humorously touched upon. There is a thrilling illustrated description of "Ghost Pictures." Miss, Mary MacLeod Moore, the distinguished Canadian writer, reminds .English readers what Christmas means to those .of their friends and relations who are helping to build Up the prosperity of the Dominion on the 'Western prairies. Mr. Charles- Eddy, the 'well-known playwright, contributes a delight- ful farce. There are poems grave and gay, in- cluding "Mr. Charles Coney's Christmas Eve," written by Miss Leslie Mary Oyler, and illus- trated by that delightful depictor of anima) life. Mr. Walton Corbould. "The Motor 'Bus at Eatanswill " is a Pickwickian vision of Mr. Atherton Fleming. The supplement is edited by Mr. Mostyn T. Pigott, .
Repartee. Mrs., Grover Cleveland at a tea in Va'ashington gave a neat definition of repartee. "This is a cruel world," she said, with a smile, "and repartee is merely insult in evening dress."
Of Course. "Now, Teddy," asked the teacher, "is Jerusa- lem a proper noun or a common noun?" _ "'Taint neither," came the prompt reply of Teddy. "It's an ejaculation."
'nit' Need of Votes.

"Breakfast eggs, ten for a shilling. Gentle- men's breakfast eggs, twopence each." We call this a nasty-spirited slur on the gentler sex. Why should they eat -eggs that only cost 11-sd. while their lords have twopenny eggs? Votes for women!

div.head: CHANCELLOR'S LAND CAMPAIGN.
div.p: THE CHANCELLOR'S LAND CAMPAIGN.
Mr. Bonar Law's " Ulsteria" Answered'.

Mr. Lloyd George elaborated the Governments land policy to a crowded audience at the Hollo- way Empire on Saturday afternoon. He re- ferred also to the Ulster agitation. ',The main points of his speech were : As far as Tory anxieties about Ulster are genuine satisfaction can be given: If religious equality ever falls into jeopardy the Tory party is not the quarter from which rescue will come.

I will guarantee those who are using Ulster's fears -to fight their own selfish battles hero that I'the fighting will not be all on one side. If revolution begins an Tory initiation Ulster 'is not the only question that will be settled. Mr. Bonar Law forgot how the aristocracy fared in the French Revolution for exploiting religious bigotry to prevent democratic progress.

We mean to confirm security of tenure to all leaseholders. The Land Commissioners will grant renewals of leases on terms and oriditions which they consider reasonable. Leases will not be allowed to stand in the way of public im- provements. Where renewals of leases are re- fused, tenants will get compensation from landlords for buildings or loss of good-will or trade fixtures.

For the greatest and richest country the world has ever seen to house its workers in slums is a scandal that cries out to be stopped. The children of the workers are more import- ant than those who step the social treadmill drearily but daintily from one year's end to another.
Our descendants will regard our present con- ditions with as much horror as we now contem- plate .human sacrifice.
During the last 50 years London has paid 30 millions more for land than it was worth.
Milliohs of pounds' worth of property, which does not now contribute to the rates, must pay their share.

A larger share of the burden of certain ser- vices must be borne by the State. We shall have a national survey of the national housing conditions. They talk about drilling the nation; we must drill the towns first and hay') a little more order 'in their. planning.
Pagan thraldom stifles liberty' in the villages.
We' are out to feed the hungry.

The new dispensation is on the road, when the resources of the country will be well ordered, well husbanded, fairly distributed. The children will be the wards of the State, the aged and infirm its honoured guests.

div.head: L tRKIN AND DUBLIN.
div.p: L tRKIN AND DUBLIN.

What Mr. Larkin will do in the City and County of Dublin is to establish new groupings of parties. A new bourgeoisie has arisen since Parnell's days, whose ideas are represented by Mr. Murphy and Mr. Healy rather than by Mr. Devlin—Nationalist, but timid, and anti-demo- cratic. The facts of Irish life are changing.

The priests in the 'eighties helped the agrarian upheavel—landlords were mostly Protestants— but now in Dublin, when rich and poor are at loggerheads, they adopt the Conservative atti- tude. Some of the largest men of business in Dublin are Roman Catholics, and the Church is, after all, not "out for revolution." On the other hand, there are Protestants in Dublin, Unionists—even Unionists with property—who have a warm corner in their hearts for Mr. Larkin—the anti-clerical, not the Syndicalist! Nothing is more remarkable than to find Protes- tants of "respectability," who used to denounce Nationalism as rapine and ruin, now describing -Ir. Larkin, the arch revolutionist, as an "hon- est man." Therefore, in spite of the "new en- qgptenment " of Socialism, sectarian animosity and prejudice are still important factors in the formation of Irish opinion, both Protestant and Roman. Catholic.—J. -M. Hone in the Deem- r "Contemporary Review."

div.head: GHOSTLY JOKES.
div.p: GHOSTLY JOKES.

NI. Maurice Maeterlinck, in his latest work, complains bitterly of the lack of intelligence dis- played by the disembodied. In a scathing pas- sage of " Life after Death" he points with marked disapproval to "their irritating and maniacal energy in clinging to the slightest facts, their sleepy dulness, their incomprehensi- ble indifference. and 'ignorance, and all the wretched absurdities which we have noticed more than once." We must :make haste to de-

fend those who have but limited opportunities Of speaking for themselves from this attack. Dulness is the last thing that the unseen can be accused of—indeed, many respectable people have left on record experiences which go to show the exact contrary. There is a merry jest known among those still on earth, especially the boy portion, as the Runaway Ring. This is a form of humour greatly, appreciated in the spirit world. Witness the exerience of Major Moor, of Bealings, near Woodbridge, in Suffolk. From the 2nd February to the 27th of March ne bells in his house did nothing but ring. No- body could account fdr the occurrences; and ,ie Major was so mystified by the extraordinary activity of his bell-wires that he wrote, and

thereafter published a history of the thing, which may be consulted by the curious. Another ad- mired form of practical joking results in objects altogether inappropriate being found in a per- son's bed. This also has been adopted in other worlds than ours. For instance, at Dwerry- gonelly, near Enniskillen, in 1877, there dwelt ' a respectable 'man whose house was the scene of many strokes of spirit-wit. Large 'stones were found in the bed of his daughter Maggie, a girl of twenty. The candles were constantly being stolen; and on one occasion a boot was 'taken from a locked cupboard and hidden in a loft. These happenings went on_for a consider- :able time, and then ceased as-suddenly asTthey: lad begun. The joke which .consists in remov- ing and. hiding small portable articles has always been a very popular one in the spirit- world. A certain good bourgeois of Bonneval was greatly annoyed with his invisible tomer'- , tors because,. at table, they were very apt to carry off plates and wineglasses. His goblet -would be snatched away just as he WaS about tO'drink.; and when he would apply himself to a slice of the roast the trencher- would inconti- nently vanish.

div.head: OLIVER CROMWELL'S tn.
div.p: OLIVER CROMWELL'S tn.

Stout old Oliver Cromwell died in 1658 and was buried in Henry ,the Seventh's chapel in Westminster Abbey. After the Restoration, on the first anniversary of King Charles the First's execution, in January, 1661, Cromwell's body was taken from its resting-place, drawn on a sledge ignominiously to Tyburn, and hung on a gallows. The body was afterwards buried at the fOot of ..the gallows tree, but the head was stuck on a pike and set up in Westminster Hall. What became of this head? In the Ashmolean Museum at Oxford is a skull purporting to be that of , General Cromwell. There is another in the possession of the Rev. H. B. Wilkinson, who claims that it is genuine.

At a meeting of the Royal Arch-Ecological Society of -Great Britain at Burlington House, London, in April, 191'1, an investigation was made into the authenticity of the two skulls. .lie\\eight bf opinion seemed to favour. ,the, relic owned by the clergyman, whose great- grandfather became its owner over a century ago. Tradition tells a curious story as follows: ‘n obscure actor named Samuel Russell (who was related or claimed relationship with the f_.:romwell family) one hundred years after the impalement of Croniv.,elfs head upon a pike, exhibited at a place in Clare Market, London, the identical' skull now in the possession of Mr. Wilkinson. Russell said that one night the head was blown down and fell art the feet of a sentry, who picked: it up putT it under his cloak, and carried it. home with him. He hid the relic somewhere in the—house and kept the fact' sccret. On his deathbed he informed the mem- bers of his family all about it, and they sold it to an ancestor of .Samuel Russell. After it had. been exhibited, it was bought by James Cox,l the proprietor Of a museum, and was by 'him shown to visitors in Meade Court, Bond-street, lin 1793. After the death of Cox, his niece fell heir to the skull, and she disposed of it to a Dr. Wilkinson, the great-grandfather of the present possessor. Flaxman, the sculptor;saw it, and declared that. he discovered in it all "the char- acteristics that anyone would expect to find who was familiar with the contemporary portraits of Cromwell.' The ,hair-covered head is trans- fixed by a spike on the broken end of a pole. There is a. quantity of .hair on the face. The spike protiddesiabout half an inch from the top of the cranium. The wood of the pole is old and worm-eaten.

Sir Henry HowOrth, chairman of the Archceo- logical Society, after listening attentively to. the evidence adduced by Mr. Wilkinson, pointed out ie fact that embalming was an extremely rare process in England in the seventeenth century. I i.:ertainly the body of a common malefactor would not be embalmed, and. the fact that, this was the-head of a body that had been embalmed showed that its owner must have been interred_ with peculiar honpur and afterwards treated with indignity. This would hardly have hap- pened, except in the case of Cromwell, and Sir Henry laid some .stress on the fact that at the time the head first came to light it was nbt known, as it is .at the present time, that Crom- well's body really was embalmed.—Henry flidgely in "The Theosophical Path."

div.head: GREAT COMPETITION.
div.p: THE GREAT COMPETITION.

My Dear Children,— The postmen looked tired and weary this vt.eek, and the office boy said he has been like to drop down. The cause of all is ascribed to our competition. Letters have been pouring in, and as 1 write a drawer is nearly full, and the office boy has, just sighed in with another batch, faintly exclaiming, "Still they comer I am inclined to sigh also when I look at the pile of letters that I shall have to read through, but I have one: satisfaction in thinking that if Santa Claus tries to fulfil half of your orders he will have to work. much harder than I shall. . I think also he will have to become a million- aire.. I hardly think it will be possible to announce the result next week, as there are so many letters to be considered, so the result will not be given until 20th December. Now, a final word to those who have not yet sent in: Get your letter away as quick as possible, for the competition closes with the last post to-night.
Your loving
UNCLE JACK.

div.head: AN UNEXPECTED ANSWER.
div.p: AN UNEXPECTED ANSWER.
A kindergarten teacher was recently review- ing her littie class in the instruction given the day previous. The following are 'a part of the questions and their answers„:—

Teacher: "Now, children, I told you yester- day about the various materials from 'which your dresses are made—silk, wool, and cotton. Let me see how well you remernber. Margie, where did the material come from of which your dress is made?"
Margie: "It once grew upon the back of a sheep."
Teacher: "Very good. And yours, Blanche?" Blanche: "My dress once grew upon the back of a sheep, land a part of it was spun by the silkworm."
Teacher: " Correct ! And yours, Lucy?" Lucy (with evident embarrassment) "My -dress was made out. of an old one of mamma's.'

div.head: VISIT TO A TORPEDO BOAT.
div.p: VISIT TO A TORPEDO BOAT.

Let me tell you of a visit I paid to a torpedo hoat, destroyer. The engineer first took me to the controlling platform, which is situated on the forecastle. Just in, front of the platform is a span gun which swings on a pivot. I was next shown the turbine engines, which are used to drive a lot of other machinery as well as the ship. AU along the sides of the engine-room are small engines for pumping oil to the fur-.,. naces and bearings of the engines, also water into the boilers. In a corner of.the room there was a small engine for compressing the air to tire the -torpedoes.. The electric generator which supplies the light for the ship is in a small room at the erxl of the engine-room. The engineer turned a small handle in the side of the room, and as the engine Slowed the lights went down. I was next shown a torpedo tube with a tor- pedo in it, then I was taken int-A a little steel box/on deck, and the door was shut -arid fas- tened. On the Boor was a hatch, which was also closed. The engineer said that both door and hatch must be open at the same time, or one would be very difficult to shut, as the air in the stokehole, where the hatch le'd to, was forced down in order to keep the place cool and airy. To get into the stokehole we had to climb down an iron ladder between two hot pipes. When we got to the bottom I was told that the furnaces used oil instead of coal. There were. eight .fires (two for each boiler), and in front of each there was a wheel and a small pipe leading to a large one below. One of the stokers gave the engineer a bit of red glass fastened in a frame, and then opened a little shutter in the furnace door. The engi- neer held the glass in front of my eyes and told me to look through the opening in the door.. did so, and saw a large fan of flame. I was told that had I not looked through the glass the glare of the furnace would have injured my sight.. We then went on deck, where the engi- neer said I had seen all there was to be seen; so,, after thanking him, I bade him good (lasi having. Spent an enjoyable hour.

THE EXAMINER, SATURD.NY, DECEMBER 6, 1913.
LIBERAL BOWLERS.
Mrs. A. H Crosfield Presents "Peter Peacock " Cup.
HOPE OF THE DEMOCRACY.

Anything undertaken by Warrington Liberals is done thoroughly, and whilst strong campaigns in favour of progressive principles are hignly successful, the enthusiasm is just as keen on the social and recreative side of the organisation. The bowling coMpetitions in summer are ex- ceedingly well organised, and the struggle for the handsome challenge cup given by Councillor Peter Peacock (the Mayor) is an intensely keen one. The various wards show a true sportsman- like attitude towards each other, and this makes the competitions run all the more smoothly. It is little wonder, then, that there was a large and enthusiastic gathering in the Co-operative Hall on Saturday evening, when Mrs. Crosfield presented the cup and other prizes to the suc- cessful competitors. 31r. J. Massey's success in carrying off the cup proved to be a very popular victory, for the audience cheered most lustily when he received the trophy from Mrs. Crosfield. An enjoyable tea was provided, Mrs. Osborne and willing members of the Women's Liberal Association giving valuable assistance at the tables. A very enjoyable evening was afterwLxis spent, Mr. R. H. Halford presiding." He was supported by Mr. and Mrs. A. H. Crosfield, Miss Trude Crosfield, Councillors Locker, Wilkinson, and Hawthorn, Messrs. J. Collins, W. Unsworth, A. Hoyle, J. Bailey, E. G. Hughes, S. H. Walker, E. Davies, E. A. Sanders, Mrs. Osborne, and others. The speeches were of a most Inspiring nature and the entertainment was one of the best. Mr. S. Aukland is a comedian-who is ever popular in Warrington; and on this occasion he was at his best. Mr. W. Ellison's cornet solos were well executed, and songs were also rendered by Mrs. Sanders, Mr. E. Walker, and Mr. J. Sephton. Mr. A. Trow was an able accompanist.

div.head: AN INCREASED ENTRY.
div.p: AN INCREASED ENTRY.

The CHAIRMAN said the large audience that evening showed what an excellent number of supporters they had in connection with the bowling competition, an institution of which they were proud. (Hear, hear.) It .had done good work, and they were also proud of that. (Hear, hear.) When they started the competi- tion a couple of years ago they had only a mod- erate entry. There had, however, been a great increase, and this year they had nearly 700 en- tries. (Applause.) Was the competition, he asked, attaining any particular object that made it worth while running? They were thoroughly satisfied it was doing a good work in the town by bringing the various Ward Committees to- gether, and also enabling the working men to enjoy the fresh air after their daily toil. He would like to ask the question as to whether they were giving too much attention to recrea- tion and sacrificing their intellectual powers? Were they exercising themselves beyond what they really ought to do, and neglecting to edu- cate themselves a little bit? If there were any of those present who felt that was the case, he urged them not to take quite so much interest in the game of bowls, but attend to the feeding of their minds as well as their bodies. They felt very proud of their new Mayor— (hear, hear)—Who had so kindly presented them with that handsome cup. They were only sorry he could not be with them that night. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: MR. CROSFIELD AND THE MAYOR.
div.p: MR. CROSFIELD AND THE MAYOR.

Mr. ARTHUR CROSFIELD, who was given a most hearty reception, said he was pleased to meet the stalwarts of the Progressive party in Warrington and to help to celebrate, as they had been doing for some months past, that won- derfully successful bowling competition, which was a most happy combination of recreation and work. (Hear, hear.) No one in the whole of the party knew better than he did the admir- able and altogether unselfish and devoted work which Councillor Peacock had been putting in for a long time past. No one knew better the value of that service to the Liberal and Progres- sive party in Warrington. (Applause.) If! he was not therein the body he was with them in spirit—(hear, hear)—but the Mayor had already shown strict impartiality, which all those aho knew him were sure he would show when he entered upon his high office. That, he felt sure, was the only reason why the Mayor was not with them that night. He put aside the party man_ to serve the town, not only/with real ability and energy, but with strict impartiality.. (Applause.) They could tiika care that they lost no ground during Councillor Peacock's tempo- rary absence from duties in the party. A fter that respite he would be all the more ready to put his shoulder to the wheel when he came back. (Hear, hear.)
Progress in Social Reform Gives Boundless Satisfaction.

Continuing, Mr. Crosfield said that tak;ng a general survey of the work which the party I v,l done in the past, and looking forward to that which was to come in the future, they could entertain feelings of boundless satibfaetion. (Hear, hear.) The work, he would venture to say, was such that would make men aid it omen —and they were delighted to see so many ladies there that night—willing to give their time and energy in honourable -public set vice. It was work that was covering the ,1401 e of the pcople and affecting their lives intim•itely. To-day the work was visibly raising the general standard of civilisation in old England, th 9 _foundation for the work having been very largely laid in the democratic finance which signalised the opening years of the present ministry. They had .230,000,000 a year coming in from death duties alone, and besides that there were the super tax and graduated income tax, the taxa- tion of luxuries. All that democratic finance had made it possible to go on with the work of social reform, in which they were engaged. A good deal of it might have been knocked on the head if the Prime Minister—with what the Chancellor of the Exchefiner referred to the other day as .his extraordinary sagacity, fore- sight, generalship and determination—had riot carried through that great reform-which wtyuld go down in the pages of English history as a re- form by which they, as democrats, had at last become, what they were never before, masters in their own households. (Loud cheers.) The way was clear for them and the work was going on. It wds too big a work for him to attempt to summarise that night, but he would give them one or two illustrations.

div.head: Minimum Wage.
div.p: A Minimum Wage.

It had struck him when he was in the, House of Commons, and sitting on that Committee which dealt for. the first time with the Minimum wage in sweated industries, that it was an epoch- making departure in English political history. The extension of that principle by the extension. of the Trades Boards was of the greatest signi- ficance, and now the principle, of the • mini- mum wage extended, as it was going to be ex- tended, to the agricultural labourer. - (Hear, hear.) -He had never suggested that the power- ful trade unions in England, capable of doing their own collective bargaining, should be in- terfere& with upon the' matter of 'wages by the State, and he would look upon it as a piece' of impertinence if they were interfered .with in that way. (Hear, hear.) But as regarded the very great mass of people—men and-. women worker's, not sufficiently organised, not powerful enough to do their 'own collective bargaining, and4ble to get a fair day's' wage -for fair day's work—he would rejoice to see the principle of the minimum wage extended to them. (Ap- plause.)

div.head: Slums Wiped Out.
div.p: Slums Wiped Out.

That was not the least important part of that great constructive work of social ,reform that was going on. They would see considerable ex- tension of that principle ~in the near future amongst men and women alike. They would also see man 3! more 'things which would give them cause for satisfaction. They would see the slums wiped out .and scant consideration would be shown to the slum owner. They would see healthier , conditions all round, and fairer conditions to all people, especially where the hours of labour were linfairly long. The people would also have better opportunities for taking advantage of all that modern civili- sation had to offer. When they got further ad- vanced with that great. constructive work of social reform in this ill-constructed world of ours, they might not then have'reached.the mil-

lenium. Ile did not believe they would, but he did -believe that before the Liberal party was through with all the work that lay before it, we would have gone pretty near realising a new heaven and a new earth. The task was a gigan- tic one, and it would. be carried out in the face of all the forces of selfishness and reaction. But big as the job was, he was certain they had got a skipper capable of steering the Ship of State— (cheers)—and a crew at Westminster worthy of him. They were confident that with such a captain on the bridge the great vessel would make a successful voyage and bring its precious cargo safely into port. (Applause.)

div.head: Committee's Unselfish Service.
div.p: Committee's Unselfish Service.

He must congratulate the chairman and mem- bers of that committee2who had given all that unselfish service in making the competition so great a success. It had helped them in every ward to get to such a strong political position as they were in to-day. No one knew how strong they were better than the Tories in Warrington. (Laughter and applause.) They knew that if they had a General Election to-day the Liberals would render a mighty good account of them- selves.

div.head: Party of Negation.
div.p: A Party of Negation.

As for the Tories, it would not be charitable to say too much about them. (Laughter.) They were a party of negation. They refused' the national demand of Wales for religious equality, and refused the demand of four-fifths of the Irish people, supported by a majority of the British people and an overwhelming majority of the whole Empire; for rational self-govern- ment for Ireland, although they knew that neither they the Tories), the Liberals, nor any one at Westminster—overworked as Parliament was—had the time or the knowledge to deal efficiently with the local government of Ireland. (Hear, hear.) And yet, they refused self-govern- ment- to Ireland, with all the healing blessings which self-government brought with it. The Tories said" No" to almost everything. (Laugh- ter.) When they did try a little bit of construc- tive work—(laughter)—they came out with their first great constructive plank. He did not know What to think- about Tariff Reform. He had never Seen any political "plank SO hacked about, chipped at, or with which the fool was played so Much. (Hear, hear.) The Tories must under- stand that the Liberals were out for solid work and solid progress, and that the democracy of England-,—with all those pressing problems for which they demanded, in the name of justice and humanity, attentiOn, work and settlement—had no use for it party of mere. negation. Good as the work of the Liberal party had been, they could tell the Tories there was much more to follow. (Loud applause.)

div.head: PRIZES.
div.p: THE PRIZES.

Mrs. Crosfield then presented the cup to Mr. John Massey, who, in reply, said he hoped Mr. Crosfield would win the next election as easily as he had won that cup. The other prize-win- ners were: J.. Gleave, E. Narroway, W. B. Smallwood, J. Cade, A. Littlewood, J. Wood, H. Jones, R. Marrow, W. Savage, E. Coyne, W. Hunt, G. Ball, jun., F. Berry, R. Smith, J. F. Naylor, E. Lunt, B. Green, J. Rigby, jun., J. Middleton, T. Jackson, F. Molyneaux, A. Gleave, W. Carter, B. Jolley, C. Llewellyn, E. Jones, T. Timmins, W. Corlett, F. Grey, J. Bennett, J. Cartwright, W. Allen, W. Crawford, C. Sut- cliffe, G. Clive, J. Lingard, J. Beardsall, G. Mar- shall, A. Gleave, J. Coyne, J. Shaw, J. Phenix, M. Llewellyn, R. Fog, J. Spillsbury, A. Davies, J. Timmins, J. Ashburner, W. Jones, B. War- burton, I. Mather, T. G. Gallop, W. Dutton, S. Sheldon, J. Pollard, H. Wright, 1.. Barlow, C. Millington, W. Madden, J. Broadhurst, jun., A. Molyneaux, F. Rigby, B. Webb and J. Graham.

div.head: LADIES' MAIN.
div.p: A LADIES' MAIN.

Mr. S. H. WALxER 'proposed a, hearty vote of thanks to Mr. and Mrs. Crosfield. He said they were under a great obligation to Mrs. Crostield, who had so gracefully presented the prizes. They had also had a most excellent speech from Mr. Crosfield, which was full of home truths.. (Hear, hear.) The competitions had been most successful. There had been keen rivalry, but a good spirit of true sportsmanship had prevailed through- out, and be could assure them they were anti- cipating even a t•etter season next year. He .would like to see a ladies' main organised, so that the wives and friends of members could take part in that splendid game. (Applause.)

MRS. •CROSFIELD AND SPORTSMANSHIP. Mrs. CROSFIELD, in reply, said the Chairman had asked whether bowling, competitions attained any particular object, and whether it was worth their while to pay so much atten- tion to sports. There was one thing about bowls, it taught them to aim straight. That might be a good thing, for they did not know what might be coming from Ulster. (Laughter and ap- plause.)

- She was pleased ,to,have been able to present the prizes that night, because she liked sports- men. She thought they could all be sportsmen and women in all phases of life—(hear, hear)— in politics as well as sports, and set a good ex- ample to their opponents. She welcomed the suggestion of a ladies' main, and thought it was an excellent idea. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The artistes had given them a most enjoyable evening, and they N'ere deserving of their heartiest thanks. (Applause.)

div.head: MR. ODOSFIELD SUPPORTS WOMEN'S RECREATIONS.
div.p: MR. ODOSFIELD SUPPORTS WOMEN'S RECREATIONS.

Mr. CROSFIELD said he had thought his better (Laughter.) He was pleased to see the ladies accepted that statement at once. (Laugh. ter.) He had thought his better half would have replied for both of them. He heartily supported the suggestion of a ladies' main. He was de- lighted to see that the women of England' were rapidly taking more interest than th 4 had done before in the various forms of outdoor reereittion. For those who lived in the thickly- populated towns he could think of no outdoor game more admirable and valuable than bowls. (Cheers.)

div.head: – Sir Alfred Mond's Speech.
div.p: - Sir Alfred Mond's Speech.

Referring to the mass meeting the previous night, he said if there was anyone present who had not read the extraordinarily interesting speech delivered by Sir Alfred Mond, he could assure them they would be well repaid by read- ing it in the columns of "The Examiner," the paper, Which ,was going ahead by leaps and bounds. (Applause.)

div.head: FAVOURITE FOR THE WESTMINSTER CUP FINAL.
div.p: FAVOURITE FOR THE WESTMINSTER CUP FINAL.

Councillor HAWTHORN proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman, committee, artistes and the lady helpers of the W.L.A. The cowmittee had worked hard during the season. -The ar- tistes had entertained them in a capital manner, and the ladies had rendered invaluable help at the tea. He was sure they all agreed that the .competition had had a most excellent .conclu- sion.

Mrs. OSBORNE, replying on behalf of the ladies, doubted if ever there had been a more success- ful gathering. She was strongly in favour of women bowlers, and someone might vev soon present them with a cup for the ladies.' (Hear, hear.) She knew they would 411 support Mr. Crosfield when he played in tWe final for the Westminster Cup. (Loud applause.) The proceedings closed with the singing of the National Anthem.

div.head: SMALL RED PIMPLES ON FACE.
div.p: SMALL RED PIMPLES ON FACE.

52, High-street; Eastleigh, Hants, Eng.—" It was about nine months ago when I first noticed the disease on My legs. It took the form of small red pimples, which itched and burned me awfully. 'Then they came on my arms from the wrist to the elbow, and my arms were swollen. I could not bear to wash them or touch them in any way, as they were so painful. "I read of horror on the first application it burned and brought my arms and legs into blisters. I fin- ished with that pretty smart. div.head: PIONEER OF REFORM.
div.p: PIONEER OF REFORM.
Was Robert Owen the First Socialist in Engla
FEATURES OF THE ADULT SCHOOLS.

The feature in connection with the Adult Schools during the week-end was the address given to, the Sankey Bridges Men's School by Mr. Pierce Williams on "Robert Owen, Social Reformer." He remarked upon tb.e ignorance displayed amongst social reformers of the work done by reformers at the time of the Industrial _Revolution. Robert Owen . was born of working-class par- ents in South Wales, and made his way in life by .pure merit, ability and force of character. Mr. Williams gave a rapid survey of the forces and circumstances which moulded the character of young Owen up to the age of 18, when he took his great plunge into the commercial world. At this time handwork was giving place. very rapidly to machinery., Owen was contem- porary with the development of cotton machin- ery and watched its evolution very closely. He saw the possibilities of the new machinery, and took advantage of his. knowledge and foresight by, at the age of 28, buying the mills at New Lanark for £60,000, to be paid in 20 yearly, in- stalments of £3,000. . It was at New Lanark that Owen's character as a humanist had its first chance to display its qualities. He had noticed that in the mills every attention was given,to the new expensive machines, and prac- tically none to the men, women and tiny chil- dren who worked them. He was of opinion that from a purely business point of 'view it would pay to improve the conditions of the workers. The state of affairs were dehumanising in thc extreme, children of ages from five to eight years were imported from all the poor-houses in the South Of. Scotland and made to work under cruel conditions in the Mills for 13 hours daily. Improving Social Conditions. •

Owen began to put his ideas into practice by improving the conditions inside and outside. He started schools, abolished punishment of all kinds, built better houses, introduced sanita- tion, And shorter hours. site met with much oppo- sition, but persevered, until he became famous throughout Europe for his humane conditions of labour, and thousands visited New Lanark every year. Owen's religion may -best, be de- scribed as a creedless Christianity. Without believing in any theological dogma, he applied the principles of Christ to his daily working life. He was a great believer in the forces of environment and circumstances on the mould- ing of character, and he sought that those under him and about him should have the best pos- sible influences around them. , Needless to say, after he had borne down the suspicion and pre- judice of his workers, he was almost worshipped by them.

Mr. Barnard, in introducing the Bible lesson, said that the passages read showed clearly that Paul knew quite well what powerful forces were at work to drag a man down. This made him sympathise with others and helped him to humble himself, realising his own weaknesses.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH MEN'S.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH MEN'S.

Mr. J. W. Crossley, on Sunday gave a very interesting account of "The Mae and Fall .of Furness Abbey." After giving a brief outline as to when and how the Abbey was founded, the speaker went on to say that although thc. methods employed by the monks in securing grants of land and money for the upkeep of . the monastery were sometimes not above suspicion, yet we at the present day have much to thank them for. Historical records of national and religious matters have been .carefully preserved by them, and possibly • our present system of Poor Law administration emanated from the ideas and methods employed by the monks of old. Whatever their Moral fanits may have been, we must not forget they were but human beings; we must admire them for their Chris- tian valour in an era of trouble and confusion. Our best thanks are due to-them for preserving the records of long centuries for the benefit of readers to-day. We ,must admire them for their exquisite monuments of skill and lavish ambition that they have left us not only at Furness, but in various other parts of the kingdom.

div.head: ACADEMY-STREET WOMEN'S.
div.p: ACADEMY-STREET WOMEN'S.

On Wednesday Mrs. Hill presided, and Mr. John Ellison gave an address on "Love Thy Neighbour," which was much appreciated. The usual light refreshments were partaken of. bringing to a close a very sociable and enjoyable evening.

div.head: LONGFORD SCHOOL.
div.p: LONGFORD SCHOOL.

The School was again without a lecturer, but as members had come prepared to discuss the Bible lesson for the day on "Paul the man; his humility and gentleness:" a real profitable hour was spent. The question was raised whether there was more temptation for evil in Paul's day or to-day.

div.head: BEWSEY MEN'S.
div.p: BEWSEY MEN'S.
On Sunday morning Mr. Jos. Elwell continued his series of addresses on "The History and Development of Modern Trade Unions." In tilt) afternoon a musical service was held in aid of the choir funds.

The Mayor presided, and after complimenting the choir on the manner in which they had acquitted themselves, spoke of the pleasure it gave him to renew acquaintance with the people of Bewsey, as it was the people of that district who had first elected him as their • representa- tive and .given . him. the first,etep. toward. the proud position he now occupied as Mayor of the town. He urged his hearers to always strive to do what was right and just, and to do their best in helping and uplifting those less happily placed than themselves, not to be deterred by any obstacle in 'their path, but to persevere in their work, until they had brought about a bater state of affairs, and made the world a better place than they found it. The choir, under the leadership of Mr. F. Gray, sang in an efficient manner, the anthems "Sun of my soul “. and "0 Lord, how manifold are Thy works." Miss Wright sang "The chil- dren's home,' and Mrs. F. Gray The Sanc- tuary."

div.head: YOUNG LIBERALS.
div.p: THE YOUNG LIBERALS.
Mr. P. M. Oliver and Social Reform.

The. Council of the Lancashire and Cheshire Federation of the League of Young Liberals met in the Manchester Reform Club on Saturday. • The Executive Committee, in their quarterly report, said it was thought desirable to empha- sise the position of the Federation in the van of Liberal thought, and announced that a Specia.! Committee had been appointed whose duty it would be to make suggestions upon political Matters for consideration and discussion by the representative meetings. The Federation, saic. the report, had reached an important stage in its development. Its efforts in the past had been directed in the main to the perfecting of organ. isation; the time had now come .to attempt tc translate political ideas into practical legisla tion. ' • , •
The President, Mr. 'Robert Hopwood, in mov- ing the adoption of. the report, said there werc many evidences of a revival of, political thought within the Federation.
Mr. M. E. ,Mitchell seconded the resolution whieli .*as carried.

Mr. P.,M.'Oliver moved a resolution expressing the opinion "that the principal social problems of the present time are closely connected with the inequalities of the existing land system," and recording sympathy with the Government's land policy as already outlined. Mr. T. F. Lister, of Birkenhead, seconded the resolution.

An amendment, which embodied the whole of the resolution; with the addition of an expres- sion of the hope that the Government's policy would include the taxation of land values, wa:- defeated. A second amendment was moved, which proposed to incorpopte in the resolution the words, "earnestly hope that it (the Gov- ernment's land policy) will prove to include the un-rating of improvements and the rate of the site value of undeveloped land." This amend- ment was carried.
The Manchester shoesmiths and farriers have presented a demand for an advance of 4s. 6d. a week.

div.head: LION AND THE LAMB
div.p: ThE LION AND THE LAMB
Amusing Discussion Over an Education Committee Appointment. A PATRONAGk STRUGGLE.

There was a lively discussion at the Warring- ton Town Council on Tuesday over a minute in which the Education Committee proposed to appoint a nurse. Alderman JAMES Evvrs moved that the minute be not confirmed, and he did not do so out of any spirit of antagonism to the Educa- tion Committee. All the-health work had been relegated to the Health Committee, and he thought the question of the additional nurse should have been left to the Health Committee. It was not a matter of such an urgent charac- ter as would warrant the step taken by the Education Committee. If the Education Com- mittee had co-operated with the Health Com- mittee a cheaper and more satisfactory way would have been found out of the difficulty, and there would be no friction. He moved the minute hack. -

Alderman BURTON seconded. He thought if the minute was withdrawn and give the two committees an opportunity of conferring, they would come to an amicable. understanding. The DEPUTY MAYOR, Dr. Joseph, said a confer- ence would be a very desirable way out of the difficulty. Councillor PEMBERTON : This is the thin end of the wedge to try to take the power out of the hands of the Health Committee and place it in the hands of the Education Committee. Such must be vetoed at all costs.

div.head: PATRONAGE QUESTION.
div.p: PATRONAGE QUESTION.
Councillor ROBERTS said the Health Commit- tee required the patronage of appointing all the officers, and then it finished with the job. Alderman JAMES EVANS : INTO, not at all.

, Councillor ROBERTS: Allow me to say so, and I am going to say it—the patronage ancl the administration should be in the same hands, and then there will be no friction between the Health: Committee and the Education Com. mittee. There is no friction at present. Alderman JAMES EVANS : I differ. Councillor ROBERTS: There is no friction and there never has been, because the work of the .Medical Officer has been so excellently done. I am not prepared to submit to another confer- ence after the lesson'we got at the last confer- ence. The Education Committee lamb and the Health Committee lion did lie together, but the lamb was inside the lion. (Laughter.) I cannot understand a committee like the Health Committee, with its enormous responsibilities and detailed work to do, seeking this paltry bit of patronage, and refusing it to the committee that is really the Health Committee in the interests of the child. You are holding, Alder- man Evans, an absolutely illogical position.

div.head: "SOMETHING TO GAIN."
div.p: "SOMETHING TO GAIN."
Alderman EVANS : Looking at it from your position._
- Councillor ROBEItTS : In your case you have something to_gaiii-

Alderman 11-1/ANEI : No, no. Councillor ROBERTS: I do not say yo.p person- ally, but you are struggling to maintain in your hands a piece of paltry patronage you have no right to- Alderman Evaxs : I am not struggling at all. My argument was on solvent lines, but Coun- cillor Roberts' is not.
The MAYOR,: Don't make another speech. Alderman EVANS : I'm not making another speech. (Laughter.) I'm rising on a point of order.

div.head: "THE LAST WORD."
div.p: "THE LAST WORD."

Councillor ROBERTS: It might ba_advisable for me to say there is no suggestion of any personal advantage to Alderman Evans. What I object to -is the retention of this patronage by the Health Committee. In the interests of the schools and the children you should allow the Education Committee a voice in the choice of the tools they require for their work. Alderman TINNION : I'm surprised at Council- lor Roberts-
Councillor ROBERTS I thought I was replying to close the debate?
Alderman TINNION : You thought you would have the last word, eh? (Laughter.)

, The MAYOR indicated that the debate had not been closed. Alderman TINNION recalled the conference which Councillor Roberts had graphically de- scribed as being attended by the lion and the lamb. Knowing something about the Educa- tion deputations he would not describe them as lambs. (Laughter.) The Education Com- mittee had a longing to extend their powers. He objected to their scheme, as it created a dual position. They.must have no overlapping.
Councillor ROBERTS finally withdrew the sec- tion of the minutes in respect of a suggested amicable settlement, and the rest of the minutes were adopted.

div.head: FIELD OF SPO
div.p: THE FIELD OF SPO
He Enables Warrington to Win a Tenacious Game by Two Fine Goals.
RUDDICK PROVES A CLEVER THREEQUARTER.

Clever forward work, improved half-back Ilitay, a dashing threequarter iit'lltiddick;.and a thoroughly sound back enabled Warrington to win a hard-fought game with Leeds at Wilders- Dool. Jolley was the man who did the scoring. Ills first goal was a penalty given for him being 'obstructed, and he _kicked a clever goal from /tear the • touch-line, half-Way down- the .pitch. ,lolley's second goal was one of the best he has eVer kicked, and he has lauded a few in his time. _

It was a really brilliant dropped goal. Gath- Cling the ball at mid-line, from a long return from Haycox, he ran a yard or two, and then, sayed a drop. The ball sailed true as an 4rrow between the 'uprights. These are the tYPe of goals the Spectators like to see, and no wonder they gave the clever, little back a rous- ing cheer. This, the only scoring happened in the second half, and Warrington 'won by four Points to nil. In both portions of the game we saw, a very hard tussle, in the course of which the War- lington forwards were in the ,forefront of the work. They dribbled well and wheeled the pack in a way that greatly puzzled the Leeds six. The ball was hooked out nicely and generally the home forwards were superior to the other pack, tlever though they were. Warrington now Possess a set of forwards as= good as any in the 14eague.

div.p: Ciever Forward Play.

Clare distinguished himself with his indivi- dual work. - He could run, down any of the I.,eeds men, and twice Clare experienced hard 'ines in not scoring. • Thomas and Chesters Ilsed their weight to advantage, and the. burly -Leeds forwards found- themselves up against a tone wall when they tried to upset the two warrington " strong men." Skelhorne and ranter dribbled with almost 'Association-like Drecision, and Cox had also a good -foot in this 'work. Taken all over, it would be difficult to lied a pack who Work more in unison than do tile Warrington. sextet. - All through the season the forwards' have been the mainstay of the side, but I do not think they. I,lave yet played a game to equal that', of Satur- ltaY. One heard a great deal about the Leeds orwards, who were said to be the smartest pack (4 the Northern Union League. • They were :Droved inferior to those of Warrington in the 41tatch at Wilderspool. I have no desire to ,111,Inimise the Leeds sextet, yet I must say that 'llls time they met their betters in every depart- anent of forward play.

div.p: Ruddick as a Threequarter.

div.head: " LAKELANDER'S " CRITIQUE.
div.p: " LAKELANDER'S " CRITIQUE.
Young Promising; Ruddick Great.

Although Warrington only beat the lads from Headingley by two goals to nil, it does not alter the fact that they were by far the smarter team. Saturday's game was the best I have seen our local men play for some weeks, and was a great improvement on the Whines match. However, it is not my intention to dwell on the run of the play, but merely to give my impressions of our. local players.

All eyes were centred on Young, and I must say the Abertillery man came through the ordeal with flying colours. I had the privilege of being present when he made his debut with the "A " team, and in my notes in "The Examiner" then I prophesied that he wonld not be long before he was partnering Nicholas at the base of the pack. After his display on Saturday I feel confident the Warrington Com- mittee have secured a half-back with original ideas, and one whose main idea is to keep the ball on the move. Some of the critics think that he Makes the mistake of standing too far back. One might 'say the same of Johnny Thomas, of Wigan—and where can one find a smarter half-back than he during the past few seasons? My idea is that it proves it is possible to make openings without running round the scrummage, and at the same time avoid being tackled. Considering that it was the first time he had played with Nicholas, I must congratu- late him on his display, especially towards the close of the game, when a better understanding between them was quite evident, and when some of his movements received their due recognition from the crowd.

div.head: Ruddick the Hero.
div.p: Ruddick the Hero.

The hero of the match was Ruddick:- and he fully justified his selection on the wing. He played a. great game, and it is a long time since we had such a fine exposition from a left wing. In fact, not since the days of .Jack Fish have I seen a player -send such thrills of excitement through the spectators as did Ruddick on Satur- day. Well might " Scrum " wear a ..beaming smile at the close of the game, for has he not all along maintained in his notes that Ruddick's place was in the ,threequarters? I should like to make one suggestion, however, to the com- mittee, and that is that he be,transferred on to the right wing. In my opinion; -I, think he would be able to make more use with his kicks. On one or two occasions I thought he ought to have kicked into mid-field instead of allowing himself to be pushed into touch. I may be wrong, but I think this was due to the fact that he is not able to use his left leg with the same advantage as his right. However, .he 'certainly made rings round the Leeds men, and. it .now only remains for the club to secure a smart centre to keep up with the pace of the little man from Cumberland. \

Howard Davis gave us a good idea of what he can do as regards defensive play, but he lacks speed and was altogether too slow when it- earns to attaek. Dickenson was the best of the centres and was a tower of strength in repelling the attacks of the speedy Leeds men.
Bradshaw Needs a Rest.

Bradshaw was again variable-7-good and bad in turn. What has come over the cEiptain? Do his responsibilities weigh too heavy on his shoulders? I think' the committee will be well advised to give him a week or two's rest, and then perhaps he will give us some of his old 'form. Whilst the committee,areleitm-building I suggest that Ruddick takes Bradshaw's place, and give C. Brown a trial On the left wing. This lad is very speedy and seems to know where the line is. And it, is high time we. had some tries scored! •

Jolley again excelled himself and proved what a great full-back he really is. Surely if any of the N.U. League Committee were .present on Saturday they could not overlook Jolley's claim for "down under." That dropped goal of his was one of the best I have seen at Wilderspool. The penalty goal, too, was a fine effort, and to Jolley it is that Warrington owe their victory. The forwards again did .magnificent Work, and Clare especially I pick out for special men- tion. He certainly had the, hardest lines in not scoring on at least two occiasions. Skel- home and he would make an ideal pair of forwards to go out to the Antipodes—and who knows • but what they are not already likely candidates? -

div.head: TO-DAY'S MATCH MTh SALFORD.
div.p: TO-DAY'S MATCH MTh SALFORD.
AVarrington Should Just About Win.

There should be a great game on the Salford ground today, when Warrington meet the Weaste men for the first time. Salford secured a fine 'Victory at Batley on Saturday, and this will give them zest to try and effect a similar result against Warrington at Weaste. If War- rington, however, play up to the standard shown" against Leeds they ought to about win. The Salford threequarters will take ti lot of careful watching. Salford won the corresponding match last year by 2 points to nil. Warrington Should reverse this result.

Warrington are to play the team which did so .well against Leeds on Saturday. The Sal- ford Committee have made two changes in the side that defeated Batley, but both will be at full strength. The men will turn out thus:—
WARRINGTON. ' Jolley. Bradshaw, Dickenson, Davis, Ruddick. • Nicholas, Young. Chesters, Cox, Skelhorne, Thomas, Clare, Tranter.

HONOURS FOR JOLLEY AND CHESTERS.

For the inter=county match, to be played be- tween Yorkshire and Lancashire at Huddersfield on Wednesday, two Warrington men have been selected. Jollo, Who is acknowledged to be one of the finest full-backs in the country, I will be the Lancashire defender-in-chief. Chesters' per- sistent fine form has again been recognised, and he will be in the Lancashire pack. .
WARRINGTON "A" v. SALFORD "A." Keen Match Expected at Wilderspool.

The meeting of these teams at Wilderspoof ought to produce a keen game. Warrington have to strive to maintain their position in the Combination table, and therefore the local lads may be expected to put their best foot forward. The teams will be:— Warrington "A."—J. Brown; Baker, Shaw, C. Brown and Waywell; A. Brown and Damn- teth; Fearnley, Harmer, Naylor, Ward, Critch- ley and Boardman. div.head: MR. wiNSTANLEY RETIRES FROM REFEREEING.
div.p: MR. wiNSTANLEY RETIRES FROM REFEREEING.

Mr. J. Winstanley, a member of the Warring- ton Committee, who has been acting as a Com- bination referee during the season, has decided to retire from the list of Combination referees and devote his spare time to the club manage- ment. It should,. of.,cnuFsc),be understood. that Mr. WinitanleY, whilst officiating as a referee, had the sanction of' the committee, and was out on behalf of the club in search of players.

div.head: LANCASHIRE JUNIOR CUP. Fourth Round. _
div.p: LANCASHIRE JUNIOR CUP. Fourth Round. _
Rylands' Recs.. Beat Ditton Recs.

Rylands' were short of A. Horrocks and Floyd. Stretford kicked off. With the wind in their favour, Rylands' were soon bombarding the Bit- ton line, but. the defence was sound, the home players making no mistake in 'their tackling. F. liorrocks, Morris and Carter were pulled up close in. O'Garra mulling the ball hi the Ditton quarters, a scrummage was formed, and from the pack the ball travelled among all the backs of the " Wiremen," and Carter scored far out. Potter failed at goal. Half-time arrived with the score: Rylands', one try (three points); Ditton, nil. With the wind in their favour the home team started pressing, but the defence of the " Wire- men " was perfect, and flinging the ball about the backs, t.:3tretford scored dat the corner. The goal kick failed. Blond dropped a fine goal for the home team. Rylands' replied with a try by Potter.- The same player failed at goal, and the game ended: Rylands', three tries (nine points) ; Ditton Recs., one goal (two points).

div.head: Rylands' Recs. "A" Beaten.
div.p: Rylands' Recs. "A" Beaten.

Warrington White Rose _ defeated Rylands' "A" in the second round of the Bardsley Cup, at Gorsey-lane. In the first half Scarisbrick scored a good try for the home- team, Barton failing at goal. On resuming Gregson scored for the visitors. Barlow missed the goal kick. Near the close Barlow kicked a goal for the Rose from a free kick, and placed his side in a winning position. Final: Warrington White Rose, five points; Rylands', three points.

St. Helens and District' League. Rylands' Recs. "A" play Westfield at St. Ifelens with: Potter; Scarisbrielr, Barton, Mor- ris and Cooper; Mannion and Warren ;.Welsby, Peers, Adamson, Myles, Weldon and Bibby.

div.head: PICKS OUT OF THE SCRUM.
div.p: PICKS OUT OF THE SCRUM.
Pithy Pars About N.U. Games.

" Jolly ' at full-back, and quite " Young' in the half-back division, "And rather Cox '-ing forward, "Warrington ought to do very well." In this way our pet punster Sums up the Warrington team. There is some point in his puns. To perpetrate the pun still further, It is quite "Clare" there is improvement, Let it be kept up, ye Warringtonians. A similar victory at Salford to-day Is just what is required—Do it!

© Ruddick proved ,great at threequarter. Surely now there will be a general Opinion that he has found his right pot. Would he have been there if " The Examiner" Had not kept saying that Ruddick Was just the man for wing threequarter? "The Examiner's" judgment has proved correct. • Ruddick simply revelled in his new place. As attacker and defender he was great. It is rare that one man can upset two Opponents at once and get the ball. Ruddick performed that feat on Stacey and Lewis.

e 0.0 'What has gone wrong with Bradshaiv? When he gets the ball he mulls it. He is not playing the game he did, And seems to have lost his fine speed. Is Bradshaw over-trained? It looks like it. A week or two's rest might do good, - And bring the genial captain back to form. Two faster centre-threequarters are wanted. Neither Dickenson nor Davis can keep Up with Ruddick when he starts, consequently The "little 'un" is not supported as he Deserves to be when he gets on the run. •

e e ee e Jelley dropped the finest goal that possibly He has notched in his clever career. It was truly a brilliant dropped goal. - He did not bring off the, second Penalty kick given because of obstruction. No one was the least sorry about it. The cltib's supporters want to see games. Won by other means than penalty goals. Nicholas and YOung worked well together. The new player is not quite up to The Northern Union game as yet, but He will improve, -without a doubt.

CCOCC Young lies a bit too far back In the position of "stand off," but this Is a relic of his Welsh R.U. days, And he will amend it as time goes on. Young was very active and as a most Willing worker all through Saturday's garde. One of his pieces of work was remarkable. He caught the ball, dropped it for a tackle, Wriggled out from below two Leeds men, Re-caught the.sphere and made off finely. Such a curious and clever bit of work Is rarely seen in a Northern Union game. CCC C C C Leeds were a weighty crowd. • They used their weight to some purpose. In Thomas and Chesters the heavy-weights Found more, than they bargained for. The two Warrington "strong men" seemed To enjoy themselves in the melees. Clare was a shilling light in the match. His speed was a most valuable asset. He dodged cleverly, and it was hard on The Thelwall lad that he did not score. If he keeps up-Saturday's form he Will yet get some good tries. .

Skelhorne and Tranter were very useful. , They often came into the picture on Saturday. Has Tranter been taking lessons In the Association code style of dribbling? His footwork was particularly good, And the way he dribbled was clever. Skelhorne used his speed to advantage. Dickenson played strong on the defensive. Ah,, if he just had Some of his old speed! Davis was a hard-working defender. There was a great improvement in the team. Keep it up bhoys—the .2100 is still on offer.
